descs.en: When a brilliant girl from nowhere drowns at a rich family’s boathouse, nobody comes for her. Fourteen months later, the family starts dying in the order they hurt her.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
A brilliant girl from nowhere drowns at the Whitmore boathouse, and nobody comes to claim her.

Fourteen months later, Ryla Whitmore is still in her wheelchair, still silent, still smiling for the Foundation’s cameras while her family counts the days to her twenty-fifth birthday. Then the Whitmores start dying, one by one, and the quiet auditor from London is the only person in the house who waits for her to finish a sentence.

He knows her language. He knows what happened at the boathouse. And he has a list.

Dark romance · revenge · captor and captive · a mute heroine · a hero who kills · Complete: prologue, 26 chapters and an epilogue.

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
I wanted to write a love story where nobody gets to be good, and where the ending is happy only in the way the characters choose to call it happy. This is that book.

It is dark, the violence is on the page, and the love scenes are 21+. Please read the content warning first.

How to read the dialogue: spoken words are in “bold quotation marks”. Signed words (ASL) are in bold italics, without quotation marks. Words typed on Ryla’s tablet are in a typewriter face. Thoughts and mouthed words are in italics.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers.

This is a dark romance with an unhappy ending.

• Murder and violence on the page

• Kidnapping and psychological torture

• Drugging, poisoning and withdrawal

• Suicide (staged)

• Coercion and restraint by the love interest

• Sexual content between adults

• Captivity

• Grief, disability and medical abuse

chapters.title: Hands Above Water
chapters.desc: Fourteen months earlier, a young woman answers a message from someone she loves and walks down to the boathouse.
chapters.epigraph: “Come to the boathouse. I want to talk. Just us.”
chapters.content:
The first thing she noticed, on a late-August night fourteen months before any of it, was that the stars were moving, just enough to make her wonder whether the sky had tilted or she had.

She stood at the edge of the garden path with one hand on the stone railing and waited for the world to settle. It didn’t.

The August night was warm and heavy, and the air smelled of wet grass and lake water. Somewhere behind the house, a piano drifted through an open window. Her phone buzzed against her hip.

Come to the boathouse. I want to talk. Just us.

She read it three times, smiling through the strange heaviness gathering behind her eyes. It was from him.

He had barely spoken to her at dinner. When she’d tried to catch his eye, he had given her a distracted smile and turned back to the people around him, and she had spent dessert wondering what she’d done wrong.

Maybe this was his way of making up for it. Are you still there?

The screen blurred while she typed it. She blinked hard, and the letters slid back into place. She laughed at herself, put the phone away and started walking.

She knew the path well: where the gravel gave way to stone, where the garden lights had stopped working, where the old oak threw its shadow across the steps.

Tonight it seemed twice as long. Her legs felt loose, and her thoughts kept arriving a little after they should have.

She remembered the drink at dinner. Someone had brought it to her and said she looked tired, and she had finished it because she didn’t want to be rude. It had tasted too sweet. After that, things were hard to put in order.

By the time she reached the boathouse, she was breathing through her mouth. The door was already open.

“Hello?”

Her voice came out smaller than she meant it to. Nobody answered, so she stepped inside.

It was dark except for a strip of moonlight from the open side facing the water. Beyond it the lake lay flat and still, holding the lights of the estate.

Someone was standing by the far wall. Then she saw another, and another. Five of them.

Her mind tried to give the shapes faces and couldn’t. One had his hands in his pockets. One leaned on a post. A phone screen lit up, and a small red light appeared beside it. Recording.

“What’s this?”

Her voice shook. One of them laughed, almost fondly, as if she’d said something funny at a dinner party.

She searched the shadows for the one who had sent the message.

“Where is he?”

A figure moved. “You’re late.”

She knew the voice, and the relief nearly made her cry. “It’s you.”

She took a step forward.

“What’s going on? I thought you wanted to talk.”

Nobody answered. She tried to focus on him, but his face kept sliding out of shape every time she blinked.

“Are you feeling all right?” someone asked.

She nodded, then shook her head.

“I don’t know. I think someone gave me something.”

Someone laughed again. “Listen to her.”

“Please. I don’t feel very well.”

The red light came closer. She lifted a hand to shield her eyes.

“Stop filming.”

“Why?”

“Because I said so.”

It came out sharper than she intended, and for a second she was almost herself again. She straightened her back.

“I’m leaving.”

She turned. A hand closed on her arm, not hard enough to hurt, just hard enough to stop her.

“Don’t be difficult.”

She looked at the fingers around her wrist, then up at his face.

“Let go.”

“You’re making a scene.”

“I said let go.”

Someone sighed. A low, impatient voice from the dark said, “She’s unstable.”

The word sat in the room. She turned towards whoever had said it. She knew that voice too, but the memory wouldn’t come fast enough.

“Please, I just want to go home,” she whispered.

Nobody moved towards the door. The hand on her arm tightened, and then the floor wasn’t there.

Her shoulder hit a wooden edge. She heard shoes scrape, felt a shove and a rush of cold air, and then she was outside, with the water under her.

For one suspended second she saw the sky. Then the lake closed over her head.

The cold came first, before the fear. It was so complete that her mind cleared, and she opened her eyes on a smear of moonlight and black.

She tried to breathe and got a mouthful of water. Her body moved before her thoughts did: she kicked and reached, and her fingers found the underside of the dock. She caught it and pulled.

A shadow leaned over the edge, then a hand. She thought someone was helping her, and she grabbed it with everything she had.

The hand turned on her wrist and pushed her head back under.

She fought. Water churned around her face, and her feet struck the posts below the dock. She twisted, but the grip didn’t give. She opened her mouth and only bubbles came out.

Above her, the surface broke into trembling pieces of light, and somewhere up there a voice was laughing, or telling the others to be quiet.

Her chest began to burn. She clawed at the wrist holding her down and felt skin tear under her nails. The hand stayed where it was.

She thought of the message, and how stupid she’d been to smile at it.

Then, out of nowhere, she thought of something much smaller.

A kitchen in winter with the electricity cut off again. A little girl at the table, trying to make her fingers hold a shape, and a boy beside her folding them into place one at a time. Thumb. Index finger. Little finger.

Like this.

She had laughed when she finally got it, and promised him she would never forget.

Her right hand moved. The fingers were clumsy with cold, but the middle two folded down, and the thumb, the index finger and the little finger came up. I love you.

For one second her hand broke the surface, and the moonlight caught it.

Then the grip tightened, the hand went under, and the lake was still.

✦ ✦ ✦

Most of the house was dark by then. On the second floor one window was still lit, and behind it a young woman in a wheelchair was awake.

She had taken the noises outside for guests leaving the garden party until she heard the splash. The evening medicine had left her hands heavy, as it always did, and she had been watching the lights on the water because it was easier than trying to read.

From her window she could see part of the boathouse and a strip of water beyond it. Five figures stood on the dock, and one of them was holding up a phone.

Her hands lay in her lap. She could hear laughter but not words, and the figures kept shifting against the lights on the far shore. Something moved in the water. An arm, and at the end of it a hand, held up for a moment in a shape she couldn’t make out at that distance.

She leaned forward. Her fingers twitched against the blanket over her knees, and she tried to lift her hand. It barely moved.

The figures began to drift apart. One walked back towards the garden. Another stood looking down at the water, then followed.

She waited for someone to come out of the lake. Nobody did. A minute passed, then another.

Her tablet was on the table across the room. It might as well have been across the lake. She tried for it anyway, and her fingers slid off the armrest, and the effort left her breathing hard.

When she turned back to the window, there was only the boathouse, the water and the moon on it.

In her lap, her right hand tried for the only sign that came to her: two fingers against the chest. A young woman had made it for her at dinner in the spring, kneeling beside her chair while she fought for breath, and afterwards told her she had beautiful hands. Her fingers wouldn’t close into it.

She didn’t know why she was remembering it now. She only knew that someone out there had been asking for help, and she had sat at the window and watched.

✦ ✦ ✦

By morning the water was calm. The guests came down to coffee and the ordinary small complaints of a summer weekend. Someone asked where the girl had gone, and someone else said she’d left early. The story was ready before anyone thought to ask questions.

Nobody asked the girl at the window. By the time her hands would hold the tablet again it was afternoon, and she had half decided it was a dream. In that house it was easier to believe a dream than to type a word nobody wanted to read.

Fourteen months later, when the first of them began to die, none of the people who had stood on that dock remembered the small hand that had broken the surface. Someone else did.

chapters.title: The Poster Child
chapters.desc: The Whitmore Foundation gala, its brave poster child, and a stranger from London who watches her hands instead of her chair.
chapters.content:
By the night of the Whitmore Foundation Gala, on the seventeenth of October, Ryla Whitmore had learned three things about charity galas.

People got far more generous when there were cameras nearby. Nobody wanted to hear about spinal injuries; they wanted miracles, ideally with a photograph, a donation and a woman in a wheelchair smiling beside them.

And if one more person called her brave, she was going to start charging for it.

Unfortunately, the Whitmore Foundation had decided long ago that her face was worth more than her opinions.

“Smile, darling.”

Ryla smiled. A camera flashed.

“Beautiful. One more. Just a little brighter, sweetheart.”

Would you like me to set myself on fire?

Her smile didn’t move. Across the ballroom, a string quartet played something expensive and forgettable. Crystal chandeliers hung from the high ceiling, scattering warm light over polished marble and tables dressed in white linen.

The gala was held at the Whitmore estate every October: politicians, hospital directors, investors, physicians, and people whose money was so old they no longer mentioned it. Ryla knew most of the faces.

She knew which women would kiss her cheek without touching it, which men would crouch and use the voice people keep for children and nervous horses, and which donors would ask about her rehabilitation and check their watches during the answer.

“Mrs. Whitmore, over here!”

Victoria turned towards the photographer, her hand resting lightly on Ryla’s shoulder.

“Of course.”

Her stepmother’s smile was flawless. So was Ryla’s.

“Ryla, darling, look at the camera.”

“Such a lovely girl. You must be very proud,” the photographer said.

Victoria’s fingers pressed against her shoulder.

“More than you can imagine.”

The photographer took another. Ryla could already see the caption in the annual report: Ryla Whitmore: A Story of Courage, Hope and Resilience. Hope was what people said when they didn’t want to talk about money, or about things that couldn’t be fixed.

“Darling, are you tired?”

Ryla shook her head.

“You’ve been sitting for quite some time.”

They had been there less than an hour.

“Then perhaps we should take a little break.”

Victoria was already turning towards the next table.

“Mrs. Whitmore!”

A woman in a silver dress approached them, accompanied by a man Ryla vaguely recognised from the foundation’s board.

“Ryla, sweetheart!”

The woman bent and kissed her cheek. Her perfume arrived first.

“Oh, look at you. You look absolutely wonderful. Such a beautiful dress.”

Ryla mouthed thank you, which was the one thing everyone in the room could read.

“And how are you feeling?”

Ryla gave her the same answer she had given the last eleven people: a nod, and a smile that said very well without making anyone wait for it.

“That’s wonderful. You’re such an inspiration. I always tell my daughter about you. Such courage.” The woman pressed a hand to her chest.

“Ryla has always been remarkably positive.”

“That must be so important. Having such a positive attitude.”

Yes. Especially around people who mistake good manners for happiness.

Ryla nodded as if she agreed. That conversation ended and another began. By the time Victoria wheeled her into the dining room, she had been kissed on both cheeks, complimented on her dress six times, and called an inspiration by a man who spoke mostly to her wheelchair.

If she died tonight, she suspected the foundation would turn it into a campaign.

“You’re doing beautifully.”

Victoria said it low enough that only Ryla could hear. When Ryla raised an eyebrow, she adjusted her shawl. “Of course you are. Just a few more photographs. Damien will be speaking soon.”

How lucky for me.

Ryla nodded. Nodding took almost no energy and let people believe they’d been understood.

✦ ✦ ✦

Damien Whitmore took the stage a little after eight, and the applause started before he reached the microphone.

He wore a black tuxedo with a white pocket square and the easy confidence of a man who had never wondered whether the world would make room for him.

Her half-brother could look sincere on command. He could make a room believe he was listening while he worked out what the conversation might cost him. He could make an apology sound like a gift, and a lie sound like something he had personally suffered.

“Good evening, everyone.”

His voice carried easily through the ballroom.

“Thank you for joining us tonight. Your presence means a great deal to the Whitmore Foundation, and, more importantly, to the families whose lives have been changed by the work we do.”

Polite applause. Damien waited for it. He was good at that.

“Four years ago, when we first expanded our spinal injury research programme, we made a promise. We promised that a diagnosis would never be the end of someone’s story.”

Her photograph appeared on the screen behind him, two years old, from a bad morning when Mrs. Pell had needed twenty minutes just to get her dressed.

The photographer had asked her to look towards the window, and she had been watching a bird. It ended up in three brochures. Damien continued.

“We promised that research would continue, that families would receive support, and that those living with spinal injuries would never be defined by what they had lost.”

His gaze found her. “And perhaps nobody represents that promise more beautifully than my little sister. Our brave little Ryla.”

The room turned to look at her. A few people seemed genuinely moved, and someone behind her whispered how lovely it was.

“She has taught our family more about courage than she will ever know. Every day, she reminds us that the human spirit is stronger than circumstance.”

You could at least have used a newer photo.

“She reminds us that hope is not simply something we talk about. It is something we choose, every morning.”

Damien laid a hand on his chest. “And that is why we continue.”

He spoke for another six minutes about research, partnerships and next year’s plans, and the room clapped in the right places.

“Little sister.”

He kissed the top of her head while the cameras flashed. “How are you doing? Enjoying yourself?”

She mouthed fine and gave him a small, radiant nod, and his smile widened.

He turned to the nearest photographer. “Get one of us.”

He put an arm around her shoulders, and she tilted her head towards him for two flashes.

“Perfect. You’re making me look good.” He glanced down.

She smiled and signed, That must be exhausting for me.

He didn’t understand a word of it. He never had. He laughed anyway, because the cameras were still there.

“Still got your sense of humour.”

He patted her shoulder. “That’s my girl.”

He was already turning away. Ryla curled her fingers once in her lap and let them go. She had stopped wasting words on people who were determined not to understand them.

✦ ✦ ✦

Arabella Langford arrived at their table shortly after the speech.

She wore a champagne gown, blonde hair in loose waves that had taken someone an hour to make look careless, and diamonds at her collarbone. She had the sort of beauty that photographed well. Ryla had once thought that was a compliment.

“Darling.”

Arabella kissed her cheek. “You look lovely tonight.”

Ryla mouthed thank you.

Arabella stepped back, and her eyes went to Ryla’s hair. “Oh. Nothing. It’s just your hair.”

Before Ryla could respond, Arabella reached forward and adjusted a loose strand near her temple.

“There. Much better.”

Ryla went still.

Arabella tilted her head at her work. “The photographer kept getting a shadow earlier.”

She smoothed the hair behind Ryla’s ear.

Of course they do.

The photographer was still hovering, and Arabella saw him. “One more, darling?”

Ryla smiled and nodded.

Arabella set one hand on Ryla’s shoulder and found her angle. Flash. She checked the screen, said “Perfect,” kissed Ryla’s cheek again and called her a sweetheart.

Ryla watched her go back to Damien. They looked beautiful together; they always did. She wondered whether Arabella knew what he was like when nobody was watching, and then whether it would make any difference.

✦ ✦ ✦

The man from London arrived late, through the east doors, with someone from the bank’s board. Ryla noticed him because he didn’t behave like a guest. Dark suit, forgettable tie, a face that gave nothing away.

He was of no particular height, but people moved around him without noticing they were doing it. Dark hair, a lean face, a mouth that looked serious at rest. Early thirties, maybe.

Ryla had no idea who he was, and that was unusual. Even people with no business at the gala usually came in on someone’s invitation. This one hadn’t come to be entertained. He was introduced to Victoria first.

“Mrs. Whitmore, may I introduce Keaton Vance? He’s joining us from London. The bank has asked him to oversee the independent review of the group’s accounts.”

Victoria’s smile didn’t falter. “How lovely. Welcome to Wrenhaven.”

“Thank you.” His voice was calm.

Damien appeared beside them. “Mr. Vance. I hope the flight wasn’t too unpleasant.”

“It was fine.”

“Come. Let me introduce you to a few people.”

Ryla filed the name away. Another banker who would spend the evening admiring the family’s generosity before asking to see its books. Nothing interesting.

Mrs. Pell was standing just behind her wheelchair. She had been with the Whitmores for nearly six years: fifties, kind eyes, a habit of worrying about things she couldn’t control.

At the moment she was watching Victoria, who was smiling at a woman from the hospital board with the careful restraint of someone who had paid a great deal to keep her forehead still. Ryla’s fingers moved low above her lap.

If she smiles any harder, something will come loose.

Mrs. Pell’s lips twitched, and she dropped her eyes.

Maybe we should ask the surgeon for a refund.

Mrs. Pell pressed her lips together, and her shoulders shook once. Ryla smiled. It was a small win, but the evening hadn’t offered many.

She was about to add something when she realised Keaton Vance was standing near the table, and he was looking at her hands, not her face.

She stopped. He probably thought it was a nervous habit. Then his eyes came up to hers, flicked to Mrs. Pell, and something moved at the corner of his mouth. It wasn’t quite a smile. Ryla narrowed her eyes. Keaton inclined his head politely.

“Miss Whitmore.”

She gave him a smile and inclined her head in return. His gaze returned to her hands.

“Enjoying the evening?”

She could have told him she’d been photographed so often she now flinched at bright lights, or that her brother had just turned her into a lesson on courage without asking. Instead she mouthed the one word everyone could read. Lovely.

“Good.”

He paused.

“Your family has put considerable effort into tonight.”

Ryla let one eyebrow ask the question.

“That’s what I understand.”

She glanced at Victoria, then back at him.

“I imagine they’ll be rewarded for it.”

There was no mockery in it, and no sympathy either. He sounded like a man answering a question she hadn’t quite asked.

Before she could think of something else to say, Victoria appeared beside them.

“Mr. Vance. I hope you’re settling in.”

“Very much, thank you.”

“Ryla, darling, have you met Mr. Vance?”

Ryla nodded.

“Wonderful. Mr. Vance is here to help us with some of the group’s financial arrangements.” Victoria put a hand on the wheelchair.

Ryla turned her head towards Mrs. Pell and signed, How fascinating.

“Very,” Keaton said to Victoria.

For half a second, Ryla thought the word had landed a little too neatly after her hands. Then she decided it hadn’t.

Victoria laughed politely. “Well, we won’t keep you.”

As she was wheeled away, Ryla looked back once. Keaton was already listening to the man from the bank, his face as still as before.

Maybe he was just one of those people who noticed details. It didn’t matter. He couldn’t have understood her. Hardly anyone could, and fewer bothered to learn.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before nine, Mrs. Pell wheeled her towards the quiet side of the house.

The second round of speeches had started, and Ryla was tired in the way she had been tired for months: a heaviness that came and went without warning and sometimes left her unable to lift her arms at all.

The doctors called it part of her condition. The family called it fatigue. Mrs. Pell called it bedtime.

“Shall we go upstairs, sweetheart?”

Ryla nodded. The ballroom noise faded behind them in the side corridor.

“That was a nice speech from Damien. He spoke beautifully,” Mrs. Pell said.

Ryla raised an eyebrow.

Mrs. Pell laughed. “All right. Perhaps a little too beautifully.”

In the lift, Mrs. Pell set the brakes and looked at her. “You’re tired, aren’t you? Your hands have been slower tonight.”

Ryla hadn’t noticed, or hadn’t wanted to. Mrs. Pell squeezed her shoulder. “We’ll get you settled.”

The doors closed. The lights overhead seemed too bright, and the lift tilted once and steadied. Ryla shut her eyes.

Dr. Albright arrived at nine with a small glass bottle on a tray.

“Good evening, Miss Whitmore.”

She had been sitting by the window watching the garden lights. Mrs. Pell straightened by the wardrobe. “Doctor.”

Albright smiled. She had known him for years: silver hair, thin expensive glasses. He had treated her after the fall and visited through her rehabilitation.

He had explained that recovery would take time, and later, gently, that she should learn to accept her limitations. She had never liked the word. It always seemed to arrive when she asked too many questions.

“How are we feeling tonight?”

Ryla gave him a small nod. He set the tray on the bedside table.

“Excellent. I’ve brought your evening tonic.”

Mrs. Pell approached.

“She was quite tired downstairs.”

“That’s to be expected after an evening like this.”

He lifted the bottle. “Let’s keep the routine consistent.”

He poured the pale yellow tonic into a small glass. Same colour as always. Nine o’clock, the tonic, then the lamp turned low, Mrs. Pell helping her into bed, and the heaviness. She held out her hand. Albright placed the glass against her fingers.

“Slowly.”

It tasted bitter under the sweetness. Albright watched her swallow and took the glass back. “Good. That should help you sleep.”

Will I be less tired tomorrow?

“Hopefully.”

When she kept waiting, he smiled.

“You’re making progress, Ryla. These things take patience.”

She looked down at her lap. People always offered her patience. It was cheaper than answers.

Mrs. Pell tucked the blanket over her knees and asked if she wanted the window closed. Ryla shook her head. Albright collected his tray, promised to see her tomorrow and left, and Mrs. Pell stayed a little longer, checking the medication sheet and plumping pillows.

Ryla tried to lift her right hand. It moved, but slowly. The familiar weight was spreading down her arms, denser than weakness. Her fingers settled on the blanket and answered the next time only after a delay.

Mrs. Pell noticed. “Getting sleepy? Good. You need your rest.”

She kissed Ryla’s forehead and said goodnight, and the door shut behind her.

It took Ryla several minutes to realise she was still awake. The heaviness had settled into her shoulders. Her arms felt far away, and her legs, as usual, were almost beyond her.

She tried to shift her left hand. Nothing. She waited and tried again, and it moved a little. Enough. She let out a breath.

The lamp and the garden lights were all that was left. Beyond the glass, the grounds ran down into darkness. The last guests were leaving, their headlights sliding between the trees on the gravel drive, and farther off the boathouse sat black against the lake.

She had never liked that view. Maybe it was the water. Maybe she had spent too many nights looking at it without knowing why.

A memory stirred: a young woman with a warm voice, hands moving in front of her.

Your hands are beautiful. Take your time. She couldn’t remember the woman’s name. Only that she had been kind, and had spoken to Ryla before she looked at the chair, and had signed slowly.

Ryla tried to make the sign herself. Her fingers barely moved, and the effort tired her.

She stared at the boathouse a moment longer, then looked away, the way she always did.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, alone in the east study, Keaton Vance had his jacket over a chair and a folder open on the desk: preliminary statements, audit letters, a list of questions. He had read all of it before dinner and found three discrepancies. One mattered. The other two were interesting.

Tucked among the supplementary papers was a group photograph from earlier that evening. Victoria in the centre, Damien beside her, Arabella smiling at the lens, and Ryla.

He studied it for several seconds. Not her face; her hands. He remembered how her fingers had moved at the table.

That had been ASL, and the girl had been making a joke, a cruel one, in a room full of people careful never to say what they meant. He had nearly smiled.

He closed the folder, then opened it again. Someone had clipped a short biographical note under the foundation overview.

RYLA WHITMORE

Age: 24.

Position: Beneficiary and public ambassador of the Whitmore Foundation.

Medical status: Spinal injury following a fall; limited mobility; non-verbal.

Keaton read the last line twice before he turned the page.

chapters.title: The Slip
chapters.desc: A groundskeeper finds Preston Whitmore in the boathouse slip. By noon, a dead man has posted a confession.
chapters.content:
Preston Whitmore’s mother was the first to notice he was missing. A groundskeeper was the first to find him, a little after seven on Sunday morning, and by the time the household understood what had happened, the police were already on the drive.

Last night’s decorations were still up. Champagne glasses stood abandoned on the terrace, the caterers were due at nine, and the gardeners had been told to start with the east lawn. Nobody had expected a body.

“Mr. Whitmore?”

The groundskeeper had been calling from the edge of the boathouse slip for several minutes. At first he thought someone had dropped a jacket in the water.

Then he saw the shoulders under it, and when the current turned the face a little towards him, he forgot to breathe.

“Jesus Christ.”

Preston Whitmore was floating face down beside the platform, his wrists tied behind his back with his own silk tie. His shoes were gone.

One sleeve was torn, and the water had turned his pale blue shirt almost grey. He hadn’t been dumped there. He had been arranged, by someone who had taken the time to make sure he would be found.

The groundskeeper stumbled back and dialled emergency services, and his voice shook so badly the operator made him repeat the address twice.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ryla woke to footsteps she didn’t know. Not Mrs. Pell, and not the breakfast trolley: heavier, hurrying. Down the corridor a door opened, and men’s voices passed it. Mrs. Pell came in a few seconds later.

“Good morning, sweetheart.”

She was dressed, but her hair was coming loose, as if she’d been interrupted halfway through something. Ryla raised her eyebrows.

Mrs. Pell hesitated. “There’s been an incident. At the boathouse.”

Her fingers moved against the blanket. What happened?

Mrs. Pell seemed to wish she hadn’t seen the question. “One of the groundskeepers found something this morning.”

Ryla’s eyes went to the window, then back. Something?

Mrs. Pell took a breath. “Preston.”

Ryla stared at her and didn’t move. Then her fingers shifted. Preston? Mrs. Pell nodded.

“I’m afraid so.”

Everyone knew Preston. Marcus’s son, Damien’s cousin, twenty-eight, permanently delighted by his own jokes and sure the world was a private club with his name on the list.

He talked to her like a slow child, and he liked photographing things people would he didn’t. Last night he had been at the bar, laughing at something with his phone held up. She couldn’t remember what. Her fingers moved again. Is he hurt?

Mrs. Pell’s face crumpled. “Oh, sweetheart. Preston is dead.” She came and put a hand on Ryla’s shoulder.

Ryla looked at the window and tried to picture the boathouse in daylight: the wooden slip, the water, the place where they’d found him. Her fingers stayed still.

Mrs. Pell brushed the hair off her forehead. “You don’t need to worry about any of this. The police are handling it.”

Ryla wanted to ask how anyone died in a house full of people who spent their lives watching each other. Whether he’d been alone. Why Mrs. Pell looked frightened. She lowered her eyes instead, and Mrs. Pell took it as the end of the conversation.

“Let’s get you washed and dressed, shall we?”

Ryla nodded.

✦ ✦ ✦

By nine the estate was a different place. The staff had been told to stay inside, police tape closed off the east lawn, two officers stood at the front door, and a police car was parked by the fountain.

Ryla watched from her window while Mrs. Pell helped her with breakfast: someone pointing at the boathouse, someone talking into a radio.

Nobody from the family came upstairs, not Damien, not Victoria, not even Arabella. Ryla supposed they had more important things to attend to. The dead, for instance. Her toast went cold.

Victoria came up mid-morning in a cream blouse and tailored trousers, her make-up camera-ready. She looked tired, but she never looked untidy.

“Ryla, darling.”

She came in without knocking, thanked Mrs. Pell, and waited until the door had closed behind her before she crossed to the wheelchair.

“How are you feeling?”

Ryla reached for her tablet. Victoria had never learned a single sign, and in five years had never once pretended to want to. The sentence took most of a minute. Mrs. Pell told me about Preston.

“Yes. It is a terrible tragedy.” Victoria straightened the blanket over Ryla’s knees.

Her face was exactly as sombre as it needed to be. Grief, like everything else in this house, had to be presented properly.

“Your uncle Marcus is devastated, of course.”

Ryla typed again. Has he seen him?

“Of course. He’s downstairs with the police.”

Victoria touched her cheek.

“Don’t trouble yourself with this, darling. The police will take care of everything.”

What happened?

Victoria’s fingers paused. “We don’t know yet.” When Ryla went on waiting, she added evenly that apparently he’d been found in the water, and that it must have been some sort of accident.

Ryla glanced towards the window. An accident?

Victoria smiled. “We should let the authorities determine that. I’ve asked the kitchen to make something special for lunch. Try to eat properly today. Be a good girl.” She stood. She bent and kissed Ryla’s forehead.

After she’d gone, Ryla stared at the door. The phrase itself didn’t bother her; Victoria said it every day. What bothered her was that she’d said it the same way this morning.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before noon the family gathered in the study, and nobody invited Ryla. She hadn’t expected them to. It was Edward Whitmore’s old room: his desk, locked cabinets, shelves of books nobody read, and the family safe.

Whenever someone opened the door, voices carried down the corridor. Ryla recognised Detective Calder’s, low and firm. She had heard it once before, years ago, when the police came after her father died.

Calder wanted Preston’s movements last night. Who had seen him, when he’d left the ballroom, how much he’d drunk, whether anyone had argued with him, where his phone was.

Mrs. Pell was helping her into a cardigan when the door opened again, and a man’s voice said, “We have reason to believe this was deliberate.”

Ryla went still. Mrs. Pell lowered her voice and said they should get her comfortable, but Ryla was listening.

“We’re treating this as a targeted killing,” the detective went on.

A silence, then Damien. “Targeted?” From him it sounded less like a question than an accusation.

“That’s what the evidence suggests, Mr. Whitmore.”

A chair scraped. “Surely, you’re not suggesting someone came onto our property specifically to murder my nephew,” Victoria said.

“We’re not ruling anything out.”

“This is a private estate.”

“I understand that.”

“With security.”

“Yes, ma’am.”

“Which is why we’d like to see the security footage.”

The door shut, and Mrs. Pell went back to the cardigan buttons. Ryla could feel something shifting. The family had always controlled what happened inside this house. Now someone from outside was asking questions they didn’t want to answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little after noon, Preston Whitmore posted a video.

It went up on his private account and spread from there. A journalist watching the police cars at the gates saw it first, then someone in the foundation’s press office, then Damien.

It was under a minute long. Preston sat in a dark room, pale, his hair wet, wearing last night’s shirt, his eyes unable to settle on the lens. No introduction, no date, no place. For several seconds he only stared. Then he spoke.

“We only meant to scare her.”

His eyes slid to something outside the frame. “It wasn’t supposed to— We didn’t think she’d actually...”

The video jumped. When it came back, he was crying.

“It was Marcus’s idea to burn it.”

“I didn’t know what was in the other one. I swear. I deleted the real one. I deleted it.” His voice cracked. He looked straight into the camera.

That was all. No name, no clue who her was, nothing about what had been burned. But it was Preston’s account and Preston’s phone, and within twenty minutes it had been downloaded and reposted everywhere. Nobody could call this an accident now.

Damien was watching it for the fourth time when Victoria came into the study.

“Turn that off.”

He didn’t look up. “Have you seen it? Then you know what this means.”

She shut the door. “I know exactly what it means.”

He paused it. Preston froze with his mouth slightly open, staring past the camera, and Damien looked away.

“Who has it?”

“Everyone, apparently.”

“Can it be removed?”

Victoria gave him a look.

“I’m asking whether it can be removed.”

“The communications team is trying.”

“Trying?”

He stood up. “Mother, it’s on every news site.”

Victoria walked towards the desk.

“Then we make a statement.”

“A statement?”

“That the video is unverified. That Preston was clearly distressed. That the family is cooperating fully with the police.”

Damien stared at her. “He’s dead. He was found in the water. So how the hell did he upload a video?”

“Lower your voice.”

Damien laughed once, and it wasn’t a nice sound.

“Someone killed him, Mother.”

“Yes.”

“And they sent us that.”

Victoria studied the frozen screen. Then she said, low, “What did Preston mean by the real one?”

Damien looked at her.

“I don’t know.”

“Don’t lie to me.”

“I’m not.”

She stepped closer. “He said he deleted the real one.”

Damien rubbed his forehead. “Maybe he meant something else. How am I supposed to know?”

“Was there something?”

He took too long to answer, and that was answer enough. Her eyes narrowed. “Damien.”

Damien turned away. “Not here.”

He glanced at the door. Victoria followed his eyes, and after a moment she nodded.

✦ ✦ ✦

By half past one, Marcus Whitmore had stopped talking. He sat in the study with his hands on his knees and his face grey. The police had finished their first interview and left him alone, and he hadn’t moved since.

Victoria stood by the fireplace. Damien paced. Arabella had arrived before noon and sat on the sofa with her phone. Nobody cried. Nobody talked about Preston as a boy, or wondered what his last minutes had been like. They watched the video, again and again.

“Turn it off,” Marcus said.

“It’s already been copied,” Damien said.

“I said turn it off.”

Damien shut the laptop.

Marcus rubbed his face. “Who has the original?”

“Preston’s phone is with the police.”

“Not the phone. The video.”

“Everyone has it, Uncle Marcus.”

Marcus shut his eyes, and for the first time his composure gave. He leaned forward with his elbows on his knees. “Jesus Christ.”

“What did he mean?” Victoria asked.

He didn’t answer.

“Burn it. What was he talking about?”

Marcus’s jaw tightened.

“Old documents.”

“What documents?”

“Things from the university.”

Damien turned. “Which things?”

“Not now. Do you want the police to hear this?”

That shut him up.

Arabella lowered her phone. “Perhaps we should all calm down. I mean, the police will find whoever did this.”

Nobody looked at her. Marcus let out a breath that wasn’t a laugh. “Yes. Of course. I need to make a call.” He stood.

When the door had closed behind him, Victoria turned on her son. “What university documents?”

He didn’t answer.

“Damien.”

“Old research.”

“Whose?”

A pause. “Elena’s.”

The temperature in the room seemed to drop. Arabella looked up. Victoria didn’t move at all, and when she finally spoke, it was only to say, “Not in front of anyone, darling.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Ryla was in the sitting room by the upper landing, where she wasn’t supposed to be. Mrs. Pell had gone for a fresh blanket, the door below stood half open, and she hadn’t meant to listen. But she had heard a name. Not hers. One she didn’t know. Elena.

Damien came out first and didn’t see her. The dinner-party smile was gone; his shoulders were tight and his jaw clenched, and he was carrying a stack of old notebooks.

He stopped at the fireplace in the drawing room and stood staring at them. The fire was already lit. He took the first one, thick, dark blue, worn at the corners, and his hand shook.

Ryla noticed because Damien’s hands didn’t shake. He opened it, read something on the first page, shut it, and held it over the flames for several seconds before he let it drop.

Ryla caught the letters on the cover just before the fire curled over them.

E.W.

There were at least six more notebooks in the pile.

Damien picked up another. He glanced at the door, at the notebook, at the fire. Why was he burning them? Ryla’s fingers moved slowly on the armrest. What are you doing? He didn’t see.

The second notebook went in. A corner of the cover curled, and the smell of burning ink drifted up the stairs. She knew those initials, or knew she had seen them somewhere, but nothing came.

Victoria appeared behind him. “Darling.”

He spun round. She looked at the fire, then at the notebooks. Her voice was quiet and not at all angry, which was worse. “Not here.”

“I know.”

“Then be careful.”

He glanced up at the staircase, and for one terrible second Ryla thought he had seen her. His eyes passed over the landing. He picked up another notebook. Victoria moved closer.

“Not all at once.”

Damien’s hand tightened on the cover. “Mother.”

“Do you want the staff asking questions?”

He set the notebook down beside the grate instead.

“Go downstairs. I’ll take care of the rest.”

Damien hesitated.

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

He left. Victoria waited until his footsteps had gone. Then she stood looking into the fire, and finally pushed the last notebook deeper with the poker. Ryla watched the initials blacken.

“Ryla? Oh, sweetheart, you shouldn’t be sitting out here.” Mrs. Pell was back with the blanket. She looked from Ryla to the drawing room.

Her fingers moved. What was Damien burning?

Mrs. Pell glanced at the fireplace. “Oh, just some old papers.”

Why?

“I don’t know.”

Mrs. Pell moved behind the wheelchair. “Come on. Let’s get you back to your room.”

Ryla didn’t let go of the armrest. A thin trail of smoke was still rising from the grate. What does E.W. mean? Mrs. Pell frowned.

“What?”

Ryla spelled the letters again.

Mrs. Pell shook her head. “I don’t know, darling.”

She wheeled her down the corridor, and Ryla let her. But she kept turning it over: the notebooks, and the three things Preston had said. We only meant to scare her. It was Marcus’s idea to burn it. I deleted the real one.

Through the windows, the boathouse showed between the trees, tape still fluttering across the path. The water looked perfectly ordinary.

✦ ✦ ✦

Late that afternoon the video reached the guest study on the east side of the house, forwarded by the bank’s security team with one line: Please be aware. Client exposure possible.

Keaton Vance watched it once without moving, then again. The third time he stopped at one sentence and played it back.

It was Marcus’s idea to burn it.

He opened his notes on the Whitmore review and added a line under the list of missing records.

M. Whitmore — “burn it” — which documents?

Then he sat with his hand on the mouse, looking at a dead man’s face, until the screen went dark on its own.

chapters.title: The List
chapters.desc: Across the water, a man cleans his tools, crosses out a name and sleeps on the sofa.
chapters.epigraph: “They would choose wrong. They usually did.”
chapters.content:
The house across the water had nothing on its walls. A grey sofa, a narrow coffee table, a television nobody had switched on since the last tenant left. In the kitchen, two plates, two glasses, one saucepan and a knife block. Everything was clean, which wasn’t the same as comfortable.

In the early evening a man stood at the kitchen counter washing his hands for the second time. No soap now, only cold water, cold enough to tighten the skin over his knuckles. He turned off the tap and dried each finger separately.

On the counter lay a small metal case, a pair of gloves, a roll of tape, a folded cloth and a bottle of cleaning solution, in a straight line. The work was finished. There was no reason to hurry.

He opened the case. The tools inside sat in order of size, and he took each one out, checked it under the light, cleaned it and put it back. Careless things became problems later. Then he wiped the counter twice.

The house stood across the lake from the Whitmore estate, on a narrow road that curved through the trees.

From the kitchen window the estate came in pieces as the light went: a roofline, a few lit windows, the dark shape of the boathouse. He looked at it for a while and turned away.

The laptop was on the dining table. He sat down in a silence broken only by the fridge and opened an encrypted folder. Inside was a list of six lines, each with a name and an empty square beside it.

PRESTON WHITMORE.

He clicked the square, and a mark appeared. He moved down the list.

MARCUS WHITMORE.

HENRY ALBRIGHT.

He stopped there and studied the rest without opening them, then closed the file.

He felt nothing about the first mark. No relief and no excitement.

A man had died, and that was all it was. He had spent fourteen months arranging for things to happen in the right order, and there was no reason to feel anything about the first of them yet.

✦ ✦ ✦

That afternoon he had driven the long way round the lake.

The road along the eastern shore was the one the delivery vans used, and it passed the estate’s lower gate close enough to see through the bars. Two police cars stood on the gravel inside, and a third was parked across the boathouse lane with its engine running. A van from the medical examiner’s office had backed down as far as the lawn would let it. Someone had strung yellow tape between two birch trees, and the wind had already found it and twisted it into a rope.

He didn’t slow down. A man who slowed down was a man who wanted to see, and people remembered men who wanted to see.

At the bend past the gate a news truck had pulled half onto the verge with its mast still folded. A young reporter in a good coat was practising her opening into her phone, saying the Whitmore family three different ways. An officer in a yellow vest waved the traffic on with the bored, circular gesture of someone who had been doing it since seven. He lifted two fingers from the wheel the way the locals did, and the officer lifted two back.

In the mirror he watched a black car come down the drive from the main house and stop at the tape. The rear window lowered. A woman’s hand, pale, with a ring on it, rested on the door and then withdrew, and the window went up again. The car didn’t leave. It sat there, as if whoever was inside had come to the edge of something and found they couldn’t go any further.

He knew whose hand it was. He had studied it in photographs: on the arm of a chair at a charity dinner, on a son’s shoulder at a graduation, holding a pen someone else had uncapped for her at a ribbon-cutting. He had never seen it tremble. It hadn’t trembled now, either. That was worth knowing.

Above the drive, the main house showed him its east wing and a row of upstairs windows. In one of them a pale shape sat very still, too still for someone watching the police, the way a person sits when sitting is all they’re allowed to do. Then a second figure in something blue crossed behind it and drew the curtain halfway, and the window was only a window again.

He had read about the youngest Whitmore once, five years ago, in a paragraph in the local paper about a gala performance she would no longer be dancing in, and nowhere since. A family that could make a girl disappear from its own newspaper could make a great many things disappear. He had counted on that. He was counting on it still.

The local station was already on it. A man with a pleasant voice said that a member of one of Connecticut’s best-known families had been found dead at the family’s lake house that morning, and that police weren’t yet saying how, and then went to a song about a highway. He turned it off at the second verse.

In the village he bought bread, apples and a newspaper he didn’t read, paid in cash and said it looked like rain. The woman at the till said it always looked like rain in October, and asked whether he’d heard about the Whitmore boy.

“Only what was on the radio,” he said.

“Terrible thing. They say he was in the water all night. Poor Victoria,” she said, with the particular satisfaction of a small town discussing a large family. She wrapped the bread in paper with the air of someone who knew the family personally.

He agreed that it was terrible. On the way back to the car he caught his reflection in the shop window without meaning to, and saw a tired man holding a paper bag, which was exactly what he had wanted to see.

✦ ✦ ✦

The photograph lived in the second drawer of the desk. It was old and soft at the edges, folded once down the middle and flattened again.

A young woman stood under trees outside a university building with a paper cup in one hand, smiling with her head tilted and her eyes screwed up against the sun. It wasn’t a smile for the camera.

He held it by the edges. His thumb lay across her face, and he couldn’t have said whether he’d meant to cover it. After a long time he moved his thumb away.

His other hand lifted, and his fingers made a small shape, then another, without his having to think. Then they stopped. Some things were harder to say once the person you said them to was gone.

There was a voicemail on an old phone that he had never deleted. The phone lived in the same drawer, with its charger coiled beside it, and it had no other purpose. He kept it charged the way other people kept a candle in a window. He plugged it in and waited for the screen to wake.

Forty-one seconds, from her first week at Hollis. He had listened to it so many times that he no longer needed to; the shape of it was in him the way the shape of a staircase is in your feet in the dark. He played it anyway, with the volume so low it was barely there.

Wind first, and traffic, and then a voice that was already laughing at something before it reached him.

It’s me. I know, I know, it isn’t Sunday, and you’re going to say I’m early. I’m not early. You’re late. Listen, the maths building has a staircase that goes nowhere, I mean actually nowhere, it stops at a wall, and I’ve decided it’s the best thing in Connecticut. Call me on Sunday. I’ve got so much to tell you. Okay. Okay. Love you. Bye. Bye.

He knew the street she’d been standing on from the traffic alone. Two goodbyes. There were always two.

It was the only recording he had of her talking rather than signing, the only one in which she sounded like the rest of the world heard her. He had never been able to decide whether that made it the easiest to play or the hardest.

He played it again and stopped it before the goodbyes. Then he unplugged the phone, wound the charger round it, put it back in the drawer, and closed the drawer with two fingers so that it made no sound.

He laid the photograph on the desk instead of putting it back, and squared its edges with the wood. Then he went back to the laptop.

✦ ✦ ✦

He ate dinner standing at the counter facing the window: two slices of bread, an apple and a glass of water, no plate. He washed the glass and turned it upside down by the sink, and the wrapper and the core went in the bin.

There were three messages on his phone. One from a number he hadn’t saved, one from work, and one he didn’t need to open. He read none of them and put the phone face down.

At the table he opened a spreadsheet of company names, transfer dates and payments between subsidiaries, figures that looked ordinary until you lined them up. He made three notes and closed it.

The next folder held photographs: the boathouse, the garden path, the west entrance, the upstairs windows of the main house.

He enlarged one window and studied it before moving on. He hadn’t forgotten the house or the people in it. He just didn’t need to look at them every day.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten he put on a dark coat and went down to the water.

The rented house had its own jetty, a short run of grey boards with a ladder at the end and a rowing boat turned upside down on trestles beside it, its hull furred with moss. The boards were slick from the afternoon’s rain, and he walked them down the centre, where the nails were. He didn’t touch the boat. He walked to the end of the boards and stood with his hands in his pockets, and the cold came up off the lake and found the gap at his collar.

Halfway across, a police launch was working the shoreline. Its searchlight moved in slow, overlapping strokes, the way a man paints a fence: the reeds below the estate’s lawn, the mouth of the boathouse, the rocks at the point, the reeds again. Now and then a voice carried across the water, thinned to nothing by the distance, and a radio answered it.

They were looking for something that had gone into the lake, and they wouldn’t find it, because nothing had.

The light swung wide at the end of a stroke and came across the water towards him. He didn’t move. Movement was what eyes caught; stillness was furniture. The beam slid over the jetty, the upturned boat and his shoes, and went on up the bank into the trees without stopping, and the launch turned its nose back towards the boathouse.

He stayed another ten minutes to be sure of the pattern. Twelve strokes and a turn. Twelve strokes and a turn. Whoever was steering was methodical and tired and wanted to go home, and in three nights they would stop coming at all. Across the water, one light still burned in the east wing after the others had gone out.

On the way back up he counted the steps, as he had the first night: thirty-one from the boards to the back door. The kitchen light he’d left on threw a yellow square onto the grass, and he walked round it rather than through it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later he went upstairs. The bedroom had a bed, a wardrobe, a lamp, and open curtains. The sheets hadn’t been touched; he hadn’t slept in it last night, and he wouldn’t tonight.

He left his watch by the lamp, took a thin blanket from the wardrobe and lay down on the narrow sofa downstairs in the dark.

His mind went back to the morning: the video, and Preston’s face as he said the words he’d been made to say. We only meant to scare her. He shut his eyes and saw another room, another camera, another night, and opened them again on the same ceiling.

Near midnight the phone buzzed with a news alert. POLICE TREAT WHITMORE DEATH AS TARGETED KILLING A minute later, another.

PRESTON WHITMORE VIDEO: WHO WAS “HER”?

He read them both and put the phone down. He thought about checking the locks, but he had already checked them.

From the sofa he could see one corner of the photograph on the table. He could have fetched it. He stayed where he was.

Across the water, the study lights were still burning in the Whitmore house, and someone moved behind an upstairs window. They were frightened, and they had reason to be.

For years they had believed the past could be managed. A document could be burned, a witness made to look unstable, a name taken off a record, a body cremated.

He couldn’t see the boathouse now, and he didn’t need to. He knew how far it was, how deep the water ran at the slip, and how long a person could fight before they began to slow.

Tomorrow he would go back to work. He would be polite and patient, and he would let the family decide for themselves who was worth worrying about. They would choose wrong. They usually did.

On the table, the list was still open. Six lines, one of them marked.

chapters.title: Interviews
chapters.desc: The bank’s review begins, a detective asks about a name the family won’t say, and someone waits a full minute for Ryla to finish a sentence.
chapters.content:
A week later, the Whitmore estate felt like a house waiting for a verdict.

There were police cars at the gates on Monday. By Wednesday they had been replaced by two private security men in dark coats who stood by the entrance and pretended not to watch the road.

Staff lowered their voices outside the study. Deliveries were inspected, visitors announced twice, and Victoria had the curtains drawn in the east sitting room without telling anyone why that room in particular was dangerous.

It was quieter, but it wasn’t peace. Frightened people made less noise. They listened for footsteps, watched each other’s faces, and stopped saying certain names.

Preston’s had become one of them. When Ryla did hear it, it was in the past tense, said with the air of someone inconvenienced by grief.

Nobody asked her whether she was frightened, or what she remembered about the boathouse. Instead, Victoria had the bank’s review moved into the house: the man from London would examine the Whitmore Group’s accounts from Edward’s study.

Apparently the family preferred being investigated by a bank to being investigated by the police. Ryla suspected they were wrong about that too.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first interviews took place in the study on Saturday. Ryla wasn’t invited, but Mrs. Pell wheeled her past the open door mid-morning, which was how she learned that Damien had changed his tie three times. The navy one matched his suit and made him look serious. His smile, when he saw her, was less convincing.

“Ryla. Morning.”

She lifted her fingers in a small greeting.

His eyes went to her hands and back. “How are you feeling?”

It was a question he had learned to ask in front of other people, now that his sister had turned out to be useful. Fine.

He nodded, satisfied. “Good. That’s good.”

He turned to the man across the desk. “Mr. Vance, you met my sister at the gala,” he said.

“Mr. Vance, this is my sister, Ryla.”

Keaton Vance stood. Charcoal suit, nothing showy, dark hair neatly cut, a face that made it hard to guess what he was thinking. His eyes settled on her face rather than the chair.

“Good morning, Miss Whitmore.” His voice was low, with small pauses between the words, as though he didn’t intend to waste any.

Ryla inclined her head.

“Mr. Vance is conducting the independent review. He’ll be with us a little while,” Damien said.

How lovely for us.

Keaton gave her a polite nod and sat down again. He didn’t ask Damien to explain her condition, and he didn’t do the face. He went back to his document.

Mrs. Pell wheeled her on. Ryla hadn’t expected anything from him, but she kept thinking about how he had looked at her. It was unusual to be seen without being examined.

✦ ✦ ✦

By noon the study had become a revolving door. Executives went in with folders and came out with different faces. A senior accountant was called back twice. Someone from legal took forty minutes to explain a transaction that should have taken ten.

“Who authorised the transfer?”

A pause. “Was that approval documented?”

Another pause. “Then perhaps you could explain why the payment went out three days before the approval was entered.”

The accountant turned a strange shade of red. Keaton wrote something down and asked the next question. His patience was almost unpleasant. It gave people room to hear their own excuses.

Damien’s interview came after lunch, and his collar was already damp. He leaned back with the ease of a man who had sat across from journalists and investors and never once felt he was answering to anyone.

“Of course, I understand why the bank needs to be thorough. The Whitmore Group has always welcomed transparency,” he said.

Keaton glanced down at the file.

“Your company has reported consistent growth over the last three quarters.”

“Correct.”

“Yet the underlying liquidity figures suggest otherwise.”

Damien’s smile remained.

“Temporary discrepancies.”

“Several of them.”

“Market conditions have been difficult.”

“That would explain reduced revenue. Not the movement of funds between entities.”

Damien shifted. Passing the door with Mrs. Pell, Ryla saw him reach for his water and hold it without drinking.

“Those structures are complicated. I wouldn’t expect someone unfamiliar with the group to understand them straight away.”

Keaton raised his eyes. “I’ve read the structure.”

“Then you’ll appreciate that—”

“I’d like to understand why the figures don’t match.”

The room went quiet. Damien’s fingers tightened on the glass, and for a second the charming young executive disappeared and something sharper looked out. Then he smiled again. “Of course.”

Mrs. Pell kept walking. When Ryla looked back, Keaton was reading again and Damien was still holding the glass.

✦ ✦ ✦

Marcus’s interview went badly.

Marcus leaned forward. He was a broad man with a heavy jaw who considered most people beneath his patience, and unlike Damien he didn’t bother hiding it.

He disliked the bank, the review and the man running it, and most of all he disliked being questioned in his own house.

“You’ve been given access to the relevant financial records. What more do you want?” Marcus said.

“Supporting documents for the transactions listed here.”

“They’re old.”

“That doesn’t make them irrelevant.”

“Some of those records no longer exist.”

Keaton turned a page.

“Why?”

Marcus’s eyes narrowed.

“Are you suggesting something?”

“I’m asking why the records are missing.”

Marcus stared at him. Then he sat back. “You’re being paid to review the company, Mr. Vance. Don’t confuse that with authority over the family.”

Keaton closed the folder. “I don’t need authority over the family. I need accurate records,” he said, in exactly the same tone.

Marcus’s face said he wanted to throw him out. Keaton waited until he stood up and said that was enough for today, then made a note on his way out. He didn’t seem disappointed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Detective Nora Calder came in the late afternoon, without any of the urgency Ryla expected from television police: a dark coat, a leather folder, a word with the housekeeper.

She was shorter than Victoria, with dark hair cut at the jaw and a face that had forgotten how to look impressed. From the landing, Ryla saw her glance up.

Calder nodded, and Ryla nodded back, and the detective held her eyes a beat longer than politeness needed before she followed the housekeeper to the study.

Victoria rose. “Detective. I wasn’t expecting you. Is this about Preston?”

“It’s about a few things.”

Calder sat without being asked and opened her folder. “I’d like to go over the timeline again.”

“Your nephew was found at the boathouse.”

Victoria folded her hands.

“Yes.”

“Do you know why he was there?”

“No.”

“Who has keys?”

“Several people, I imagine.”

“Could you give me their names?”

“Of course.”

Calder wrote it down. “Did Preston have any reason to think someone wanted to hurt him?”

Victoria’s mouth tightened. “Preston was not an easy young man. He had disagreements. But nothing that would justify—”

“That’s not what I asked.”

Victoria stopped. For the first time, staying composed seemed to cost her something. “No. I don’t believe so.”

“Did he ever mention a woman named Elena Ward?”

A stranger wouldn’t have noticed anything. But Victoria’s fingers, resting neatly together, pressed tight.

“Who?”

“Elena Ward.”

“I don’t know that name.”

“She attended Hollis University.”

“I wouldn’t know.”

“She died fourteen months ago.”

Victoria went still. “Why are you asking me about her?”

“Because Preston’s video talks about burning something. Because her university tells me she was working on Whitmore Group data when she died. And because nobody in this family has said her name to me once.”

“Preston said a great many things in that video. Some of them were incoherent.”

“Some of them were specific.”

Victoria glanced at the door, and Calder saw it. “Is there something you’d like to tell me?”

“No.” It came too fast.

Calder closed the folder and stood, and Victoria looked relieved. “Thank you for your time, Mrs. Whitmore.”

“Will that be all?”

“For now. One more thing.” At the door she turned.

“The boathouse.”

“What about it?”

Calder looked out of the window, where the lawn ran down through the trees to the boathouse.

Victoria said nothing. Calder turned back towards her.

“Do you use the boathouse yourself?”

“No.”

“Neither does your son?”

“I wouldn’t know where Damien goes every evening.”

Calder studied her a moment longer and left.

✦ ✦ ✦

Twenty minutes later Ryla saw her again from the east window. Calder hadn’t gone to her car.

She was down on the path to the water with the groundskeeper, hands in her coat pockets, listening while he pointed. Then she walked to the edge of the slip and stood looking down.

She wasn’t searching for a dropped object or a mark on the boards.

Her eyes stayed on the water where Preston had been found, and Ryla knew that face. She had seen it on people at graves: less sadness than recognition, the look of people who had been told something by a place once and weren’t sure they could stand to hear it again.

Calder bowed her head, stayed like that, and turned away.

Ryla’s fingers tightened on the armrest. She remembered lights at the boathouse once, a brightness in the dark, and watching something she couldn’t reach. She hadn’t thought about it in months. Or she had thought about it every day and refused to call it remembering.

“Miss Ryla? Would you like to go downstairs?” Mrs. Pell had come up behind her.

Ryla looked at the water once more and nodded.

✦ ✦ ✦

The library was the one room where people sometimes forgot she was there, not because they liked her but because nobody else used it.

Edward had filled it with books he’d actually read, which was rare among rich men with libraries: cracked spines, turned-down corners, notes tucked between pages. It smelled of paper and polish, and it was one of the few rooms that still felt like Edward’s.

She was there before dinner when Keaton Vance stopped in the doorway with a thin folder under his arm.

“Miss Whitmore.”

She lifted her hand.

“May I?”

She nodded at the chair opposite. He sat, put the folder down and saw her glance at it. “Nothing urgent. I was looking for somewhere quiet to read these.”

He didn’t open it straight away. He looked at the shelves instead. “Your father had a particular interest in economics.”

Ryla’s fingers began to move before she remembered that he wouldn’t understand. She stopped, picked up the tablet and typed it instead. He liked collecting books.

Keaton read the screen. Then his eyes went to her hands, which had started the sentence first, and stayed there a fraction longer than she expected.

“That too,” he said.

Ryla went still. It was a small thing, but he had looked at her hands. He opened the folder, and she woke her tablet.

Typing was hard when she was tired. Her right hand was more reliable than her left, but even it refused sometimes, and a sentence that took anyone else a few seconds could take her a minute.

People rarely waited. They guessed, interrupted, answered questions she hadn’t asked, or wandered off. Keaton turned a page and didn’t look at his watch. Do you always work in other people’s houses?

She deleted the first word and started again, and it was close to a minute before she turned the screen to him. She turned the tablet towards him.

He read it. “Not always. Only when the work requires it.”

She tilted her head. And does it?

“Apparently.”

His face was perfectly serious, and she wondered whether that had been a joke. Then the corners of his eyes creased, and she realised he was teasing her, just slightly. She looked down at the tablet before her face could give her away. She typed again. My family must be interesting.

Ryla stared at him, and then she smiled. It wasn’t the smile she gave photographers. Keaton went back to his folder and didn’t seem to notice she was still looking at him. Or he did. After a while she typed again. What are you looking for?

“In the accounts?”

She nodded.

“Discrepancies. Transactions that don’t have sufficient supporting documentation. Money moving between companies without a clear business reason.”

He explained it in the same even voice. “Sometimes a company keeps poor records. Sometimes complicated ones. And sometimes the records are built to make something hard to find.”

Which one is this?

“I haven’t decided.”

My family doesn’t like being questioned.

“I’ve noticed.”

They don’t like being told no, either.

“That seems less surprising.”

Do you know how long it takes me to write one sentence?

He read it. “About a minute. Sometimes less, sometimes more.”

She blinked.

He had noticed. Not the disability: the time. She didn’t know why that made her feel so exposed.

She typed: Most people don’t wait.

“Then most people are impatient.” His face didn’t change.

It wasn’t a comforting answer. He hadn’t called her brave or an inspiration, or promised her things would get better. He had named the problem and put it somewhere outside her. She couldn’t think what to write.

Keaton closed the folder. “May I ask you something? Did you know Preston well?”

It was an ordinary question in a voice that wasn’t. She picked up the tablet. He was family. He waited, and she said: I knew him.

“Did you like him?”

Ryla’s mouth tightened. She could have typed something harmless that wouldn’t find its way back to Victoria. She wrote: He was good at making people feel small.

He didn’t look surprised. “Was he like that with you?”

She nodded. His eyes went to her hands and came back. “I’m sorry.”

It was so plain she almost didn’t recognise it as an apology. No sympathy, no claim to know what it was like. Just the fact, acknowledged. She looked at the tablet again. He wasn’t the worst.

Keaton didn’t ask who was, and she was grateful.

A clock ticked somewhere in the shelves, and the light outside was going. This had lasted longer than most conversations she had with the people she lived with.

Nobody had asked her to smile or be patient, and nobody had made her feel that talking to her was a favour.

You don’t seem to like my family very much. Keaton read it.

“I don’t know them well enough to like or dislike them.”

She raised an eyebrow.

“Professionally speaking, I find them difficult to interview,” he said.

Ryla’s shoulders shook with a silent laugh. When he looked at her, she saw his face ease, the way it seemed to when he wasn’t busy listening. It wasn’t warmth exactly. It looked like something that had been there before he remembered to hide it. You can say unpleasant.

He read the screen, then looked at her. “Noted.”

He gathered his folder and stood. At the door he said, “Good evening, Miss Whitmore,” and when she lifted her hand, he lifted his.

The library went quiet again. Ryla looked at the empty chair.

She had spent five years learning to make a minute shorter: fewer words, sentences dropped halfway, an eye for the moment people stopped listening, answers simple enough that nobody had to wait. She had learned to be grateful for scraps.

And a man she barely knew had sat across from her and let her finish.

The last line was still on the screen. Noted, he had said. She was smiling at it when footsteps came down the corridor.

It disappeared when she heard footsteps in the corridor.

“Ryla, darling. I’ve been looking for you. Mr. Vance has a great deal of work to do. You shouldn’t distract him.” Victoria stood in the doorway, immaculate as always.

It was said gently. It was still a reprimand. Ryla lowered her gaze and typed. I wasn’t.

Victoria glanced at the tablet. “Of course not, darling. Come along, it’s nearly dinner.”

Ryla locked the screen, and Mrs. Pell came to wheel her out. On the way past she looked at Keaton’s chair. The folder had gone. There was only a dent left in the cushion.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across the hall, Keaton listened to one of the bank’s people, asked for a document, and made a note when the answer didn’t match his figures. When the man asked whether the family had been cooperative, Keaton glanced towards the library.

“Not particularly.”

The man laughed. “That’s the Whitmores for you.”

Keaton went back to his notes. Records had gone missing. Certain names appeared in old documents and vanished from later versions, and not at random. He had seen patterns like it before.

He would need the original records, and he would need to understand why a company that had spent years looking impeccable had grown so careless with the evidence of its own decisions.

From the end of the hall came the sound of a wheelchair on the wooden floor. He didn’t turn round. But he remembered her hands, the pause before she typed, the look she gave him when he waited, and the smile she had tried to hide.

She had asked whether he knew how long one sentence took her. He did. He had been counting. He always counted.

chapters.title: Ashes
chapters.desc: Marcus Whitmore drinks alone, wakes somewhere he has been before, and is read his own accounts.
chapters.content:
Marcus Whitmore didn’t like drinking alone, and on the last night of October he did it anyway.

The hotel bar was nearly empty: brass fittings under amber light, a football match playing silently above the shelves, ice settling in a bucket behind the counter. He sat at the far end with his jacket on the next stool, finishing his second whisky.

He had picked the place because it was far enough from the estate that he wouldn’t see anyone he knew and close enough to get back in twenty minutes if Victoria called. He had told the driver to wait and the housekeeper he had a meeting. Neither was quite true.

His phone lay by his glass and had been buzzing all evening: three calls from Damien, one from Victoria, one from a number he didn’t know. He didn’t want to speak to any of them.

The video had made everything worse. Preston’s glassy face on every news feed, the broken confession, the line about burning things, and underneath it thousands of strangers guessing what the Whitmores had buried. Then the police.

Calder had been back to the estate twice. Marcus had seen her with the groundskeeper and at the boathouse, and he had heard that she’d asked about Elena Ward. He had told himself it meant nothing, several times.

“Another, sir?”

“Yes.”

While the bartender poured, Marcus turned his phone over.

Damien: We need to talk. Tonight.

Marcus: Not now.

He pushed it away again. The fresh glass tasted slightly bitter. He frowned.

“Something wrong, sir?”

“No. What? Stop staring.” He swallowed and found the man still there.

The bartender lowered his eyes, and Marcus finished the drink.

For a while nothing happened. Then the room moved a fraction out of line, the way a picture hangs when someone has brushed it. He put a hand flat on the counter, and the glass slid under his fingers. His hand was shaking.

“Get me some water.”

He tried to straighten up. His legs felt as though they belonged to the man on the next stool.

The bartender came back with a glass and a white cloth and said something Marcus couldn’t make out. He reached for the water and missed, and it tipped across the polished wood. He tried to stand. The floor came up to meet him, and then there was nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

When he woke, he was cold, and the cold seemed to be inside him. White ceiling tiles. A fluorescent tube humming to his left.

He tried to move his arms and couldn’t. He pulled harder, and a strap tightened across his chest.

His wrists were fastened at his sides and his legs were held down, and he was lying on something metal and narrow. He jerked his head round, and the room tilted.

“Hello?” It came out thin. He tried again. There was a door a few feet away, its small window dark, giving him back the room.

His suit was gone. He was in a white shirt open at the collar, no shoes, and the metal under him ran on past his feet.

He knew that shape. Slowly, then all at once, he knew the room. A funeral home: the one he had used fourteen months ago.

“No. No. No, no—” He hauled at the straps.

The door opened, and a man came in wearing dark trousers and a plain black shirt. No uniform, no badge, nothing that said he belonged there. He carried a leather folder.

“Who the hell are you?”

The man shut the door, put the folder on the counter and looked at him. His face was calm, almost polite. “Good evening, Mr. Whitmore.”

Marcus strained against the chest strap. “Get me out of here.”

The man glanced at the restraints.

“You’re uncomfortable.”

“Untie me.”

“I don’t think that’s wise.”

“Do you know who I am?”

“Yes.”

“Then you know what happens to people who do this.”

The man opened the folder. “I know what happens to people who arrange certain things.”

He took out a sheet of paper: a photocopy of an old ledger, handwritten entries in narrow columns. Marcus’s stomach dropped.

“I thought we might begin with the accounts.”

“Take these off. Now.”

The man ignored him and came to stand by the table, holding the page at a comfortable reading distance.

“First entry. August twenty-third. Payment to Sergeant Peter Haines. Two thousand five hundred dollars.”

Marcus stopped struggling.

“Description: traffic incident involving a vehicle belonging to a university student. No report required.”

“That’s not—”

“August twenty-fourth. Payment to Detective’s Office Administration. Five thousand dollars. Description: expedite closure of accidental drowning investigation.”

Marcus’s mouth went dry.

“Where did you get that?”

The man turned the page.

“August twenty-sixth. Payment to Wrenhaven Municipal Services. One thousand eight hundred dollars. Description: collection and transfer of personal effects.”

“That’s enough.”

“August twenty-seventh.”

“Shut up.”

“Payment to—”

“I said shut up!”

The man raised his eyes. He didn’t look angry, which was worse. He waited until Marcus’s breathing was the loudest thing in the room, then went back to the page.

“September second. Payment to the funeral director. Four thousand dollars. Additional payment, September third. Two thousand dollars. Description: unclaimed. No next of kin.” He turned it over.

It hung between them. It took Marcus a moment to find his voice. “Where did you get that?”

The man lowered the paper.

“Does it matter?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because it belongs to me.”

“Yes.”

“You’re stealing confidential documents.”

The man looked at him. “That’s what concerns you?”

Marcus swallowed. “Listen. Whatever you think you know, there’s an explanation.”

“Then explain.”

Marcus opened his mouth, and nothing came. There was no handle on his side of the door. The little window showed only his own face, pale and bent out of shape.

“Who sent you? Was it Damien? The police? Calder.” No answer. Marcus licked his lips.

Something moved in the man’s face. Not surprise. Marcus seized on it.

“She sent you, didn’t she? That woman has been digging for weeks in things that have nothing to do with her.”

“She asked about Elena Ward.”

Marcus’s face tightened.

“Who?”

“Elena Ward.”

“I don’t know her.”

The man glanced at the ledger. “That’s an interesting answer. Your handwriting is beside her name six times.”

The room seemed to shrink.

“Six payments. Three to the police, one to the funeral home, one to the man who collected her belongings, one to a disposal company.”

Marcus’s mind raced. The original ledger was in the safe behind the shelves in the old study, where he had kept it for years because he trusted nobody else to remember what had been paid, when and why. Nobody else knew it existed.

“You’re not a police officer.”

“No.”

“Who are you?”

The man didn’t answer, so Marcus tried something else. “Money. Whatever this is, I can pay you. More than whoever hired you. Name a number.” It came out hoarse.

The man glanced at the ledger.

“You’re offering money?”

“Yes.”

“How much?”

“Whatever you want.”

“That’s not a number.”

“Ten million.”

Marcus forced a smile, which was hard with a mouth so dry. “Ten million dollars. Cash. Offshore. No questions. You get me out of here and you disappear.”

The man considered that. “What would you have paid to make her name disappear?”

Marcus’s smile faded.

“What?”

“Elena Ward.”

“Listen—”
