“What was the price?”

Marcus hauled at the straps. “You’re making a mistake.”

“How much did it cost to make her unclaimed?”

“She was already dead.”

It was out before he could stop it. The man didn’t move. Marcus tried to take it back. “I mean she was found in the water. There was nothing we could do.”

“Nothing?”

“It was an accident.”

“Then why did you pay the funeral director?”

Marcus’s breathing went ragged. “Because the family didn’t want a scandal.”

“Which family?”

“Mine.”

He had expected anger, a threat, some sign he’d hit a nerve. Instead the man looked almost tired. “Go on. You were explaining.”

Marcus shook his head. “No, you don’t understand. I was protecting the family.”

“From what?”

“From a scandal.”

“She was a person. She had a name,” the man said.

Marcus looked away. “She was making trouble. She was blackmailing—”

“Was she?”

Marcus stopped.

The silence stretched until he broke it. “You don’t know what happened. She was involved with Damien. She was unstable, obsessed with him. We were trying to prevent something worse.”

“Something worse than drowning?”

Marcus’s throat worked. “I didn’t drown her.”

“I know.”

That frightened him more than anything yet.

The man picked up another sheet. “Preston brought her to the boathouse. Damien held her under. Victoria arranged the rest, and Dr. Albright signed the report. And you made sure there would be no one left to ask where she’d gone.” He glanced down at the ledger.

Marcus’s face had lost all its colour. “How do you know that?”

When there was no reply, he began to pull at the restraints again.

“You’re going to kill me. Because of her?”

“Because of what you did.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first time Marcus saw the cremation room, it had been empty. Disinfectant, a polished floor, the funeral director’s careful voice.

He had stood with his hands in his pockets while she explained there would be no viewing, no service and no collection of belongings. He had asked whether anyone would be able to identify the body.

She’d said the authorities had completed the necessary procedures. He had asked whether there would be a record, and she’d said everything would be documented.

He had paid and left. It had taken less than an hour to erase a woman who had spent years making herself useful to his family.

Now he was lying on the same kind of tray, under the same white walls, facing the same door.

He began to shake. “Please. Listen to me. I can give you names. People who were involved, people you don’t know about. Albright. Victoria. Damien. Preston—” He tried to lift his head.

“Preston is dead.”

Marcus flinched. “Then Victoria and Damien. I can tell you where the documents are. There are originals. At the estate, in the old study, a safe behind the shelves. I can give you everything.” The man didn’t react, and he swallowed.

“Everything?”

“Yes.”

“Then why didn’t you give it to the police?”

The answer was obvious, and impossible to say.

The man leaned a little closer. “Why didn’t you tell Detective Calder? Because you were protecting the family? Or yourself?”

Marcus closed his eyes.

The man straightened. “Do you know what she was buried with? Nothing. No family, no belongings, no photograph. Nobody to say her name.”

“She had nobody. Nobody came. Nobody asked. If anyone had cared about her, they would have come,” Marcus said, offering it as a defence.

The man’s fingers rested on the edge of the ledger. “Is that what you told yourself?”

“Please.”

The man looked at him and then picked up the folder, and Marcus started to cry. The tears ran sideways into his hair while he fought the straps.

“Please don’t. I have children. I have—”

He had had a son. Preston was dead. There was a nephew who wouldn’t cross a room for him, and a family name he had spent his whole life protecting.

“I have people. People who’ll look for me,” he tried.

The man opened the door. “People looked for her. Nobody found her.”

The door began to close, and Marcus pulled until his wrists burned. “WAIT! Tell me what you want!”

He looked back, and for the first time his face gave something away. Something much older than anger. “Nothing you can give me.”

The door shut, and the lock turned. Marcus stared at it. Then he shouted, for the man, for the funeral director, for anyone, and his voice came back off the walls. Nobody answered.

Somewhere beyond the room a motor started, and the tray under him began to hum.

“No. NO!” The sound grew.

He couldn’t see what was happening past the door. He could only hear the machinery and feel it in his spine, steady and indifferent, built to do the same thing thousands of times.

He had once listened to a funeral director explain the process to a grieving family and thought it efficient.

Now he knew the difference between understanding how something worked and being the one who went into it.

The tray jolted and began to slide. The air changed first, dry and then scorching, a wall of heat that stripped the water from his eyes before he understood that the dark beyond his feet had a glow at the back of it.

He smelled his own hair. He heard someone screaming in a voice he didn’t recognise, and then understood that it was his.

He shouted until his throat tore. He promised money, names, a confession, anything. The door stayed closed, and the machinery went on.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, Detective Nora Calder was halfway through her first coffee when a courier came to the front desk with a flat brown package.

She signed for it and carried it to her office. There was no return address and no sender, only her name on a typed label.

She had been reading the Preston Whitmore file for the third time, still unable to decide whether the video was a confession or a message, and she left the package on the desk for a minute before she reached for the scissors.

Inside was an old black-bound ledger, its corners worn and its spine coming away. No note. The first pages were ordinary: dates, amounts, initials, expenses.

A few pages on, her face changed. Some payments had names, some had account numbers, and some had descriptions that meant almost nothing without context. Then she reached the twenty-fourth of August.

Detective’s Office Administration — $5,000.

Her eyes narrowed. She turned the page.

Funeral Director — $4,000.

Beneath it, in a different hand:

Additional payment — $2,000.

Unclaimed. No next of kin.

She stopped turning pages and sat back. Fourteen months ago she had worked a drowning for two days before it was taken away from her and she was told there was nothing to pursue. She remembered the body and the report and the lack of any family.

She remembered asking who had identified the girl and being told the paperwork was complete, and the speed of the closure, which had bothered her even then.

Now there was a record on her desk saying someone had paid to keep a dead woman exactly what the paperwork called her. Unclaimed.

She took a fresh evidence envelope from the drawer, then stopped. Beside the funeral director’s payment was a small handwritten reference number. She copied it down and picked up the phone.

“Get me the original case file for Elena Ward. Yes, the Wrenhaven drowning, summer last year. And find out who signed the cremation authorisation.”

Outside her office the day went on: phones, someone laughing at reception, a printer starting and stopping. Calder sat with one hand on the open ledger.

She had spent over a year wondering why the case had closed so fast. Now she wanted to know who had been so sure nobody would ever come looking.

There were more names, more payments, and in the margin between two entries, two small letters.

E.W.

She closed the ledger. For the first time since Preston died, it felt like a case.

chapters.title: House Call
chapters.desc: A late visitor at Dr. Albright’s clinic wants a post-mortem rewritten.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t know what they’re doing to the mute girl.”
chapters.content:
Dr. Henry Albright had never liked staying late, and the first Tuesday in November was no exception. At sixty-three he had earned the right to leave before the cleaners started.

His patients were mostly rich, mostly demanding, and nearly all convinced that money entitled them to a longer life, and he managed them with a soothing voice, a steady hand and the occasional carefully worded prescription. The Whitmores were different. They didn’t need soothing. They needed discretion.

By nine the corridors were empty, reception was dimmed, and the last of the staff had gone.

He had stayed because he didn’t want to go home, and he didn’t want to go to the estate. For five years he had driven out to the Whitmore house every evening at nine, and tonight, for the first time, he had sent the bottle with his driver and a note in his own hand. Evening dose as usual. H.A. He told himself it was the paperwork.

The paperwork was an excuse. Marcus was the reason. Marcus Whitmore had died a few nights ago at the funeral home the family had used fourteen months earlier, and the police were saying very little in a way that told Albright a great deal. Preston before him, in the water by the boathouse. Albright had spent his life reading patterns in bodies. He didn’t like the one he was reading now.

He sat in his examination room with his glasses low on his nose, going through lab results beside a cold cup of tea. He had just reached for his phone when someone knocked, three even taps.

“Come in.”

A man in a dark coat came in and shut the door behind him.

Albright frowned. “I’m afraid we’re closed.”

“I know.”

His face was neutral and his movements economical, and Albright had the brief sense that he’d seen him somewhere before.

“Do you have an appointment?”

“No.”

“Then you’ll have to call reception tomorrow.”

“I won’t be here tomorrow.”

Something in the voice made Albright take his hand off the phone. “Have we met?”

The man came further into the room. “Not properly.”

“Who are you?”

Instead of answering, the man laid a folded sheet on the desk. Albright glanced at it, and his eyes stopped moving. He knew the date before he read it, and the signature, and the conclusion.

Cause of death: accidental drowning.

He took his glasses off slowly.

He thought of Marcus. He couldn’t help it. A funeral home, and now a report with his own signature at the bottom, laid on his own desk by a man who hadn’t given a name. Someone was going back over the summer before last, document by document, and returning each one to the person who had made it.

“I don’t know what this is.”

“Yes, you do.”

“You’re mistaken.”

Albright reached for the phone, and the man moved. The blade was under his jaw before he understood what had happened.

“Don’t.”

The room lost its ordinary proportions. The door was too far away. The phone, an arm’s length off a moment ago, might as well have been in another building. The man stood close enough that Albright could see the fine lines at the corners of his eyes.

“Sit down.”

Albright sat.

“Listen to me. I don’t know what you think I’ve done, but this is a misunderstanding,” he began.

The man pulled the visitor’s chair round and sat facing him, and laid the knife on the desk, out of Albright’s reach but not out of his mind.

“You signed a post-mortem report fourteen months ago.”

Albright swallowed.

“I sign hundreds of reports.”

“This one was for Elena Ward.”

The doctor’s face changed, only slightly, and the man saw it.

“She drowned,” Albright said.

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“I don’t know what you want me to say.”

“The truth.”

Albright’s eyes went to the door.

“No one’s coming.”

“You’re threatening a doctor in his own clinic.”

“Yes.”

“Do you understand the consequences?”

“I understand them.”

Albright’s mouth tightened. “You’re making a serious mistake.”

The man put a blank sheet of paper in front of him, and a pen beside it. “You’re going to write the report again.”

Albright stared at the paper.

“What?”

“Your original findings. What you saw. What was in her body. What you were instructed to omit.”

“I can’t—”

“You can.”

“That isn’t how medical examinations work.”

“Then you should have no difficulty describing one accurately.”

The knife stayed where it was. “Who sent you? Is this about the Whitmores?”

The silence answered him. Albright’s breathing changed. “Oh, God.”

“Listen. Whatever they’ve told you—”

“Write.”

He picked up the pen with unsteady fingers and stared at the sheet, trying to arrange his thoughts into something that wouldn’t condemn him. He had written the original in under twenty minutes. He remembered the room where Victoria had waited, Marcus by the window, Damien on his phone, the three of them watching him after he’d finished with the body.

He remembered the money and the pressure, and telling himself he wasn’t responsible for what had happened before the body reached him. He had been responsible for what happened after. The pen touched the paper.

Post-mortem examination — Elena Ward.

He stopped. “Go on.”

He described the condition of the body, the bruising, the injuries that hadn’t made it into the official version. At the shoulders he hesitated.

“Both shoulders,” the man said.

Albright looked up. “How do you know that?”

“Write.”

Multiple contusions over the posterior and lateral aspects of both shoulders.

Findings consistent with forceful restraint.

His hand was shaking. The man watched each word appear.

“Next.”

Albright swallowed. “Water in the lungs. That’s consistent with drowning.”

“Write what you found.”

He wrote it. Then the man laid a lab result in front of him, and Albright knew the numbers and what they meant.

“Sedative detected in blood,” the man said.

“That isn’t—”

“Write it.”

“Those levels were—”

“Write it.”

His hand tightened on the pen.

Toxicological analysis detected a sedative substance in the blood. Concentration inconsistent with incidental therapeutic exposure.

The ventilation hummed overhead. He could hear his own breathing and the pen scratching. He wrote the findings he had seen and the conclusions he had deliberately avoided, and at the bottom of the page he stopped, because the last line was waiting.

“Please. I was told what to do.”

“By whom?”

Albright hesitated.

“Victoria.”

The man’s face didn’t change.

“Marcus arranged the payments. Victoria spoke to me. She said it was necessary, to protect the family. Damien was involved with her. There had been trouble. They said she was unstable.” Albright looked down.

“Was she?”

“I don’t know.”

“You examined her.”

“I—”

“You examined her body.”

Albright’s lips parted. The man waited, and slowly the doctor wrote the last line.

Manner of death: homicide.

He put the pen down, and for a while neither of them moved. Then Albright began to cry.

“Take it. Take it to the police. I’ll testify. I’ll tell them everything, the payments, the false report. I can give you names.”

“You’ve already given me names.”

“Then evidence.” He leaned forward, closer to the knife, without seeming to notice.

“There’s something else. You don’t know what they’re doing to the mute girl.” He lowered his voice.

The man’s eyes narrowed. “What?”

“The girl. Ryla. You’re looking at the wrong thing. You’re asking about a dead woman, but there’s someone alive in that house who—”

“Don’t.”

The man stood. “You’re trying to bargain. You’re trying to stay alive.”

The doctor reached for the paper. The man moved the knife, and Albright shrank back. “Wait.”

He seemed to be weighing something. Then the doctor’s eyes flicked to the telephone, pure instinct, and his hand followed them.

The man caught his wrist, pulled him off balance and drew the blade across his throat in one movement.

The chair overturned. A glass fell from the desk and shattered against the floor. Albright clutched at his neck with both hands, as if pressure could hold in what he had spent forty years teaching other people to keep inside them.

He made one wet, startled sound. Then his knees went, and the room was quiet.

Then there was only the ventilation. The man stood looking down until he was sure the doctor wouldn’t move again.

He put the knife down and checked the report. The handwriting was uneven but legible: the bruising, the toxicology, the conclusion. He folded it once and slid it into the leather folder.

He felt only tired. Men like Albright always bargained once the consequences of their choices finally walked into the room with them.

The girl had come up too late, from a man who had already lied about one woman’s body, and it could easily have been one more attempt to buy time.

He hadn’t come here for the doctor’s unfinished sentences. He had come for the truth about Elena, and he had it. The doctor had spent his career understanding bodies.

He had known exactly what his report would hide. The man took the surgical marker from the counter, drew a neat Y across the doctor’s shirt, and put the original false report in his mouth. A falsified examination returned to its author.

Then he went over the room. The overturned chair was the only obvious disturbance, so he set it upright, swept the broken glass into the clinical waste bin and wiped the desk.

Last, he took the doctor’s bag, an expensive monogrammed case marked H.A. Stethoscope, blood-pressure cuff, prescription pads, a few bottles. At the bottom were three small brown vials with handwritten labels.

NERVE SUPPORT · Rx 0417 · H.A.

The code meant nothing to him. Private prescriptions, probably, for a family that treated its medical arrangements like property management. He closed the bag without a second look.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the staff washroom at the end of the corridor he locked the door and ran the cold tap. He washed his hands twice, took off his coat and folded it, and checked his cuffs, collar and shirt front.

A damp cloth for his wrist, then his neck. The man in the mirror looked tired and a little pale, and nothing else. He changed into the clean shirt from his bag and fixed his hair with his fingers. His phone buzzed.

The bank: The Whitmore review resumes tomorrow. Mr. Whitmore asks whether you could come to the estate tonight.

He put the phone away, wiped the sink dry, checked the mirror once more and left by the back corridor before the night staff arrived. Outside, a fine rain had started.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the Whitmore house, nine o’clock had come without Dr. Albright.

Ryla noticed because she always noticed. For five years the evening had kept the same shape: his knock, his tray, his silver hair in the lamplight, the small glass and the word slowly. Tonight the knock was Mrs. Pell’s, and the tray was in Mrs. Pell’s hands.

“Dr. Albright telephoned. He’s kept late at the clinic. His driver brought this over,” Mrs. Pell said, before Ryla could ask. She set the tray on the bedside table. The pale yellow bottle stood on it with a folded note tucked underneath, the doctor’s narrow handwriting on the outside.

He has never missed a night.

“Well, he’s allowed one, sweetheart. He’s not as young as he was.”

Mrs. Pell poured, holding the bottle the way she had seen him hold it, and frowned at the level in case it was marked wrong.

“There. Same as always.”

Is he ill?

“He sounded tired. Everyone’s tired this week.” She didn’t say since Mr. Marcus. Nobody in the house said it. The name had gone into the same place as Preston’s, behind closed doors, where the staff stopped talking when someone came in.

Ryla took the glass. It tasted the way it always did, sweet and then bitter, and Mrs. Pell watched until it was empty, because that was the routine, and the routine was kept even when the man who made it wasn’t there to keep it.

“Lamp?”

Ryla nodded. The lamp went down. Mrs. Pell tucked the blanket over her knees, drew the curtains against the lake and stood for a moment at the door, on the point of saying something else.

“He’ll be back tomorrow,” she said, and closed it.

Ryla lay listening to the wind come off the water. Her hands were already growing heavy. She thought, without knowing why, that she would have liked him to come himself. Not because she liked him. Because in this house, when one small thing changed, it was usually the first sign that something larger had already moved.

✦ ✦ ✦

Close to eleven, he came in through the front doors of the Whitmore house in a dark suit, carrying a document case.

“Good evening, Mr. Vance. Mr. Damien is expecting you,” the housekeeper said.

He handed her his coat, and she took it without looking at his face. From his inside pocket he took a plastic badge and clipped it to his jacket.

VISITOR · KEATON VANCE · WHITMORE GROUP · EXTERNAL FORENSIC REVIEW

He straightened it and walked to the study.

Damien was waiting with a drink. “Keaton. Glad you could make it.”

“Mr. Whitmore.” They shook hands.

Damien hadn’t slept, by the look of him. His tie was off and his collar open, and the drink in his hand wasn’t his first. “Long night?”

“A meeting ran late.”

“At least yours ended.”

Damien gave a short laugh with nothing in it.

“The police were here half the afternoon. Calder again. She wants Marcus’s diary, Marcus’s car, the name of every bar he ever drank in. As if any of that brings him back.”

He looked into the glass.

“It’s been a week.”

“I was sorry to hear about your uncle.”

It was said in the same level tone Keaton used for everything, and Damien seemed grateful for that. People who had been told I’m so sorry forty times in a few days often were. “Thank you. He was difficult. But he was family.”

He set the glass down.

“Which is why I need this review to be clean. Whatever’s in those accounts, I’d rather hear it from you than read it in a newspaper.”

“That’s sensible.”

“Sorry to drag you in so late. There’s a discrepancy in one of the subsidiary accounts, and I thought it was better to talk before the next report goes out.”

Keaton set down his case. “Which account?”

Damien pointed at a stack of papers. Keaton read the figures for a while without speaking, then pulled out a chair. “Show me where you think it begins.”

Damien sat down opposite him and started explaining. Upstairs, Ryla was asleep with the lamp off and the curtains drawn, a glass of water untouched beside her tablet. The tonic had left its usual weight in her limbs. Her hands lay loose on the blanket.

In the study, Keaton listened, asked a question and made a note. He didn’t look at the staircase. Halfway down a page, his pen stopped.

You don’t know what they’re doing to the mute girl.

He had gone to the clinic for a dead woman and come away with a true report. The rest could wait until he had something better than the word of a frightened man. He started writing again.

“Go on,” he said, and Damien did.

chapters.title: Funeral Season
chapters.desc: Two funerals, a tonic that still arrives at nine, and a trust that changes everything on Ryla’s twenty-fifth birthday.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t imagine we’ll need to worry about that.”
chapters.content:
After Marcus died, the Whitmore estate became a house with too many locks.

There was a guard at the main entrance now, another on the west drive, and two at the boathouse, where the slip had been scrubbed and the doors were kept bolted. Victoria called it a precaution.

To Ryla it looked more like a confession. The staff were forbidden to discuss the deaths, visitors had to identify themselves at the gate, the gates stayed shut in daylight, and the downstairs curtains were drawn whenever a car came up the drive.

Most telling of all, Victoria moved everyone into the main house. Marcus’s rooms were locked. Preston’s things were boxed and carried upstairs. Damien moved his office from the east wing into the study, and Victoria took the bedroom nearest the central staircase.

Nobody wanted to be alone, and nobody said so. The estate had once been big enough to give everyone privacy. Now it was too big for anyone to feel safe.

Marcus was buried on Thursday under low grey cloud, in the old walled cemetery on the hill outside Wrenhaven. Ryla wore a plain black dress with long sleeves and a high neck that Mrs. Pell had chosen and Victoria had approved because it photographed well.

Her chair was placed near the front. Damien stood to her right with his hands clasped, Arabella beside him in a black coat and dark glasses, and Victoria a few steps ahead, accepting condolences with a grief she had clearly rehearsed.

Marcus hadn’t been a pleasant man. He had talked about Ryla as if she were furniture left in the wrong room, sighed whenever she needed time to type, and looked at her in a particular way when he thought nobody was watching.

She didn’t feel sad, and she wondered whether that made her a bad person. Then she remembered him at her father’s funeral, one hand on Damien’s shoulder, already discussing the arrangements. Maybe the dead weren’t owed grief. Maybe the living could feel it or not, as they liked.

The priest began, and two men lowered the coffin on ropes. For no reason she could name, Ryla thought of the boathouse.

She hadn’t seen Preston’s body or Marcus’s, but both deaths had left the same feeling behind: something unfinished, in a place where nobody should have been alone.

At the edge of the cemetery, a security guard was scanning the mourners. His eyes went past the grief to the gates. He was watching for someone.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dr. Henry Albright was buried three days later, and fewer people came. He had been well known in certain circles but never much loved, and the papers called his death “a shocking incident at his private clinic”. The police had said little. Victoria stayed home with a migraine; Ryla suspected she didn’t want to be photographed beside another coffin. Damien went, and he made sure Ryla came too. He shook hands with the doctor’s family and two men from the hospital board, and on the drive home he asked the driver to take the long way round. Nobody asked why.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the second week of November the family had a new routine. Doors were locked. Meals were eaten together. A security report went to Victoria every evening, and Damien made phone calls in the study so that Ryla couldn’t hear them from the corridor.

And the tonic kept coming. That was the one thing that hadn’t changed. It still came every night at nine, only now Mrs. Pell brought it.

The first evening after Albright died, she carried in the pale yellow bottle with a small glass of water. Ryla looked at it, then at her. Where is Dr. Albright? Mrs. Pell’s expression had tightened.

“Oh, dear. You know what happened.”

Ryla signed again. Who made this?

“Mrs. Whitmore arranged it.”

The doctor?

“No, darling. Mrs. Whitmore.”

Did he leave instructions?

Mrs. Pell hesitated. “Everything has been arranged.”

It wasn’t an answer. Ryla typed the question out as well, in case it was her hands Mrs. Pell was pretending not to understand. Did he leave instructions?

Mrs. Pell glanced at the door. “I don’t know, Miss Ryla.”

Ryla pushed the tablet away and left the glass where it was. She didn’t drink the tonic.

Mrs. Pell looked unhappy. “Your stepmother asked me to make sure you take it. Please, darling. Don’t make this difficult.”

Ryla had been hearing that for five years, in one form or another. Don’t make this difficult. Don’t tire yourself. Don’t upset your stepmother. Don’t make people wait. In the end, she picked up the glass.

It tasted the way it always did, sweet and then bitter. Mrs. Pell watched until it was empty.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three nights later Victoria brought it herself. Ryla was by the window when the door opened and her stepmother came in with the tray.

“You’re still awake. I thought I’d bring this up myself tonight. Mrs. Pell has been rather busy, and I don’t want you missing your medication.”

Ryla reached for her tablet. What is it?

“Your nerve support.”

Who prescribed it?

Victoria’s smile stayed put. “Dr. Albright.”

He is dead.

The room went quiet. Then Victoria gave a small, patient sigh. “His treatment plan, darling. He left instructions. You know how these things work.”

Ryla lowered her hands.

“Besides, it’s been helping you sleep. There.” Victoria poured, and Ryla watched the level rise. Not a drop more than necessary, not a drop less.

Ryla didn’t reach for it. Victoria waited, then came closer and put the glass in her hand. “Drink it while it’s fresh.”

Ryla thought about refusing, and she could see exactly how it would go. Victoria would call Mrs. Pell, Mrs. Pell would apologise, the tonic would come back tomorrow, and someone would mention her difficult temperament at dinner. Nothing would change. She drank.

Victoria took the empty glass. “Good girl. Now get some rest.” She touched Ryla’s cheek, almost fondly.

Ryla listened to her footsteps fade down the corridor. Her hands had already started to feel heavy.

✦ ✦ ✦

Walter Greaves came on Tuesday, with no security and no entourage: an old dark blue car, a leather briefcase and a box of biscuits from the bakery in town.

He was seventy, silver-haired and slightly stooped, and he had been Edward’s solicitor for more than thirty years. He was the only person in the family’s orbit who had never treated her as an inconvenience.

He spoke to her directly and waited for her answers. He had even learned some sign, slowly and carefully, and could follow her if she kept it simple.

And he never let Victoria speak for her unless Ryla asked. She liked him, maybe because he remembered her father as a man rather than a fortune.

“Well. Hello, my dear,” Walter said, coming into the sitting room.

She smiled. He set the biscuit box on the table.

“I brought the almond ones. Your father used to say they were too sweet.”

Ryla signed, He ate them anyway. Walter laughed.

“Yes. He was a hypocrite about biscuits.”

He pulled a chair close. “How have you been?”

Fine.

Walter gave her a look. “That’s the answer you give when you don’t want to tell me anything.”

When she only smiled, he nodded.

“Very well. I’ll ask something else,” said Walter.

He took a thin folder from his briefcase. “Your birthday is coming.”

Her smile faded a little. The twenty-first of December, a little over a month away. Whitmore birthdays were productions: flowers, photographers, a cake nobody ate, speeches about how lucky they all were to have each other. She knew her twenty-fifth would be different. She didn’t know why.

“Your father was very particular about the arrangements he made for you. When Edward died, his will put most of his estate into a trust for you. Seventy per cent of the Whitmore fortune, including his controlling interests, is held in that trust,” Walter said, choosing his words.

Ryla blinked. Seventy per cent. She glanced at the doorway.

Victoria was standing there. She had come in so that Ryla hadn’t heard her.

“Victoria. Good afternoon.”

“Mr. Greaves. I didn’t realise you were going through the trust documents today.” Victoria came in with a pleasant smile.

“I thought it was time we went through them with Ryla.”

Her smile tightened. “Of course.”

Walter returned his attention to Ryla.

“Your father wanted you to have independence, my dear. He wanted to ensure that you would never be entirely dependent on anyone else’s goodwill.”

What happens when I turn twenty-five?

Walter smiled. “That’s the important part. At twenty-five you take full control of the trust. You’ll direct the assets, vote the shares and make your own financial decisions.” He turned a page.

She had known she was rich, and that there was a trust. She had never understood how big it was, or how carefully her father had put it out of Victoria’s reach.

“Until then the trustees manage it for you. On your birthday that changes, and what happens next is up to you.”

I can decide?

“Yes.”

Everything?

“Everything covered by the trust.”

Walter’s voice softened. “Your father wanted you to have that choice.”

Ryla remembered Edward’s hands, broad and warm around hers the week she moved into the estate, when he insisted on teaching her to waltz in the front hall and stepped on her feet twice.

She remembered his laugh when she got it wrong, and him telling her never to let anyone make her feel small. She had been eighteen when he died and nineteen when she fell. Five years later she was still trying to remember what it felt like to choose.

Victoria hadn’t moved, and her smile hadn’t either, but her fingers were curled tight round the handle of her bag. Damien had come up behind her with his phone in his hand. His eyes were on Walter. Walter continued.

“There is one other provision. It covers what happens if you die before your twenty-fifth birthday without children. In that case, the trust passes according to your father’s instructions. I don’t imagine we’ll need to worry about that,” Walter went on.

Nobody said anything.

Victoria gave a small laugh. “Edward always was rather dramatic with his legal arrangements.”

Walter didn’t smile.

“He was careful.”

“Of course.”

“And very clear about what he wanted.”

Victoria’s eyes went to the folder. “Yes. He was.”

Her face barely changed, but the warmth went out of it, and the performance with it. For one unguarded second she looked at Ryla the way you look at a locked door. Then the smile came back.

“Well, darling. Your father certainly wanted you to be secure.”

Ryla lowered her eyes. She signed, Yes. Walter closed the folder.

“I’ll arrange another meeting before your birthday. We’ll go through everything properly, and you can ask me anything you like. Now. Your father would never forgive me if I left without making you eat at least one,” Walter said, closing the folder. He stood and opened the box of biscuits.

Ryla smiled, and for the first time that afternoon it was easy.

✦ ✦ ✦

After he’d gone, Victoria and Damien stood at the sitting-room window and watched his car disappear down the drive. Then Victoria turned.

“Did you know?”

Damien slipped his phone into his pocket.

“Know what?”

“That he intended to discuss the trust today.”

“No.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because I didn’t know.”

“You should have known.”

Damien’s jaw tightened. “Mother, I’m not his solicitor.”

“No. You’re Edward’s son.”

He looked away.

Victoria picked up the folder Walter had left, read the first page and closed it. “Forty-one days.”

“I can count, Mother.”

Damien poured himself a drink at the sideboard. “There’s still time.”

“Not much.”

“We’ll deal with it.”

“How?”

Damien didn’t answer.

Victoria glanced towards the staircase. “She doesn’t understand what she has.”

“She understands enough.”

“Does she?”

He turned, and their eyes met before she looked away. “She has always been more perceptive than people think.”

Damien didn’t answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ryla kept thinking about Albright’s funeral, more than she wanted to. The cold, the flowers, the priest, and Damien standing beside her the whole time with one hand on her wheelchair.

At first she’d thought he was being attentive because people were watching. Then she had looked up and found him staring at her.

Not at her face or the black ribbon on her wrist: at her. There was no grief in it and no tenderness, only a still, focused attention, and it went on long enough that she felt it.

When she turned her head, his eyes didn’t move. Then, slowly, they went to the coffin.

She knew that look. It was the one he gave a balance sheet when he was working out what something would cost him, and whether a problem could be removed without creating another. He was doing arithmetic, and somehow she had become part of the sum.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she didn’t sleep straight away. The guards changed outside, and a door closed downstairs. She lay looking at the ceiling while Walter’s words came round again.

At twenty-five you take full control. Victoria’s hand on her bag. Damien watching her. The way the room had changed when Walter said the word trust.

Then the tonic. Albright was dead, and Marcus, and Preston, and still someone brought her the same medicine every night. The empty glass stood beside the lamp.

Ryla lifted her right hand and made the sign for wait. It was the first sign she learned in rehabilitation, and the one she had used most since. She held it, and let her hand fall.

Forty-one days. For the first time in five years, the future had a date on it. And downstairs, they were counting too.

chapters.title: Greenhouse
chapters.desc: Victoria Whitmore believes every problem can be solved by controlling what people see. In her greenhouse, someone tests it.
chapters.content:
Victoria Whitmore believed almost any problem could be solved by controlling what people were allowed to see.

She had believed it long before Edward, the estate, the foundation and the society pages. People weren’t complicated.

They wanted to be admired and loved, and to believe the world was fair as long as fairness kept favouring them. Give them the right picture, and they would forgive almost anything.

A photograph could turn cruelty into discipline, a headline could turn greed into ambition, a funeral could turn a suspicious death into a tragedy. And a girl in a wheelchair, presented properly, became proof of a family’s compassion. Victoria had always been good at presentation.

She stood in the greenhouse with a pair of pruning scissors, examining a pale orchid. It was her favourite room on the estate: warmer than the house, humid enough to soften the skin, quiet enough to hear the irrigation ticking.

Outside the glass the trees were losing their leaves. Inside, everything stayed green. She liked flowers that needed attention.

Orchids wanted exactly the right heat, light and water; too much affection killed them, and too little and they stopped flowering. Victoria understood that. She snipped off a dead stem. Her phone buzzed.

Damien: Calder called again. She wants to speak to us tomorrow.

Victoria: Tell her to arrange it through our solicitor.

Damien: She’s asking about Elena Ward.

Victoria’s fingers stopped. The name was turning up far too often. She put the phone down.

For over a year, Elena Ward had been a problem that no longer existed. An inconvenient history, an inconvenient attachment to Damien, and a habit of mistaking closeness to money for belonging.

Edward had never met her; he was dead before she started coming to the house. It was Damien who brought her in.

A clever girl, he’d said, brilliant actually, helping with the fund’s mathematical model. He talked about her mind as if it were something he had found and acquired.

Victoria could tolerate that. What she couldn’t tolerate was the girl believing she was anything more: too familiar, too comfortable, too sure she could talk to the Whitmores as an equal.

And then there was the other one. Edward’s other daughter.

Ryla had her mother’s face and none of her mother’s sense. Annika Holt had been an ordinary woman with an extraordinary talent for making men feel important, and Edward had mistaken that for depth.

He brought the girl into the estate and called her his daughter, and Victoria said nothing, at least in public.

She allowed Ryla her rooms, her schooling, her place at the table, the staff’s indulgence, even Edward’s sentimental insistence on putting her in family photographs. Then Edward died, and the girl fell.

Victoria looked across the lawn at the main house. Ryla was twenty-four, nearly twenty-five. For five years she had been cared for, and for five years Victoria had arranged that care.

The girl couldn’t walk or speak and could barely hold a glass. And somehow she had become the most expensive problem in the family.

Damien: We need to do something.

Victoria: We are doing something.

She put the phone away. One of the orchid’s petals had a small brown mark on it. She bent closer. It would have to come off before it spread.

✦ ✦ ✦

She heard the greenhouse door open as the light was going.

“You’re late,” she said without turning.

Nobody answered. In the glass she saw a man standing behind her and took him for a guard until she recognised the suit. Keaton Vance, the auditor.

He had been at the estate on and off for a month, so quiet and professional that she had nearly forgotten he was there. She had stopped asking when he came and went, which was exactly how men like him made themselves useful.

“Mr. Vance.”

“Mrs. Whitmore.”

She set down the scissors. “I wasn’t expecting you. Is there something you need?”

He looked round the greenhouse. “Not from you, necessarily.”

She frowned. “Then why are you here?”

He shut the door behind him. “I wanted to speak to you privately.”

She laughed without humour. “About the review?”

“Among other things.”

She studied him. Average height, dark hair, a controlled face. She had met dozens like him: accountants, advisers, lawyers, men paid to notice things without having opinions about them.

“Anything concerning the review should go through Damien.”

“I’ve spoken to Mr. Whitmore.”

“Then I suggest you speak to him again.”

“I don’t think he’ll be able to help me.”

Victoria picked up her phone. “Then perhaps you should leave.”

He didn’t move. When she looked pointedly at the door, he took one step closer. “Do you remember Elena Ward?”

Her fingers tightened on the phone. That name again. “Why?”

“I’d like you to answer.”

“I don’t know what you’re talking about.”

“That’s unfortunate.”

He reached into his coat.

“What are you doing?”

She didn’t see what he was holding until he was already beside her. A quick, sharp pressure in her arm, and then a feeling she couldn’t name. She stepped back with her hand on her sleeve. “What did you—”

Her knees went soft. She caught the edge of the table, and the pruning scissors slid to the floor. She told herself she’d nearly fainted. Then she tried to lift her hand, and it stayed curled on the table.

“Help.”

The word came out clearly. Her voice still worked, and somehow that frightened her more than anything.

She tried to take a step, and her legs didn’t answer. She fell against the bench and knocked a ceramic pot to the floor, where it broke, shockingly loud.

“Help!”

Keaton caught her before she hit the tiles.

He lowered her into the chair by the workbench. She tried to push him off, and her arm hung there. Her eyes flicked from his face to the door. “Call— Call someone.” Her tongue felt thick.

“No.”

He turned the chair to face the bench. He wasn’t breathing hard and he didn’t look excited. He had the look of a man who had finished one task and was moving on to the next.

“What have you done?”

He glanced at the broken pot. “Something you’ve done before.”

Nothing she said after that made sense. He took her phone, set it beside the laptop on the bench, and then opened the laptop. Her personal computer, the one she used for the foundation, her private finances and the messages she didn’t want going through the household office.

“Don’t,” she whispered.

It had no password. He had already found that out. The screen lit, and her fingers twitched. She could feel them. She couldn’t move them.

He set the laptop on her knees, angled the screen so she could see it, and opened a blank document. The cursor blinked.

“What is this?”

He pulled the other chair round to face her. “Your statement. You’ll want to read it.”

She shook her head, barely.

“Yes, you will.” He started typing.

At first it was ordinary. A date. A line about wishing to make a final statement. Then a name.

I am writing this because I can no longer live with what happened to Elena Ward.

Victoria’s eyes widened. She tried to lift her hand, and it moved a fraction. He glanced down. Victoria tried to lift her hand. Nothing. She tried again. Her fingers moved a fraction. Keaton glanced down.

“Don’t tire yourself.”

Her eyes filled with fury. He went back to the screen.

Fourteen months ago, Elena came to the Whitmore estate believing she was meeting Damien privately. She was drugged before she reached the boathouse. She was humiliated, restrained and held under the water. She didn’t die by accident.

He stopped and looked at her. “Is that accurate?”

“You’re insane.”

He waited, then went on.

Her death was covered up. The medical report was falsified. Her belongings were destroyed. Her body was cremated without anyone being told. She was filmed and laughed at and treated.

Victoria opened her mouth, and only a faint sound came out.

I knew what had happened. I ordered the arrangements that let her death be called an accident. I told Marcus Whitmore to make sure nobody asked questions.

He paused. “That’s the part you should have been most careful about.”

“Who are you?”

He didn’t answer.

I knew that Elena had worked for the Whitmore fund. I knew that the financial model she developed had been used to conceal losses and misrepresent the fund’s performance. I allowed her work to be taken, her name erased and her death concealed.

Victoria’s face changed, because it was dangerous. The fund. She tried to shake her head. “No.”

The model wasn’t Damien’s work. It was Elena’s. The research and the papers were hers. Her intelligence made the profits possible, and the same work she trusted us with was used to hide the losses.

“That is not true,” Victoria said.

“Which part?”

She couldn’t answer.

I have spent fifteen months telling myself that what happened was necessary. It was murder, followed by a deliberate attempt to erase the person who was murdered.

Her eyes went to the greenhouse door. Beyond the glass the garden was going dark and the house stood across the lawn with its windows lit.

She could see the security lights and almost see the guards. Someone would come eventually. Someone would notice the broken pot and wonder why she hadn’t come in. She tried to make a noise.

Keaton glanced at the door and back at her. “Nobody is coming.”

He read the note through once, deleted a sentence that sounded defensive, roughened one that was too polished, and added a last paragraph.

I am responsible for Elena Ward’s death, for the false report, for the destruction of her work, and for leaving her without a name or a family to claim her. I can’t undo it.

Victoria’s eyes were wet now and her breathing ragged.

He leaned in. “Do you want to say something?”

A word took shape. “Money. I can—”

He looked back at the screen. “That’s what you offered everyone else. You paid people to keep quiet, to change records, to make sure a dead woman had no one. You thought that meant nobody would ever ask.” He looked at her again.

Her lips trembled.

I have no excuse.

He saved it and opened her email, already signed in, and chose the press list. Victoria’s eyes followed the cursor, and she understood.

“No. Please.”

He attached the statement under the subject line A PERSONAL STATEMENT FROM VICTORIA WHITMORE, added the foundation’s press office, several journalists and two newspapers, and looked at the screen. “Anything else?”

She had nothing. He clicked send. The first reply came within seconds, from the foundation’s communications director, then another and another. Journalists opened it and forwarded it, and someone rang the foundation, and the laptop chimed and chimed.

Victoria watched her name stack up in the subject lines: her confession, her words, her photograph. She couldn’t reach the screen or close the lid or call anyone. The words weren’t hers any more.

He asked, “Do you remember what you wrote for Elena? The message from her phone that night, the one that made her sound unstable. You wrote hers. I wrote yours.”

The fear stayed in her face, but something else came into it. This wasn’t a threat or a shakedown or a demand for information.

He had come with a decision already made. He had brought the words and the means, and he had already decided how the world would remember her.

Her fingers trembled against the edge of the laptop. He stood, took a second syringe from his coat, and drew it full from a small brown vial. She knew the colour of that vial.

He took her limp right hand, closed her fingers round the barrel one by one, and pressed the needle into the crook of her left arm with her own thumb on the plunger.

She watched it go in. He held her hand there until it was empty, then let the syringe fall into her lap.

It didn’t hurt. That was the worst of it. The heaviness that had been in her arms climbed into her chest and settled there, and every breath took more work than the last.

The irrigation clicked on, and a thin line of water ran off the edge of a pot and onto the tiles.

On the screen the first alert appeared, WHITMORE MATRIARCH ADMITS ROLE IN STUDENT’S DEATH, then a second, then a third that used the word murder.

Her breathing slowed to a catch, and then a long gap, and then a smaller catch. Her lips went grey. Her eyes stayed open on the screen until there was no one behind them.

Keaton closed the laptop and put it on the bench.

For the first time he looked round the room properly: the orchids, the glass walls, the chairs set just so, the tools in their rows, everything exactly where Victoria had wanted it. Then he left the way he had come.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first call reached Damien in the study, where he was sitting with Arabella.

“Mr. Whitmore, you need to look at the news. Your mother has issued a statement.”

“What statement?”

“I think you need to see it.”

He opened his email and found it at the top. A PERSONAL STATEMENT FROM VICTORIA WHITMORE. He read the first paragraph and the second, and by the time he reached Elena’s name his face had gone completely still.

Arabella looked up. “Damien? What is it?”

He scrolled, and his hand began to shake. “Who sent this?”

She read over his shoulder, and her face changed. “Elena?”

“Call the press office. Tell them it’s fake.”

“Damien—”

“Now.” He stood so fast the chair hit the wall.

He rang his mother twice and got nothing, then rang the security office. “Where is my mother?”

The guard hesitated. “Mrs. Whitmore went to the greenhouse, sir. About an hour ago, I think.”

“Go there. Now.”

The guard found her in her chair with the syringe in her lap. By the time the ambulance came up the drive, the note had been copied across the country. The Whitmore Group’s first statement went out twenty minutes later.

It called the document a forgery, suggested Victoria’s accounts had been hacked, and said the family was cooperating fully with the police. Damien spoke outside the gates, exhausted, his voice steady.

“My mother has been the victim of a cruel and calculated attack. The document circulating online is fabricated, and we intend to find out who is responsible.”

A reporter asked about Elena Ward.

His face hardened. “Elena Ward was an associate of mine. Her death was a tragedy. There is no evidence my family was involved.”

When someone asked about the financial model, he walked away.

✦ ✦ ✦

By midnight, half the country believed Victoria had confessed and the other half believed she’d been framed. Elena Ward’s name was everywhere. Someone found her university photographs.

Someone else circulated her papers, a classmate posted a picture of her collecting an award at Hollis, and an old video of her presenting her research went round.

The comments piled up. Who was she? Why would the Whitmores kill a student? Was she Damien’s girlfriend? Why was there no funeral? Who paid to have her cremated?

Damien sat in the study with the statement open on his laptop. Marcus, Preston, Albright, and now his mother: four people who had known what happened at the boathouse, and every one of them made to pay.

He stared at Elena’s name. He hadn’t thought about her properly in months.

Clever, useful, occasionally difficult. He remembered her in his office with papers all over his desk, correcting his calculations before he’d finished explaining them, telling him the model wasn’t ready, and how much that had irritated him. He remembered the last argument.

And something else, just out of reach: a night at his apartment with rain on the windows, Elena saying something she obviously thought mattered. He couldn’t remember what. He hadn’t been listening.

Now someone had killed four people over her. He shut the laptop. Damien closed the laptop.

Arabella was standing at the window. “She was just a girl,” she said.

“What?”

“Elena. She was just a girl who worked for you.”

“Don’t.”

“Someone has killed four people, Damien.”

He stood. “You don’t understand what you’re talking about.”

She looked at him. Then she said, “I think that’s what frightens me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

After one in the morning, Keaton let himself into the rented house across the water without turning on the lights. Coat over a chair, keys in the dish, hands washed.

On the laptop at the kitchen table, the story had moved on from the confession: pictures of Victoria and of Elena, a map of the estate, an old photograph of the boathouse. He looked at the last one before he closed the browser.

The worn photograph lay beside it. He rested two fingers on it, moved them slowly, and took his hand away.

The list wasn’t finished. But tonight they had all had to say her name, and the whole country had learned it. He turned off the light.

chapters.title: Taken
chapters.desc: The night of Victoria’s wake, the lights go out.
chapters.epigraph: If you’re going to kill me, do it fast.
chapters.content:
By the time the first guests arrived for Victoria Whitmore’s wake, the house smelled of lilies.

White arrangements stood on the hall console, up the staircase, outside the drawing room and beside the portrait someone had chosen: Victoria at a charity lunch three years ago, in pearls, with a smile that suggested she had just forgiven someone for something unforgivable. Ryla thought it was an accurate photograph.

The house was full of people who had come to say they were sorry. They said it to Damien and Arabella, and to each other over wine and tea.

They touched Damien’s arm and told him his mother had been a remarkable woman and that he must be strong. Nobody seemed interested in what had happened to her.

Ryla sat by the drawing-room window in black, beside a small table with a vase of white roses. Mrs. Pell had done her hair that afternoon and fastened a pearl clip at her temple, which had been Victoria’s choice. Ryla had thought about taking it out, but she didn’t want to give anyone the satisfaction of asking why. She had become good at choosing her battles.

A woman in navy bent to kiss her cheek in a cloud of heavy perfume. “Oh, darling. How are you holding up?”

Ryla smiled. The woman waited, so Ryla reached for her tablet, and the woman watched her fingers with the strained patience of someone waiting for a lift. I’m all right. Thank you for asking.

“Oh, you poor thing.” She patted Ryla’s shoulder.

Ryla kept smiling. She had never understood why people asked questions when they only wanted one answer.

Across the room, Damien was talking to two men from the foundation. Black suit, tie a little loose, a face drawn in all the right places. He hadn’t slept, by the look of him.

He had spent Monday night at the hospital and most of every day since with the police, who had questioned him twice. Reporters had camped at the gates since the statement went out, and every hour brought another one asking about Elena Ward.

Elena. A student who had worked for Damien, whose death was tied to the Whitmores in ways nobody would explain.

Ryla remembered her, though not her name; it had slipped away even when the news first broke. What stayed was a young woman crouching beside her chair at a dinner, smiling as if she had all the time in the world. Your hands are beautiful. Take your time.

Ryla remembered how warm she had been, and how she signed: not slowly and carefully, the way people sign to a difficult child, but naturally.

She had been kind. That was all Ryla knew about her, and now she was dead.

The television above the fireplace had been left on low, and Elena’s photograph came up beside Victoria’s.

ELENA WARD: QUESTIONS MOUNT OVER WHITMORE CONFESSION

Then Damien stepped in front of it and stood beside her. He stood beside her.

“Are you comfortable? Do you need anything?”

I’m fine.

“Good. Tell Mrs. Pell if you get tired.” He moved the vase of roses a few inches from the edge of the table.

He smiled, but it wasn’t his party smile any more. This one took effort. He touched the pearl clip in her hair. “Mother would have liked that.”

Ryla held his eyes and smiled back. She doubted Victoria would have liked anything about her dressed for a funeral.

When he went back to the guests, she wondered whether he’d been thinking about Elena when he said Mother, or whether he had ever thought about her at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

Security had doubled, and the guards had stopped trying to be invisible.

One stood at the front door, one at the foot of the stairs, two outside the study, one in the corridor to the private rooms, and a broad man she didn’t know, with an earpiece and orders not to chat, stood by the garden doors.

Everyone in this house watched everyone else now. Ryla hated it. She had never liked being watched, even before she lost the ability to leave a room on her own.

At half past nine Mrs. Pell came to her side. “Shall I take you up, dear?”

Ryla was tired in the way that sat behind her eyes and made rooms too bright. She nodded. Mrs. Pell checked the footrests and asked whether her medicine was in her bag. Ryla pointed to the small medical bag hanging from the back of the chair.

“Good. I’ll give it to you upstairs. Mrs. Whitmore wanted you to keep taking your tonic, even with everything.”

Victoria had been dead three days and was still giving instructions. That seemed about right.

As they passed the television, the anchor’s voice rose. “—police have not confirmed the authenticity of the statement. However, investigators are understood to be examining the death of Hollis University doctoral candidate Elena Ward—”

Mrs. Pell walked faster. “Don’t listen to that nonsense.”

Ryla watched the screen until the doorway cut it off. She wondered whether the woman from the dinner had been afraid when she died, and whether anyone had waited for her to come home.

✦ ✦ ✦

The power went out halfway down the corridor.

It was so sudden that the house seemed to vanish. One moment there were sconces and light spilling from the drawing room, and the next there was nothing. Downstairs someone cried out, a glass smashed, and a chair scraped. Mrs. Pell stopped. “Oh.”

A man called from behind them, “Stay where you are. The emergency lights will come on.”

Ryla gripped the armrests. In the drawing room a woman laughed nervously, and someone asked whether the generator had failed.

Then footsteps, not hurrying and not searching. Coming towards them.

Mrs. Pell turned. “Who’s there?”

A hand settled on Ryla’s shoulder, then moved to the side of her neck. A sharp sting. She jerked. Mrs. Pell made a small sound, and something heavy hit the wall.

Ryla tried to turn her head and saw nothing. A gloved hand covered her mouth. She tried to bite, but her jaw wouldn’t close properly, and the hand held her still while her heart hammered in her throat. She tried to scream, and nothing came.

A man’s voice spoke close to her ear. “Quiet.” It was almost gentle, which was worse.

The edges of the dark began to blur. She tried to lift her hand, and her fingers barely moved. The last thing she felt was the chair under her and the push forward. Then the dark went deeper.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke to the sound of breathing and didn’t know at first whose it was.

The room was cold, a deliberate, empty cold that had got into the walls. No linen, no furniture polish, no perfume in the curtains, no footsteps from the service corridor. Only a dry, clean smell and her own breath.

White ceiling. One light behind a metal grille. Bare walls, a narrow door on her left, an empty table opposite. No window. No clock.

She tried to move, and her hands closed on armrests. She was still in her own wheelchair. Slowly, then all at once, she understood that she wasn’t in her room, or on the estate at all.

Her heart started to race. She looked down: the black dress, the pearl clip, the clothes from the wake. Her medical bag was gone, and her shoes, and her phone. She was alone.

Her throat was dry. She tried to call out, and no sound came, of course. She tried harder. Nothing.

The panic came too fast to hold. She began to shake. Her arms trembled on the chair, her fingers curled and opened looking for something to hold, and her breath came in short, uneven pulls.

She wanted to know where she was. She wanted Mrs. Pell, and her own room, and anywhere with a window.

Footsteps outside. She went still. A key turned, the door opened, and a man came in and shut it behind him.

She couldn’t make sense of him. Then the face fitted together: the dark hair, the controlled expression, the eyes that had watched her hands at the gala. The man who had waited while she typed in the library. Keaton Vance.

He looked exactly as he had at the estate, dark trousers and a pale shirt with the sleeves rolled neatly. No mask, no weapon, no explanation.

“You’re awake,” he said.

Her breath broke. She tried to back away, but the chair was already against the wall. He didn’t come closer.

“You’re safe for the moment.”

It was so absurd that something in her gave way. She had been taken out of a house full of people and woken in a locked room, and the man asking her questions about her family was telling her she was safe.

A wet, silent sob came out of her. Tears slid down her cheeks, and she shook her head.

“Ryla.”

She flinched at her name. He took one step forward, and she lifted her hands, though they were shaking too much to sign cleanly. Where am I? He didn’t answer. Why? Nothing. It hurt to breathe. Are you going to kill me?

His face changed, only slightly. His eyes went to her hands, then her face. She wiped her cheek with the back of her hand and tried again, stumbling and correcting.

If you’re going to kill me, do it fast. Don’t make it a show. He didn’t move.

The only sound was her breathing. Then he raised his hands and signed. I’m not going to kill you.

He signed like a native. His hands moved with the ease of someone who had never had to translate a thought on its way out, and his face and shoulders carried the grammar without his thinking about it.

Nobody learned to sign like that from a book. He had grown up inside the language.

Ryla stared and forgot, to cry. She had known people who signed: the therapist who taught her, a woman in rehabilitation who knew a little, and Elena at the dinner, warm and easy. This was different. His hands were his first voice. You sign. Yes. You know ASL?

A faint crease appeared between his brows. It’s my first language. Her hands stopped. She looked at him. Why didn’t you tell me?

He lowered his hands. “Because you didn’t ask,” he said aloud. Then he signed again.

You were talking to me in a language your family didn’t understand. You didn’t need another person making it about himself.

It was so unexpected that she almost forgot where she was. Almost. Her eyes filled again. She signed: You took me. Keaton nodded. Yes. From my home. Yes. In the dark. He didn’t look away. Yes. Her hands shook. Why? He seemed to weigh the answer. Because I needed you away from them. She stared. Who? Your family. Ryla’s expression tightened. They are my family. Keaton’s face remained still.

I know. She shook her head. You don’t know anything. He let that stand without arguing. They will look for me. Yes. They will call the police. Yes. They will find you. Keaton’s gaze held hers. Perhaps.

It wasn’t reassuring, or even really an answer. Her hands fell into her lap, and she looked young. Not helpless: she had been frightened for so long that fear had become familiar, and now there was something new to be afraid of. She started to cry again.

Keaton looked away. When he turned back, he took a folded blanket from a shelf and laid it over her legs without touching her. “You’re cold.”

She watched him with wide eyes. The ordinariness of it frightened her more than a threat would have.

He set her phone on the table, then her shoes, which he’d carried in by the heels. Black, low, chosen because Mrs. Pell said they suited the dress. She hadn’t noticed them coming off, which meant someone had handled her while she was unconscious. Her stomach turned.

From behind the door he brought her medical bag and went through it: a folded list, tissues, spare clothes, medication, and a small bottle. Her tonic. The liquid caught the light when he lifted it. Her hands moved at once. That. My medicine.

He read the label. “Is this important?”

She nodded quickly. What is it for? She hesitated. She was frightened and muddled, and her hands felt heavy. My nerves. My muscles. Do you need it now? Every night.

He read the label again and put the bottle back in the bag. “I’ll keep it.”

No. I need it. His face tightened. I’ll keep your medication. You won’t be given anything until I know what it is. Her fingers curled. It’s prescribed. By whom? Dr. Albright.

Something moved in his face, for a fraction of a second, and she saw it. Whatever he was thinking, he kept it to himself. He zipped the bag shut. “I’ll look at it later.”

He carried it to the other side of the room. She tried to speak and couldn’t, so her hands came up again. Please. Don’t take my medicine.

He looked at her. “I won’t throw it away.”

It wasn’t what she had asked, and he knew it. He didn’t change his answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was no clock, so Ryla measured time by the silence. He moved without hurrying: checked the door, put her phone in a drawer, examined the lock, set a glass of water within her reach. She didn’t drink it, and he didn’t push.

After a while he brought in a second chair and sat a few feet away, not close enough to touch and not far enough to pretend they were strangers. Her breathing had slowed, but her hands still shook. She signed: Where are we? In a farmhouse. Where? North of here. How far? About two hours from Wrenhaven.

Two hours. She tried to picture it: the gates, the long drive, the interstate. She had slept through some of it.

Why did you bring me here? Keaton’s hands rested on his knees. I need to ask you some questions. Ryla’s expression hardened. Then ask me at home. I couldn’t. You could have. Not without your family knowing. She stared at him. They know everything. Not everything.

She thought of Victoria and Damien filling her silence with whatever suited them. She signed: What do you want?

He didn’t answer straight away. He was looking at her hands, the way he had at the gala, the way he had waited in the library and never once looked at her chair while he spoke.

She had thought he was different. Remembering it now was humiliating. She had mistaken a lack of pity for kindness. At last he signed.

I want to know what happened to Elena Ward.

The name meant nothing. Then it landed. Elena. The woman at the dinner, who had signed to her. Ryla’s eyes widened. You knew her? Keaton’s face didn’t change. Yes. From Hollis? He paused. I knew her.

Something had changed in his hands. Under the fluency there was a carefulness now. She signed: She was kind.

He lowered his hands. His face stayed composed, but something behind his eyes shut. She waited, and he gave her nothing. She signed again.

She spoke to me at dinner. She said my hands were beautiful.

For the first time since he’d walked in, his composure slipped, a pause too long to be accidental. I know. How?

He lowered his hands. “Because I knew her.” He stood up, and the conversation was over.

She lifted her hands. Wait. Are you going to hurt me?

He turned at the door and looked at her without speaking. Then he signed. No. Can I go home? Not yet.

That landed harder than she expected. She looked down at the blanket over her legs. Her shoes were on the table, her phone was locked away, and her medicine was in a bag she couldn’t reach.

And the only person in the room who could understand everything she wanted to say was the man who had taken her.

He opened the door and looked back. “Try to rest.”

Her hands moved once more. Please don’t leave me alone.

He went still, and for a second she thought he might come back. “I’ll be outside,” he said, and left, and the lock turned.

She listened. Nothing came through the wall: no cars, no television, no voices. The room was soundproofed, or near enough that the silence felt made. Her hands were still shaking, and she pressed them together in her lap.

She pressed them together in her lap, trying to steady them.

Her body felt wrong. Her muscles were weak, as always, but tonight the weakness was heavier, and her thoughts kept sliding away, and the edges of her sight blurred when she tried to focus.

She wanted her tonic. She wanted it so badly she could taste the bitterness. Nerve support. Mrs. Pell measuring it, Victoria insisting, Dr. Albright saying it would help her sleep. She closed her eyes.

Somewhere past the door was the quiet man who had waited for her to type, who signed her language better than anyone she had met in five years, and who had known Elena.

There was one question she hadn’t asked. It had started to form the moment he signed Elena’s name.

She lifted her hands in the empty room and signed it slowly. Who are you? Nobody answered.

chapters.title: Forty-Eight Hours
chapters.desc: A ransom call, forty-eight hours, and a brother who cries on cue.
chapters.epigraph: He was crying because you might not do it.
chapters.content:
Keaton had always disliked phone calls. A voice could hide too much. People cried when they wanted sympathy, laughed when they wanted to intimidate, and lowered their voices to sound sincere, and without a face it was hard to tell the feeling from the performance.

He preferred documents. Documents had dates, signatures and amounts, and they could be laid side by side until they contradicted themselves.

But this needed a voice. He stood in the farmhouse kitchen looking at a phone that wasn’t his: bought for this, activated under someone else’s name, used once before.

A voice-changing app was already running, set to flatten and slightly delay whatever he said. Damien had sat across a desk from him for weeks. He wasn’t going to hear that voice today.

Behind him the house was quiet. Ryla had been awake for nearly an hour; he had heard the chair shift now and then, a footrest scraping.

She hadn’t called for him or tried the door again. He had left her water and a sandwich, and she had barely touched them.

Forty million dollars, a public confession, forty-eight hours. None of it was arbitrary. The money would be hard to move without setting off alarms.

The confession would be worse: Damien would have to say, in his own words, that the work he had passed off as his own was someone else’s, and that his fund had hidden its losses with it.

It wouldn’t bring back Elena’s research or undo the cremation. But it would make the truth public in a way no document could. He dialled. Damien answered on the fourth ring.

“Hello? Hello?”

“Mr. Whitmore.”

A pause. “Who is this?”

“You know why I’m calling.”

Damien’s breathing changed. “Where is she?”

Keaton glanced down the hall at the closed door. “Good morning to you too.”

“Where is my sister?”

He said it fast. Sister.

“She’s alive.”

Damien made a sound, not quite a breath and not quite a sob.

“Let me speak to her.”

“No.”

“Please. Just let me hear her voice.”

Keaton glanced at the kitchen clock. “You have forty-eight hours.”

“What?”

“Forty million dollars. Transferred to the account I’ll provide. No police, no private investigators, no attempts to trace the call.”

“Forty million? That’s—”

“Not negotiable.”

Damien talked over him.

“Listen to me. I don’t know who you are, and I don’t know what you think you’re doing, but she’s disabled. She needs medication. She needs—”

“She has water. She has food. She’s not being harmed.”

“She needs more than that!”

For the first time he sounded truly upset, and Keaton could imagine how it would sound to anyone else: a frightened brother, a family already shattered by four deaths, now facing the kidnapping of the one who had survived. It was almost convincing.

“There’s a second condition,” Keaton said.

Damien stopped. “What?”

“You will make a public statement.”

“About what?”

“Elena Ward.”

Silence.

“You will admit that the dissertation you submitted under your name was built on her work. You will admit that your fund’s mathematical model was hers, and that you used it to hide the fund’s losses.”

“That’s absurd.”

“You have forty-eight hours.”

“She’s got nothing to do with this.”

Keaton’s hand tightened on the phone. “Everything has to do with this.”

“You don’t understand what you’re talking about.”

“I understand the documents.”

“Those documents were stolen.”

“From whom?”

Damien didn’t answer, and Keaton waited. “From Elena?”

“She worked for me.”

“That wasn’t the question.”

“She was part of a research team.”

“She was the research team.”

Damien was breathing loudly now. “You don’t know her. You don’t know anything about what happened between us.”

Outside, the fields were pale under the morning sky, and mist lay in the low ground. Keaton had heard this argument before.

People who took things from other people never called it theft. They called it a collaboration, an arrangement, a misunderstanding. They remembered the benefits and forgot the terms.

“Your dissertation. Her work,” Keaton said.

“That is not true.”

“Your fund.”

“You’re making a mistake.”

“Her model.”

“She agreed to help me!”

“She told you it wasn’t ready.”

Damien went quiet.

“She told you the assumptions were wrong. She told you the model was being used outside its limits. You ignored her.”

“How do you know that?”

“Because I read her work.”

A pause. Then Damien’s voice changed. “Who are you? How do you know Elena?”

Keaton looked at his free hand. There was a faint pale line across one knuckle from a broken glass in a childhood kitchen; he had forgotten it until the light caught it.

“That isn’t relevant.”

“It is to me.”

“Forty-eight hours, Mr. Whitmore.”

“Wait.”

Keaton said nothing.

“Please. Please don’t hurt her,” Damien said, and his voice broke.

Keaton had never heard that sound from him. It wasn’t the polished voice from the gala or the confidence of a man who assumed rooms would make space for him. It was smaller and more frightened.

“She’s my beloved little sister. She’s all I have left.”

Keaton went still. The farmhouse seemed to lose its sound. My beloved little sister. He saw Elena at the boathouse, the cold water, the hand holding her under.

“I’ll do anything. Do you understand? Money, the fund, whatever you want. Just let her go.”

Keaton looked at the clock. “Forty-eight hours.”

“Please—”

“And Damien? Don’t call her your sister again.”

He ended the call. He stood with the dark phone still against his ear, then lowered it. He had expected anger, denial, threats, some hurried attempt to bargain. He hadn’t expected Damien to cry. Or he had, and had been waiting to find out whether the sound would satisfy something in him.

It did. Not the suffering itself. It was that, for once, Damien had been made to beg for something he couldn’t buy. He put the phone down, oddly calm.

The next two days would show how much of the Whitmore money could move without tripping an alarm, how fast Damien could write a confession that wasn’t one, and whether the golden son would give up his reputation for someone he claimed to love. Keaton almost smiled.

Behind him came a small, uneven sound, and he turned.

Ryla was in the kitchen doorway. He hadn’t heard her come. She was still in the black dress from the wake, the pearl clip gone and her hair loose round her face, the blanket trailing one corner on the floor.

Her cheeks were wet, and her mouth was open in a silent, helpless shape that might have been laughter.

Keaton stared. She pressed her lips together to stop it, and it didn’t work. Her shoulders shook without a sound. She was crying and laughing at once.

“How long have you been there?”

She wiped her face and didn’t answer.

“Did you hear the call?”

She nodded. He took a step towards her. “How much?”

Her hands were shaking when she lifted them. All of it. He stopped. She looked at him. You made him cry.

Keaton said nothing. Her face twisted with no pleasure in it at all, only an exhausted disbelief. He sounded so sad. He said he loves me.

Her fingers faltered. She pressed them together and lifted them again. He called me his beloved little sister.

A tear slid down, and she laughed again without a sound. It was the laugh that comes when something is so cruelly absurd that crying alone isn’t enough.

“You think he was lying?”

She nodded, and he frowned. She signed: He wasn’t crying for me.

Keaton’s face hardened. He was crying because you might not do it.

Keaton stared at her. She wiped her face with the back of her hand and signed more slowly.

He doesn’t want to lose me. He wants to keep me. Keaton didn’t answer. She looked at the phone on the table.

He wants me back where he can see me. Where he decides what happens to me.

Her hands dropped, and she was breathing too fast again. Keaton pulled a chair out from the table to make room. “Come here.”

She hesitated, then wheeled herself in. Her right hand slipped on the rim and she had to correct with her left. He didn’t reach for her. He waited until she was beside the table.

“You’re saying he doesn’t care whether you’re safe.”

He cares that I belong to him.

Keaton’s jaw tightened. “That’s not the same thing.”

She gave a small, bitter smile. I know. He hadn’t expected this. He had prepared for fear and questions, for bargaining, for her asking whether he meant to hurt her and whether the police would come. He hadn’t prepared for her to understand Damien better than he did.

“He’s your brother.”

Half-brother.

“And he loves you.”

Her face changed. She looked down at her hands, and when she signed again the movements were small.

Does he? He says he does. He says it when people are watching. He says it when he wants me to smile. A pause. He says it when he wants something.

Her hands settled in her lap. The strange laughter had gone and left a quiet sadness that made her look older.

“How long has he treated you like that?”

She thought about it. Since my father died.

Keaton leaned on the edge of the table. “And before?”

She shook her head. My father loved me. There was no hesitation in it. Then she looked away. He didn’t make me earn it.

That stayed with him. He thought of Elena: the money every month, the tuition, the Sunday calls, the steady promise that she could build the life he’d never been able to give her. He had thought it was enough. He had thought he’d kept her safe. You think I’m wrong.

“About Damien?”

She nodded.

He was quiet. “I think people can be more complicated than they look.”

You can believe that if you want. He wanted to tell her he had seen the video and read the reports, that he knew what Damien had done at the boathouse, that Damien had held Elena under until she stopped moving. The words wouldn’t come yet.

“You should rest,” he said instead.

She looked tired, but not obedient. You should listen. You asked me what happened to Elena. Then listen to what I tell you about people.

Keaton didn’t move. Then he pulled out the chair across from her and sat down. “All right. Tell me.”

She seemed surprised. She looked at him before she began. Then she signed:

I don’t know if Damien loved Elena. I didn’t know her well enough. But I know Damien. She swallowed.

When he wants something, he makes you feel special. When you give it to him, he acts as if it was always his.

If you stop giving it, he gets sad. Not because he misses you. Her fingers moved slowly. Because he misses what you gave him.
