Keaton looked down at the table. It was too close to something he had already suspected, and he didn’t want to hear it from her. Not because she was wrong. Because he hadn’t decided what to do if she was right.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later he brought her a glass of water, and she drank half. She shook her head when he offered food, and he didn’t push.

When he moved towards the door, she raised her hand. The money. He stopped.

“What about it?”

Forty million.

“Yes.”

What will you do with it?

His face closed. “That isn’t something you need to worry about.”

You took me for money?

“No.”

Then why ask for it?

“Because they have it.”

And if they don’t give it to you? He said nothing. Her fingers closed on the armrest. Will you kill me?

“No. I didn’t take you to kill you.” She didn’t look convinced.

She looked down. You took me because you wanted them to be afraid. He didn’t answer, and she nodded.

You wanted Damien to feel helpless. But I was the one who woke up here.

It landed. He looked at the wheelchair, the blanket, the water glass, the little table with her things on it.

He had thought of her as leverage: a living person who would make the family move. He had told himself she would be fed and kept safe and returned when the work was done. He hadn’t thought about what it meant to wake in a locked room with no way to call for help, after five years of other people deciding when she moved, ate, slept and what she was allowed to know.

He had carried her from one locked life into another.

The only difference was that he meant to be kind, and he couldn’t find a defence in that.

“I know,” he said.

Ryla looked at him.

He stood. “I’ll leave the door unlocked while I’m in the next room.”

It wasn’t freedom, and it wasn’t trust, but he could do that much.

As he reached the doorway, she lifted her hands. Keaton.

It was the first time she had used his name. He turned.

If you want to know what happened to Elena, don’t only listen to the people who hurt her.

He nodded once. “I won’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, after Ryla had gone quiet, he sat at the kitchen table. No missed calls. In the encrypted folder the demands, the account details and the statement Damien would have to read were all ready.

He went over the statement once and then sat looking at the screen without reading it, hearing Damien’s voice. My beloved little sister. He shut his eyes.

He saw Elena on their last video call, tired, hair tied up, eating from a bowl while she explained a problem with her research.

She had complained about the fund, about Damien, about a stubborn professor, and then she had smiled and asked whether he was eating properly. He had said yes, and she hadn’t believed him.

Her hands had moved while she laughed, and at the end she had made the sign she used when she wanted him to stop worrying. I’m here. He opened his eyes.

The phone stayed silent. He had expected Damien’s tears to feel like something, and they had, for a few minutes. Ryla’s words had stayed longer.

Down the hall her door stood open a crack, and a thin line of light lay across the floor. He watched it for a while before he went back to the table and the deadline.

chapters.title: The Cold Room
chapters.desc: Darkness, cold, water, and a gun that clicks on an empty chamber.
chapters.content:
The first thing Keaton learned about keeping someone alive was that fear had a sound. It wasn’t always screaming.

Sometimes it was a small catch in the throat when a door opened, or uneven breathing after a nightmare, or a silence so complete that he had to stand outside the room and listen until he was sure she was still awake.

Ryla had gone quiet. Not the quiet of the estate, where she watched people with bright, assessing eyes and saved her words for the tablet or her hands. She was guarded now.

He had filmed the first proof of life the evening before: Ryla in her chair with a blanket over her knees, hair untidy, face pale, frightened but composed, holding her right hand up beside her face when he told her to.

He sent it to Damien, and the replies came within minutes.

Damien: I want to hear her.

Damien: I want to speak to her. Please.

Damien: She gets confused when she’s frightened. You need to understand that.

He read the last one twice. He couldn’t tell whether Damien was giving him useful information or reminding him she could be frightened. He put the phone away.

On Saturday morning he stood outside her door with a cooling coffee and heard a faint scrape inside, then nothing.

When he opened the door, she looked up at once. She was in the soft grey cardigan from her bag, her hair brushed badly, her hands folded in her lap.

“There’s going to be another recording today.”

Her expression changed. Why?

“Your brother wants proof that you’re alive.”

He saw me yesterday.

“He wants another.”

“Look at me.”

She did.

“You understand what happens if your family thinks you’re dead?”

Ryla’s fingers moved. They will be sad. Keaton said nothing. For a while.

He studied her. “You’re very sure of that.”

She lowered her hands, and he lifted the phone. “Let’s get it done.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By Saturday evening, Damien had stopped pretending the money was what mattered most. The calls came more often, and his voice was hoarse.

He asked the same questions in different words: was she eating, was she warm, was she taking her medication, was she frightened, had she cried. Keaton answered only what he had to.

“She’s alive.”

“That isn’t enough.”

“It will have to be.”

“She’s not well. She needs her medication.”

“She has what she needs.”

“You’re not listening to me.”

Keaton glanced at the bag on the shelf. The tonic was still inside it. He had read the label and the dosage and found nothing that looked dangerous; he wouldn’t give her anything he couldn’t check for himself.

He called that caution. It hadn’t crossed his mind that withholding it might be what was hurting her.

“She has food and water. She’s being looked after,” he said.

Damien made a frustrated sound.

“You’re keeping her like an animal.”

Keaton’s eyes narrowed.

“Careful.”

“She can’t even tell you what she needs.”

“She can tell me.”

“She can’t speak.”

“She signs.”

A pause. “You understand her?”

Keaton looked at the closed door. “Better than you do.”

Damien let out a breath. “Three more days. That’s all. I’ll get you the money, I’ll make the statement, whatever you want.”

Three days would take them past the deadline and give Damien time to bring in the police, move assets, call people in London and maybe find out enough to become dangerous. Keaton had already given him too long.

“She’s my sister.”

Keaton’s face hardened. “Then act like it.”

Damien’s voice cracked. “Don’t do this to her.”

Keaton ended the call and stood in the kitchen with the phone in his hand. Then he walked down the hall.

Ryla had been trying to read a book he had left her, but the words kept blurring, and the room felt colder than it had that morning.

When he came in and shut the door without a word, she sat up straighter. She knew the difference between his ordinary silences and the kind that came before something bad.

He put his phone on the table. “Your brother called.”

Ryla’s hands moved. What did he say?

“He asked for more time. Three more days.”

She looked down. He waited for her to ask whether Damien would get them, but she didn’t. Did you say yes?

“No.”

She nodded once. It was a small movement.

“You don’t seem surprised.”

He always asks for more time. When he wants something, he promises tomorrow. Tomorrow becomes next week, next week becomes later. She looked at him. Then he says I misunderstood.

“You’re going to make another recording.”

She shook her head.

“Ryla. I need you to cooperate.” He stepped closer.

Her fingers tightened on the armrests. He saw the fear, and he went ahead anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t leave marks. That was his rule. No blows, no bruises, nothing that could be photographed and turned against him. He needed her alive and recognisable, frightened on camera but unharmed. So he made the room do the work.

The first time, he left her in the dark. He told himself it would be short. He switched off the light, shut the door and waited outside.

At first he heard her trying to find her bearings, hands on the armrests, the chair shifting a fraction, and then nothing. When he went back, she was sitting rigid with her face turned towards the door and her eyes wide. She flinched at the light.

“You’re all right.” He checked her hands and face and the chair. No marks.

“Do you understand why you need to cooperate?”

I don’t know what you want.

“I want your family to take this seriously.”

They know I’m here.

“They need to know what happens if they don’t listen.”

Her eyes went to the door and back. You said you wouldn’t kill me.

“I won’t.”

Then why are you doing this? He didn’t answer. He brought her food, and she barely touched it.

The second time, it was cold. He turned the farmhouse heating down and left the unit in her room blowing cold air.

She couldn’t reach the controls, her cardigan was too thin, and once the blanket slid off her lap her hands were too weak to pull it back.

He found her shivering and stood in the doorway. “You’re cold.”

He tucked the blanket back over her knees, and she thought he would turn the heat up. Instead he said, “I can’t keep doing this indefinitely. Damien has to believe I mean it.”

Her hands were shaking too hard to sign. She managed to lift one. He believes you.

“How do you know?”

Because you took me. He had nothing to say to that, and he left. The third time, he used water.

He didn’t think of it as the boathouse. He didn’t say the word or look at the photographs on his laptop or the frame he had kept from the night Elena died.

But when Ryla began to panic, he remembered the sound of water against the boards and the silence between one breath and the next, and it came so hard that he heard nothing else.

He tipped her chair back against the wall, laid a folded cloth over her face and poured water from a jug onto it, slowly and steadily. The cloth clung to her mouth and nose.

Every breath she dragged in was water. Her hands jerked against the armrests, and her whole body bucked against the chair. He counted under his breath, the way he had read it was done.

He stopped before she passed out and pulled the cloth away. She dragged in air, eyes wide, her whole body trembling, trying to turn away from him in a chair that wouldn’t let her.

Keaton stepped back. He told himself it was enough, that she would recover, that the next recording would be clean.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the third day Ryla had stopped trying to understand the room. There was a door. The light could vanish. The cold could become unbearable.

The water had woken a fear she hadn’t known was in her. She had never been afraid of water. Before the fall she had loved swimming; Annika took her to the coast every summer, and Edward complained that they came home smelling of salt and sun cream.

When Keaton came in that afternoon, she was sitting with her hands folded, and he was carrying a small camera. She went white.

“One more recording. You’re going to tell Damien that you’re alive and that you’re safe.”

Her hands moved. I am not safe.

His face tightened. “You’re not injured.”

That isn’t the same.

“Ryla.”

She turned her face away.

He put the camera down. “Your brother asked for three more days. I told him no.”

Her fingers tightened. What happens now?

“That depends on him.”

No. It depends on you. She seemed to gather herself. You’re the one who keeps coming in here.

✦ ✦ ✦

The mock execution wasn’t in his plan when he first took her. He had thought of the gun as a last resort, a way to make Damien believe the deadline.

He hadn’t imagined it from Ryla’s side: that she would know the sound of a gun being handled before she saw it, or know from the way he stood that this time was different.

Keaton set the camera on the table. Then she saw the gun, and the fear emptied her of everything else. She tried to back away, and the chair hit the wall.

He stood in front of her. “Listen to me.”

She shook her head. No.

“Your brother asked for more time. He hasn’t met the conditions.”

She was crying now. Her hands moved again. Please.

He stepped closer. “Look at me.”

She couldn’t. Her eyes were fixed on the gun. He put a hand under her chin and turned her face up, and she flinched so hard a sob broke out of her. Her eyes met his for half a second and slid away.

He raised the gun, and she began to shake so badly the chair shook with her.

“Your brother’s time ran out this morning.”

Her lips trembled, and nothing came. He pressed the empty gun to her temple. She shut her eyes and opened them again, and her whole body pulled away from the cold metal while his hand held her chin. He pulled the trigger.

Click.

It was a small sound. For one second she didn’t seem to understand it. Then she broke.

Her face crumpled. She sobbed with her shoulders heaving, breathing too fast and too shallow to catch, tears running into the collar of her cardigan. She tried to turn away.

Keaton lowered the gun. He had expected a scream, or rage, or her cursing him in the language she couldn’t say aloud. She just kept crying, and she couldn’t stop.

“Ryla. Ryla, it’s—”

She raised one hand so weakly he nearly missed it. She was trying to sign, and her fingers shook too badly to make the shapes. She had to stop and start again, and he waited. I’m scared.

He stared at her. She swallowed, trying to steady her hands. Please. Just do it.

His face changed. She looked straight at him, eyes swollen, cheeks wet. Don’t make me go back.

He heard nothing: not the room, not the heating, not the wind on the farmhouse. Only that. He had expected her to beg him to stop, to promise anything, to ask for her life. He hadn’t expected her to ask him to end it.

He crouched in front of her and put the gun on the floor. She flinched at the movement. He didn’t reach for her. He looked at the tears caught on her lower lashes and her mouth opening and opening as she tried to pull in enough air.

“Ryla.” He reached for her hands, and she jerked away. He stopped at once.

Then, without thinking, he touched two fingers to his chest. Breathe.

It was a home sign, not ASL, one that had never belonged to anyone outside one kitchen and one childhood.

He had made it when Elena was small and frightened, when she woke from nightmares, when their father shouted, when the electricity was cut and they sat under a blanket listening to the rain on the roof, when she cried so hard she forgot how to breathe.

She had made it for him too. It had meant more than the word: stay here, stay with me, one breath at a time. He made it now without remembering that anyone else might know it.

Ryla went still. Her eyes went to his hands, then his face, and the sobbing stopped. Not because she was calm. Something had cut across the fear.

A memory stirred: a crowded dinner, the smell of flowers and expensive food, a young woman crouching by her chair, and a small movement of fingers against a chest.

She remembered the woman’s face better than the sign, and her smile and the kindness in her hands. But it was faint and broken, and she had no way of knowing why the same gesture was in front of her now.

Keaton lowered his hands. He didn’t seem to know what he had done. Then he saw how she was looking at him, and he stood up fast.

“Try to breathe.”

His hand missed the door handle the first time.

✦ ✦ ✦

He made it as far as the yard. The cold hit his face. He went past the bins and the low stone wall until the kitchen window was out of sight, bent over and was sick.

He stayed there with one hand on the wall while his stomach kept heaving over nothing, then wiped his mouth and straightened up in air cold enough to hurt. He had killed four people. He had watched Preston beg, listened to Marcus bargain, made Albright write the truth before he died, and stood in a greenhouse while Victoria watched her confession cross the country.

He had never been sick afterwards. He had washed, changed, cleaned up and gone back to work, and he had eaten and slept and thought clearly.

But Ryla wasn’t one of them. She hadn’t held Elena under or written a false report, burned notebooks or arranged a cremation. She had sat in a wheelchair at a window and been unable to help. And he had made her afraid of him, deliberately.

He pressed the heel of his hand to his mouth. Across the yard, the kitchen light was still on.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ryla didn’t move. The gun was gone and the door was shut. Her breathing had slowed, though a tremor still ran through her shoulders every so often. She looked at the place where he had knelt.

She lifted her own unsteady hand and touched two fingers to the middle of her chest. The memory came back in pieces. The woman at the dinner signing to her, crouched by the chair, smiling, saying something about taking her time.

Then a glass breaking, a noise, someone calling the woman from across the room, and the woman’s two fingers against her own chest before she went. It slipped away again.

Ryla lowered her hand. She didn’t know why Keaton knew that sign, or why it had felt familiar. For one moment when he made it, it was as if someone had reached across years and touched a part of her life she had left behind.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came back twenty minutes later with his face washed, his shirt changed and no gun. She looked up at once. He stopped by the door, and neither of them moved.

“I’m sorry,” he said. The words sounded strange in his mouth.

He didn’t explain. He didn’t tell her the gun had been empty or that he would never have fired. Both were true, and both were worthless.

“Do you need anything?”

She hesitated. My medicine.

He glanced at the bag and nodded. “I’ll look at it.”

Tonight.

“Tonight.”

He took the bag down, read the brown bottle’s label again and set it on the table. He didn’t give it to her, but he didn’t put it away either. He stood a moment.

When he left, he didn’t lock the door straight away. She heard him stop outside, and then his footsteps went away.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night he went to the kitchen to check the recordings and found himself in an older folder instead: scanned documents, photographs, and a video from a foundation dinner in the spring before she died, which he had downloaded because Elena’s name was in the file details and had never watched.

The footage was poor. A long table, people talking, a young woman moving through the frame at the far end. He closed it. He didn’t need it to remember her.

He sat in the dark with his hands on the table and touched two fingers to his own chest. He hadn’t used the sign in years, and he had never thought he would make it for someone else. Tonight it didn’t comfort him.

He switched off the kitchen light and, in the dark, made the sign once more. He couldn’t make himself believe it.

chapters.title: Stalling
chapters.desc: Damien learns to look desperate without doing anything. A recording reaches the farmhouse.
chapters.epigraph: “A dead one is worth everything by Christmas.”
chapters.content:
Damien Whitmore had learned that panic was most useful when it belonged to someone else.

He spent the first day after Ryla was taken making calls and the second making arrangements, and by the third he had discovered several ways to look desperate without actually doing anything. He was good at all of them.

On Sunday morning he stood in the study with his phone to his ear, watching rain gather on the windows.

“No. I understand what the bank is telling me. I’m asking whether there’s a way around it. Then find one. Forty million isn’t an extraordinary amount for a group this size. Don’t tell me what compliance will allow. Tell me what you can do.” He listened, and his jaw tightened.

He hung up, stared at the phone, and dialled again.

That call was shorter. “The funds are temporarily inaccessible. We’re dealing with a security review. Yes, I know the timing is unfortunate. No, I can’t give you a date.”

A photograph of Ryla stood on the desk beside a silver letter opener, taken last summer: a pale blue dress, her hair tied back, her hands in her lap. She looked younger in it, or less tired. He picked it up.

He had told the kidnapper she was his beloved little sister. He had meant it to sound sincere. He hadn’t expected the man to hang up on him, and he hadn’t expected to hear his own voice crack.

That bothered him most. He put the photograph down and called his lawyer.

✦ ✦ ✦

The kidnapping hadn’t reached the papers. At the FBI’s request, the press had been told that Miss Whitmore had been moved to a private facility after her stepmother’s death, and the press, which had a great deal else to write about the Whitmores that week, had believed it.

By Monday the police had three leads. A local man had seen a dark car outside an abandoned farm near the Massachusetts line; it was vague, but specific enough to tie up two officers and a search team for an afternoon.

A witness at a private airfield had seen a wheelchair loaded into a van, and turned out to have the wrong day and the wrong van.

And a former estate worker, dismissed after a row with Victoria, had a record of petty theft and money trouble; he was questioned for six hours before the police established he had been in another state that night.

Damien had supplied all three. He didn’t invent every detail. He just made sure the police found the wrong ones first.

✦ ✦ ✦

Detective Calder called him late on Monday afternoon.

“Mr. Whitmore. We’ve been following up on the information you gave us.”

“Have you found anything?”

“Not yet.”

“I’m sure you will.”

A pause. Her voice stayed polite. “I’d like to go through the timeline of your sister’s disappearance again.”

“Of course. Whatever you need.”

“Where were you between nine and ten on Thursday evening?”

“At home.”

“Can anyone confirm that?”

“Several people. The house was full.”

“Mrs. Pell?”

“Yes.”

“And the security staff?”

“Naturally.”

Calder waited. Damien moved to the window. “Is there a reason you’re asking me these questions again?”

“Your sister vanished from a house with heavy security, during a power cut, at your mother’s wake.”

“Which is exactly why I want her found.”

“I understand,” she said, in a voice that suggested she didn’t.

“There’s another matter.”

He closed his eyes for a second. “Go on.”

“The statement attributed to your mother mentioned a doctoral candidate named Elena Ward. We’ve obtained additional records from Hollis University.”

“Then you should speak to the university.”

“We have.”

“Good.”

“Her academic work appears to be closely connected to the Whitmore fund.”

Damien turned from the window.

“That’s an old matter.”

“Was she involved in the development of the fund’s risk model?”

“She was a research assistant.”

“Was the dissertation you submitted based on her research?”

“No.” It came too fast. Calder let it pass.

“Detective, I appreciate that you’re investigating. But my sister is missing. I would prefer we concentrate on that.”

“We are concentrating on it.”

“Then perhaps we can avoid wasting time on a dead university student.”

There was a silence. When Calder spoke again, she was measured. “Elena Ward’s death is part of an active investigation.”

Damien looked at the photograph on his desk. “Then I wish you luck.” He hung up.

✦ ✦ ✦

The FBI agent came on Tuesday. Special Agent Miriam Foster had driven down from the New Haven field office and asked for a private meeting with Damien, his lawyer and Detective Calder.

She was courteous, direct and hard to distract, and Damien disliked her on sight. They met in the small drawing room with the curtains drawn against a grey afternoon.

“Mr. Whitmore, I understand you’ve been in contact with the person who abducted your sister.”

“Yes.”

“How many times?”

“Several.”

“Have you recorded those calls?”

“Some.”

“May we have copies?”

“I’ll need to speak to my lawyer.”

“Of course.”

She waited. Damien glanced at the lawyer beside him. “He’s handling it.”

Agent Foster nodded.

“I’d also like to know whether the caller has provided an account for the ransom payment.”

“Yes.”

“Has the account been verified?”

“My financial team is looking into it.”

“Have they been able to establish the recipient?”

“Not yet.”

“Have you transferred anything?”

“No.”

She made a note. “Why not?”

“Because the banks have frozen everything.”

“All of them?”

“There’s a compliance review.”

“Is that connected to the financial allegations involving the Whitmore fund?”

His eyes sharpened. “I don’t see how that’s relevant.”

“The caller demanded a public confession about your academic work and the fund. If those allegations are connected to the kidnapping, we need to understand how.”

“They aren’t.”

“So the demand is arbitrary?”

“Yes.”

She studied him. “Mr. Whitmore, I know this is difficult. But we need to know what he wants, what resources he has, and what might make him escalate.”

“He’s already escalated.”

“I understand.”

“No, I don’t think you do. My sister is twenty-four. She can’t walk or speak. She’s been taken from her home by a man who has already killed four people, and I am trying to get her back. I don’t need another person explaining to me how serious this is.” The lawyer touched his arm, a small warning, and Damien shook it off.

Foster closed her notebook. “I’m not questioning your concern.”

“Then help me.”

“We’re trying to.”

“With respect, I haven’t seen much sign of it.”

She stood. “If the caller contacts you again, don’t negotiate without telling us. No transfers. No meetings. And please don’t feed us information you know to be wrong.” For the first time she stopped sounding merely polite.

Damien held her gaze. “I would never do that.”

“Good.” She nodded once and left.

When the door had closed, Damien said, “Get her away from Calder.”

“She’s federal. Don’t make an enemy of her,” the lawyer said.

Damien laughed shortly. “I don’t need another person telling me what not to do.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening Damien poured two glasses of Scotch. Simon Hargreaves had been the family’s lawyer for eleven years. He had handled the group’s acquisitions, Victoria’s private affairs and several deals that never reached the papers.

Edward had kept his will with Walter Greaves, which Simon had never quite forgiven. He didn’t frighten easily, and he didn’t mistake loyalty for affection.

“You’re making this harder than it needs to be. You’re giving the police too much to chase,” he said, taking the glass.

“They need to believe I’m helping.”

“They need to believe you’re frightened. You can manage that without sending them round every abandoned barn in Connecticut.”

“One of those leads might have been real.”

“It wasn’t.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I know you.”

Damien put his glass down. Rain tapped on the windows. The study had become an unpleasant room.

Victoria’s letters were still on the desk, the shelves still held the books Edward had collected before Damien was old enough to know what they meant, and the place seemed to have soaked up every death of the last month.

He looked at the empty chair by the fire. “He’s going to kill her.”

“Possibly.”

“Then we need to make him think he has a reason not to.”

“Which is why you should stop provoking him.”

Damien laughed without humour.

“He’s asking for forty million dollars and a public confession. Do you understand what happens if I give him the confession?”

“Yes.”

“The fund collapses.”

“It may.”

“My position becomes indefensible.”

“Yes.”

“My dissertation—”

“Damien.”

Simon waited until he looked at him.

“Your dissertation is not the immediate problem.”

Damien stared at him.

Simon sipped his Scotch. “The immediate problem is Ryla.”

Damien looked almost offended. “Of course I know that.”

“Do you?”

Damien got up and went to the desk, turned a pen in his fingers, put it down. “She’s my sister.”

“Yes.”

“Don’t look at me like that.”

“I’m not looking at you in any particular way. I’m thinking we need to be realistic.”

Damien sat down again, and Simon leaned forward. “Edward’s will is the problem. She turns twenty-five on the twenty-first of December.”

“I know when her birthday is.”

“Then you know what happens.”

Seventy per cent, the voting rights, the control Edward had put beyond Victoria’s reach and so beyond Damien’s.

For years he had treated it as an inconvenience that would sort itself out. Ryla had never shown any interest in the business, never asked for a board seat or the accounts.

She stayed in her rooms with her books and her little routines.

But she had to reach twenty-five, and once she did, she could appoint people, open up the fund, make the decisions Damien had spent years making sure nobody else could. She could leave the money to someone who wasn’t a Whitmore.

“She’s not going to do anything with it,” Damien said.

“That isn’t the point.”

“She doesn’t understand the business.”

“She may understand more than you think.”

Damien’s eyes narrowed. Simon continued.

“Her father wanted her to have control. He made that very clear.”

“Her father is dead.”

“His will isn’t.”

Damien looked into his glass and turned it slowly, so the ice shifted.

Then he said, “A missing girl is worth nothing for seven years.”

Simon said nothing.

“A dead one is worth everything by Christmas. Keep pushing him. If he loses his temper, he does our work by the twentieth.” Damien leaned forward.

The words sat between them. Simon put his glass down. “You’re talking about a young woman who is already in the hands of a murderer.”

“I’m talking about the only outcome that protects this family.”

“Your mother is dead.”

“Exactly.”

Simon held his eyes. “Be careful.”

Damien smiled, and it wasn’t the gala smile. “That’s what everyone keeps telling me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Two hours north, the farmhouse kitchen was cold, as it always was. Keaton was typing when the receiver connected to his laptop clicked into life: a hiss through the speakers, a chair moving, then Damien’s voice. He stopped typing. He knew that room.

He had put the bug under the study desk in October, during one of his first review meetings, small enough to vanish among the cables, and tested it twice before he left the estate. He hadn’t needed it often. He turned up the volume. Simon spoke first.

“The immediate problem is Ryla.”

Keaton glanced at the doorway. Ryla was in the next room with a book he doubted she was reading. Over the past few days she had grown sharp to every sound; she knew his footsteps from across the hall. He had left her door open.

The recording went on: the trust, the birthday, the twentieth. Keaton didn’t move. Then Damien said it.

“A missing girl is worth nothing for seven years. A dead one is worth everything by Christmas. Keep pushing him. If he loses his temper, he does our work by the twentieth.”

There was only the hum of the laptop. Keaton played the last few seconds again, twice. The calendar by the desk said the twenty-fourth of November: twenty-seven days to her birthday, twenty-six to the twentieth.

He had known about the trust. He had read the will and understood what Ryla’s death was worth before he took her. What he hadn’t known was how closely Damien was counting. He had assumed the family wanted her back and would pay to get her.

It was worse than that. They wanted the problem solved, and they were happy to let him believe he was the one in control.

Ryla was in the doorway. He could tell from her face that she had heard enough. Her eyes were dry and fixed on the laptop, though not really on the recording; she had heard Damien’s voice, and the word dead, and the date. Keaton stopped the playback. Play it again.

“Are you sure?”

She nodded. He played it. Damien’s voice filled the kitchen, then the lawyer’s, then Damien’s again. If he loses his temper, he does our work by the twentieth.

When it ended, Ryla stayed still with her fingers curled loosely on the armrests. She didn’t wipe her eyes or look away. She nodded once, small and deliberate, as though someone had finally answered a question she had carried for years.

Keaton lowered the screen. “Ryla.”

The twentieth. Before my birthday.

“Yes.”

If I die before then, they get the money.

“That’s what they’re counting on.”

She nodded. There were no tears and no shock, only an understanding that seemed to settle into her body with terrible precision.

I thought they were waiting for me to get better. Her fingers hung in the air. They were waiting for me to die.

Something cold moved through his chest. He had heard it from Damien and understood it, but hearing her say it made it different. He went towards her, and she didn’t flinch, though her eyes followed him.

“Your brother doesn’t get to decide that.”

You don’t either.

He stopped. There was no accusation in her face, which was worse. She had said something true. It took him a moment to answer. “No.”

Ryla lowered her hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night he copied the recording to an encrypted drive and made a second copy somewhere else. It was clear, Damien was clear, and what mattered about the lawyer wasn’t what he said but that he hadn’t argued.

Keaton sat at the table until the screen dimmed. He had spent months arranging the order of deaths. He had thought of himself as the one who had put time back into the story: over a year of waiting, four names, one reckoning.

But the Whitmores had been counting too, towards the same date, and they had no intention of letting Ryla reach it.

Her door was open, and a small lamp lit the edge of the bed. She was awake in her chair beside the blank wall, looking at her hands.

He stood in the doorway. “Do you want the light off?”

No. He stayed where he was. After a moment she lifted her hands again. You heard him.

“Yes.”

You believe him.

“Yes.”

So now you know he won’t come for me. His face tightened. He’ll wait.

She didn’t need to explain. The forty million, the confession, the fake leads, the careful performance of a desperate brother: he had thought Damien was stalling to save his money.

Damien was stalling so that the killer would lose patience and finish the family’s problem for it. Ryla had understood that before he did. Maybe long before.

He stepped into the room. “I’m not going to let him have what he wants.”

She didn’t nod this time. You already gave him what he wanted once. You made me afraid to close my eyes.

He had no defence. “I know.”

He went back to the kitchen and shut the laptop. The words stayed. Twenty-six days. He had taken her to use against a family that, it turned out, had never meant to bring its youngest daughter home.

chapters.title: Bridgeport
chapters.desc: A torch, a bedtime story told with hands, an airport, and nineteen years of Sundays.
chapters.content:
The first stories Keaton ever understood, as a boy in Bridgeport, Connecticut, were told with hands.

His mother sat on the edge of his mattress with a torch balanced beneath her chin, casting an unsteady circle of light against the bedroom wall. The electricity had been cut off again.

Ruth Ward couldn’t hear any of it, and she didn’t look round. She had a book open on her lap, though the words didn’t matter; she had stopped pretending to read years ago.

She signed the stories instead and made the characters move through the dark with her fingers. A fox crept under a fence.

Ruth gave each of them a face: eyebrows up for the fox’s suspicion, a solemn mouth for the king, and when the little girl got frightened, both hands close to her chest, trembling.

It was a story about a bird that had lost its way home, and by the end Elena was asleep. Keaton wasn’t, and Ruth saw it. She moved the torch away and signed in the dark, slower now. What is it? He hesitated. Is Dad coming home?

In the morning there was a notice from the electricity company under the front door. By the end of the week there would be another. There were always more.

✦ ✦ ✦

Thomas Ward had once been a clever man. Keaton remembered that much.

It started with a business: a small contracting firm, a partner who vanished, a loan secured on a house already worth less than the debt.

✦ ✦ ✦

The professor came into their lives at a state mathematics competition. A teacher had made Keaton enter. He had no proper shoes, so Ruth cleaned his school ones with a damp cloth and polished them until they looked almost new. Thomas promised to come and didn’t. Keaton won.

Professor Alastair Vance taught economics, had no children, a house in Edinburgh and a particular interest in the mathematics of financial systems.

“Mathematics.”

“Why?”

Keaton thought about it. “Because numbers don’t change their minds.”

The professor looked at him and smiled. The smile of a man who had found something valuable.

Two weeks later he came to the house. Thomas let him in. Ruth sat at the kitchen table with her hands folded, and Elena stood beside her, watching the stranger’s mouth.

At the second meeting the professor brought an interpreter and explained everything carefully. He had no children. He wanted to give Keaton a home, pay for his education and open doors Bridgeport never would.

Ruth asked whether Keaton could come back. Yes. Whether he could see his sister. Yes, again. Whether he could keep his name.

He heard her from the hall and stood there gripping the suitcase handle. He had seen her frightened and angry and exhausted, and laughing until her shoulders shook, but he had never seen her cry. She kept her grief quiet, like another household expense she couldn’t afford to put on them.

He went back into the kitchen. She looked up, and neither of them moved. Then she crossed the room and held his face in her cold hands. You aren’t leaving because we don’t want you. He swallowed. I know.

You aren’t leaving because you are too much trouble. I know. Her hands were shaking. You are leaving because you have a chance.

✦ ✦ ✦

Thomas wasn’t there. Keaton hadn’t expected him. He had expected Elena.

Now she stood behind the glass with their mother, holding a paper bag of biscuits she had insisted on buying with her own coins, though he had told her he would eat on the plane.

He put his hand up to the glass, and she came closer and lifted both hands in a sign she had invented herself, back when she was too young to know that other people didn’t talk with their hands. Come back. He pressed his palm to the glass. I will.

She shook her head, eyes filling, and made it again. Come back. I will.

Elena put her hand on the glass opposite his. Their fingers didn’t touch. Ruth stood behind her with a hand on her shoulder. She didn’t tell him to be brave, and she didn’t tell him to go. She held his eyes and signed. I love you. He signed it back.

Elena kept her hand up, and her mouth moved. He couldn’t hear her, but he knew what she was saying. The glass stayed between them until he turned the corner.

✦ ✦ ✦

Edinburgh was cold. The professor’s house was big, orderly and quiet, with books in every room, floors that didn’t creak, a full fridge and electricity that never went off.

The calls started on his first Sunday. Elena was five years younger and already able to make any conversation about herself. She showed him drawings, missing teeth, biscuits their mother had baked, new curtains, the neighbour’s dog, a school project on the solar system.

Ruth died the winter Elena turned sixteen. He flew back for the funeral and stood at the back of a small chapel while Elena signed the eulogy to a room that couldn’t understand it.

Thomas outlived his wife by two years and most of a bottle a day. After that there was nobody else. There were only the Sundays, and he arranged everything else in his life around them.

✦ ✦ ✦

The last call began with laughter. Elena appeared in a dark sweater with her hair tied back loosely, tired but bright-eyed.

Now she was smiling at him in a way he had never seen, and he noticed at once. What? She shook her head. Nothing. That’s not a nothing face.

She looked away. He waited, and she sighed and lifted her hands. I’m seeing someone. Keaton’s eyebrows rose. Someone? Don’t. I haven’t said anything. Your face has. He smiled. Who?

She hesitated, and that was the first thing that made him uneasy. Elena told him everything, including things she should probably have kept to herself. Embarrassed, she laughed; frightened, she joked. Now she was choosing her words. His name is Damien. Damien Whitmore.

He knew the name. Whitmore Group was a big investment and property group that had recently expanded into private funds, and his firm had been asked to look at parts of its structure for a lender. He had seen the name in reports. He had never met Damien. How long? She smiled.

Properly? Almost a year. We’ve worked together since my first year. Keaton stared at her. Almost a year? She laughed. I knew you’d do that.

He’s clever. Really clever. He understands the work. He doesn’t treat me like I’m hard to understand. What does he do?

He works with his family’s investment group. He’s involved in a new fund. And you’re involved? She hesitated. I’m helping. His eyes narrowed slightly. Helping how? With the model.

He knew what that word meant when Elena used it. How much are you doing? Keaton. I’m asking. It’s complicated. Then explain it. She rolled her eyes, still fond.

I’m building a risk model for the fund. It started as research. Damien thought it could be useful, and we’ve been developing it together. Together? Yes.

You don’t have to work for someone to make him love you. She shook her head. That’s not what this is. Then what is it? She looked down, smiling to herself. We’re partners.

He didn’t like the word. It wasn’t wrong in itself, but he couldn’t tell whether she was describing the relationship or defending it. Does he make you happy? Yes.

I told him you left when we were little. That you changed your name. That you work in finance. A small unease settled in his stomach. Why? It came up. We were talking about family. Does he know my name? She hesitated. Not your old one. Elena. You shouldn’t have told him anything. I didn’t tell him everything. She lowered her hands and, looked hurt. She looked hurt.

Then she signed: He’s the person I love. I wanted him to know.

His face softened despite himself. I understand. Do you? He nodded.

I asked him to keep it secret. Just a little longer. She signed again, faster.

It’s not because I’m ashamed. You know that, don’t you?

His firm worked for the banks that lent to companies like theirs. He understood the risk. He also understood that telling her not to trust Damien would only make her defend him, so he chose words that might keep her safe without making her feel judged. Tell him when you’re ready. Elena smiled. Thank you. He raised his hand. I’m here. She answered immediately. I know.

The call ended. Keaton sat at his desk for a few minutes and then went back to work. He didn’t know it was the last time he would see her alive.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next Sunday, she didn’t call. He had finished work early and made coffee, and the laptop was open on the dining table. At six there was nothing. At a quarter past he messaged her. You’re late.

At half past he called, and it rang out. He tried again at seven, and at eight sent another message. Everything all right?

By Monday morning he had called twice more. On Tuesday he rang the university and gave her full name to an administrator who didn’t know him. He said he was her brother. There was a pause, and then she asked him to prove it.

He couldn’t. Elias Ward didn’t exist on any record she could see, and Keaton Vance had no relationship to anyone at Hollis. She was sorry, she said, but she couldn’t give out information about a student to someone who wasn’t family.

The police said the same. So did the department. Every door he tried had someone polite behind it, asking for a document he didn’t have. It was nearly three weeks before a man in student services, worn down by his calls, finally told him off the record.

“I’m sorry, Mr. Vance. Ms. Ward passed away.”

He heard the words one at a time, and they didn’t seem to belong to the same sentence.

“When?”

“Late in August. Nearly three weeks ago.”

He looked at the calendar and counted back. Three Sundays. He had been waiting for three Sundays.

He hung up and stood in the middle of his kitchen. He didn’t remember putting the phone down or sitting.

Just a little longer.

After that he called everyone again, and each of them gave him one small piece, carefully cut off from the rest. Elena had died in Connecticut. There had been an investigation. It had been ruled an accident and closed. No next of kin had been identified.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three days later he found the article, under a university fundraiser and a crash on the interstate. Three paragraphs. A graduate researcher at Hollis had died after an incident at a private estate in Wrenhaven.

The death was believed to be accidental. Elena Ward, twenty-seven, doctoral candidate in applied mathematics. The university sent its condolences. No funeral was listed.

There was a photograph. Elena, smiling, from her first year at Hollis, with shorter hair, a dark sweater and one hand up by her face. He knew it.

He couldn’t make himself believe she had been dead for three weeks. He read the article three times.

The word accident appeared once. The word family didn’t appear at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The cremation record was harder. He made calls and filed requests and paid for searches, and explained over and over why a man in London wanted to know about a woman cremated in Connecticut.

The first person told him there was no next of kin, the second that the costs had been paid, and the third gave him the name of the funeral home.

A woman answered, and when he gave Elena’s name there was a short silence. “Yes. We handled that.”

“Who authorised my sister’s cremation?”

“The arrangements were made on behalf of a generous local family.”

His grip tightened on the phone. “Which family?”

“I’m afraid I can’t disclose that.”

“We were informed that she had no next of kin.”

“She had a brother.”

The woman said nothing.

“She had a brother,” he said again.

“I understand, sir.”

“No. You don’t.”

He heard himself, too loud, and stopped. His hands were shaking. He shut his eyes and tried to breathe.

“Where are her ashes?”

The woman hesitated.

“I believe they were handled according to the standard procedure for unclaimed remains.”

“What does that mean?”

She explained. He didn’t hear all of it, only enough. There was no grave, no funeral, no box of ashes waiting for someone who could prove he had the right to collect it.

There was only a payment from a generous local family. He thanked her, hung up and sat at the kitchen table until the room went dark.

He didn’t cry that day. He cried the next Sunday.

At six he opened the laptop, as always, and the call window came up by itself. He stared at the empty screen. Then he signed, slowly. You’re late. He waited. Elena. Nothing.

He cried with his hands on the keyboard. Because he had missed three Sundays. Because he had sent money the week before she died. Because he had been annoyed that she hadn’t called. Because he had believed anyone could be reached if you knew where to look.

And because the last thing she had asked was for him to stay a secret. He had done exactly what she wanted, and when she died, the world took her without ever knowing there was someone who would have come.

✦ ✦ ✦

The year that followed didn’t begin with revenge. It began with paperwork.

Whitmore. He found the foundation, the investment group, the university ties, and the people photographed with Elena: Damien, Victoria, Marcus, Preston, Dr. Albright.

He found the dissertation, and the work she had described on their last call, and a version of her risk model inside the fund’s internal documents. Her name wasn’t in any of the public material. Damien’s was.

Not because he trusted the institution, but because he knew how institutions worked. He knew what a bank could demand from a borrower it suspected of lying about its finances, and what an audit could dig out from under layers of legitimate business.

Whitmore Group had lenders, the lenders had obligations, and a review done properly could open doors a grieving brother couldn’t. He made himself useful, and he waited.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first time he saw Ryla Whitmore, he didn’t know what to make of her.

Her photograph came up in a foundation presentation he was reviewing: Edward Whitmore’s youngest daughter, a former dancer, a catastrophic accident, a wheelchair. The slide called her an inspiration. He looked at it a long time.

He asked for financial records, correspondence, internal reports and access to the people who ran the fund, and the bank approved it, and the Whitmores welcomed him: a quiet forensic accountant from London with a good education, a clean record and no connection to the family.

✦ ✦ ✦

The list took shape on a winter evening, with the documents spread across his dining table, sorted by date, then by payment, then by name.

Preston had brought her to the boathouse and filmed it. Marcus had arranged the cover-up, and burning her notebooks had been his idea. Albright had falsified the post-mortem.

Victoria had ordered the cover-up and written the message sent from Elena’s phone that night, the one that made her sound unstable. Damien had held her under the water.

There were other names in the records, people who had looked away or signed forms or taken money, but these five had made it happen.

He thought of her last call. We’re partners. The way she smiled when she said Damien made her happy. Her asking him to stay secret a little longer. Her hand on the glass at the airport.

He put a blank sheet in the middle of the table and wrote at the top:

PRESTON WHITMORE.

Under it, what Preston had done. Then the rest.

MARCUS WHITMORE.

HENRY ALBRIGHT.

VICTORIA WHITMORE.

DAMIEN WHITMORE.

He stopped at that name. He didn’t doubt it. It was only the one he couldn’t look at without remembering the water. Then, at the bottom, he wrote a sixth.

RYLA WHITMORE?

He didn’t know what she was, a witness or one of them. She had lived in that house and been at that dinner, and she was the one thing every other name on the page wanted.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the farmhouse, Ryla shifted in her sleep, and Keaton looked up from the laptop.

The old memory and the present sat in the same room: a small girl behind glass, a young woman in a wheelchair, two pairs of hands on either side of something neither could cross.

Damien’s recording was still saved on the screen. He closed it and opened the list. Six lines. Four boxes marked. Damien’s still empty, and under it a name with a question mark that he couldn’t look at any more.

He had thought the list was the shape of justice. Now there was a woman in the next room who had asked him not to decide her life for her, and a man in Wrenhaven who wanted him to end it.

From the next room came the faint sound of the chair shifting. He got up and went to check on her.

chapters.title: Fever
chapters.desc: Days without the tonic. Ryla’s body turns on her, and Keaton finally reads the label properly.
chapters.content:
The first sign was the trembling. Keaton saw it on Tuesday morning when Ryla reached for the water by her bed. Her fingers closed on the glass, but it rattled against the edge of the table and slopped over her knuckles.

She stopped and stared at her hand as if it belonged to someone else, then tried again, and the tremor was worse. He crossed the room from the door and took the glass.

“Let me. I’m not taking it away.”

Her face said she hadn’t thought he was. He held it while she drank through the straw, and after a few sips she turned her head aside.

“Have you felt like this since you woke up?”

A little.

“How long is a little?”

Since yesterday. He looked more closely. There were shadows under her eyes, her colour had gone, and the small shifts she made in the chair seemed to cost her more than they should.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

Ryla raised her eyebrows, and he understood. She had told him plenty. He hadn’t always listened. He crouched by her chair. “All right. That’s fair.”

The corner of her mouth lifted for a second, and then she closed her eyes. He had spent half the night on Damien’s recording, counting the days to the twentieth, and he told himself his unease was only tiredness. He was wrong.

✦ ✦ ✦

By noon she was shaking hard enough that he could hear her teeth. He thought at first it was the cold; the heating was temperamental, and the night had been colder. He brought another blanket, and when she tried to help him tuck it, her fingers wouldn’t work. “Don’t. Just let me.” He checked the thermostat. The room was warm. He turned it up anyway.

When he came back, she had both hands pressed to her stomach and her shoulders hunched. He crouched. “Where does it hurt?”

Everywhere.

“Your head? Your back? Your arms?” She nodded to both.

She closed her eyes.

He reached for her hand, and the muscles in her forearm felt rigid. When she flinched, he let go. “Sorry.”

She swallowed and signed with visible effort. It hurts inside.

“Inside where?”

She pressed a hand to her chest and slid it down towards her stomach. Everywhere inside.

He found the thermometer in the medical supplies, and she let him put it under her tongue, her eyes following him while they waited.

Thirty-eight point nine. He had lived in Britain too long to think in anything but Celsius. He checked it again and got the same number.

Nothing he had was right for a fever with no known cause: a first-aid kit, basic painkillers, things bought for a situation he had never expected.

He called a doctor: not the family physician, nobody connected to Wrenhaven, but a private medical service he had used during the investigation. He described the symptoms without names.

The doctor asked how long they had been present.

“Since yesterday, possibly earlier.”

“Any known medical conditions?”

Keaton glanced at Ryla. “She’s been disabled for five years. Limited mobility, no speech. I don’t know the original diagnosis.”

“Medication?”

“She was taking a prescribed tonic. She hasn’t had it since Thursday.”

“Why not?”

“It was in her bag. I didn’t know what it was.”

A longer silence. “Can you describe it?”

Keaton read him the label.

“Bring her in.”

“I can’t.”

“Then you need to arrange for someone to assess her. Fever, tremors and worsening pain in a patient with a complicated medical history are not something you should manage alone.”

“I understand.”

“Then keep her under observation and get medical help as soon as possible. If she becomes confused, has difficulty breathing, loses consciousness or develops a seizure, call emergency services immediately.”

Keaton thanked him and hung up. The medical bag was still under the table where he had left it. He hadn’t thought about it since the night he took her.

✦ ✦ ✦

By evening the fever had risen, and she couldn’t sit up without support.

He carried her across the hall to the bedroom with the window, the one he had been using, because the cold room was no place to be ill. She tried to help, and it made her gasp.

“Stop helping. I know you don’t like being handled. But you’ll hurt yourself if you keep trying to do everything.” She gave him an irritated look.

I can still do things.

He stopped and looked at her. Then he nodded. “I know.”

He laid a damp cloth across her forehead. Her skin was clammy. Thirty-nine point four.

For the next hour he kept the cloth cool, gave her sips of water and watched her breathe. She slept in short stretches, and every time she woke her hands went to the blanket or her chest, looking for a position that didn’t hurt.

Once she woke with a sharp breath. She tried to sign, and her fingers jerked, and she stopped, frustrated.

“Slowly.”

She swallowed and tried again. Burning.

“Where?”

She pressed both hands to her legs, then her arms, then her chest. His stomach turned.

“Is it the same pain?”

She shook her head, and her eyes filled. Worse. He sat back.

Nothing in the medical bag or the first-aid kit or the little she had told him explained this.

He had spent months finding patterns hidden under ordinary transactions, and he could spot an irregularity when the figures looked reasonable. He had no idea what was happening to the woman in front of him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second night was worse. She didn’t sleep. She drifted towards unconsciousness and jerked awake with a tremor that ran through her whole body, and her breathing went shallow whenever the pain climbed.

Sweat soaked her hair and the collar of her nightshirt. He changed the cloth, the pillowcase, and her shirt when it was wet through, and each time she apologised with her hands, and he ignored it.

At one point she tried to push herself up. “Don’t. Ryla.”

Her eyes flashed. She signed: I can’t lie like this.

“You’re ill.”

I know.

“Then stop fighting me.”

Her hands moved sharply. I’m not fighting you. She was shaking so hard the sign was barely readable. I’m trying not to hurt.

At three in the morning she began to cry. Not the silent, controlled tears he had seen before. Her face twisted, and a broken sound came out of her that wasn’t a word, because her throat couldn’t make one. Her back arched.

He was on his feet. “Ryla? Look at me. Ryla, look at me.” He held her shoulders to stop her sliding sideways.

Her eyes opened, wet and unfocused, and he felt a sudden irrational fear that she would stop breathing. “Stay with me. I know. I know it hurts.”

Her hands searched the sheet, and he caught one, and she gripped his fingers with surprising strength. He held on while it passed. It took several minutes, and when her body finally let go, she was spent.

He could have said he had seen worse, or that it didn’t matter, or that she was safe. “I’m sorry,” he said instead. She didn’t answer, and he sat with her until she fell asleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday morning he went looking for the tonic. Not because he was sure it was to blame, but because it was the only thing that had changed.

She had taken it every night at the estate and not once since he took her, and the timing was too exact to ignore.

The brown vials were in a small compartment of her medical bag, wrapped in a cloth.

NERVE SUPPORT · Rx 0417 · H.A.

On the back, a narrow printed strip: a pharmacy code, a dosage, and the prescribing physician. Dr. Henry Albright.

Keaton stared at the name. He remembered the doctor’s bag from the clinic and the vials in it, and Albright’s bloodless face as he tried to bargain.

There’s someone alive in that house who— He had been so fixed on the confession that he had heard the rest as a final trick and thrown it away.

He took Albright’s bag out of the locked cupboard. Nothing in it had been touched since that night: instruments, paperwork, sealed packets, and several small brown vials. Same label, same code, same prescriber. He set one of each side by side on the table.

Keaton placed the two vials side by side on the table.

It hadn’t occurred to him that they might be keeping her ill on purpose.

Through the doorway, Ryla was asleep, breathing unevenly. He picked up the vials.

✦ ✦ ✦

The laboratory didn’t advertise. He had used it twice before, once for a fraud case involving counterfeit medicines and once for a substance from a warehouse. It didn’t ask why a client wanted something tested. It asked for payment, identification and a clear description of the work. He called before noon.

“I need a comparison of two prescription preparations.”

He paid, photographed both labels and recorded the batch numbers, and sent the package by courier.

✦ ✦ ✦

By late afternoon her fever was forty, and he stopped pretending he could manage alone. He called the medical service again and gave them his location.

They could send a clinician, they said, but if she got worse he should call an ambulance. Her eyes were open, but she wasn’t tracking him properly.

“Can you hear me? Ryla? Do you know where you are?” Her eyes found his face, and he knelt.

Your horrible house.

He let out a breath he hadn’t known he was holding. “Good.”

When she opened her eyes again, there was fear in them. Not the old fear of being held against her will. Something more immediate, that her body no longer let her hide.

He sat on the end of the bed. “You’re going to get through this.”

She stared at him, and he said it again. Don’t lie.

He nodded. “All right. I won’t.” And he stayed.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she woke screaming without a voice. Her body went rigid so the blanket slid off her legs. Her hands clenched, her shoulders pulled back, and her head pressed into the pillow. He was beside her in seconds. Her eyes were open but couldn’t settle. He moved the pillow behind her. “Ryla. Look at me.” She found his face, and her fingers made a frantic movement towards her chest and arms that wasn’t even a whole sign. He understood only that she was frightened.

He took her hand. “You’re in the farmhouse. You’re in bed. I’m here.”

She shook her head.

“Tell me.”

Make it stop.

He had no answer. He had brought her here and taken away the medicine she had been given for years. He had assumed she would tell him if she needed it, and that a woman who couldn’t walk or speak had been badly cared for. He had never asked what happened when she missed a dose, or what the tonic was for, or why someone who barely slept seemed so afraid of bedtime.

✦ ✦ ✦

The clinician arrived after midnight: a middle-aged woman with a tired face and a medical bag who introduced herself as Dr. Sethi and went straight to Ryla. Keaton had given the service a name that wasn’t his. If Dr. Sethi recognised the face from a foundation brochure, she didn’t say so; the service’s clients paid a great deal not to be recognised. She took temperature, pulse and blood pressure and asked for a history, and he gave her what he knew, which was little.

“How long has she been taking this medication?”

“At least several months. Possibly years.”

Dr. Sethi looked up, and he met her eyes. “I stopped it when I took her.”

Dr. Sethi went back to the bed and spoke to Ryla directly, slowly and clearly, explaining each step before she did it. When she touched Ryla’s wrist, Ryla flinched, and she stopped. “Does that hurt?”

Ryla lifted a hand, weak but deliberate. Yes.

“All right. I’ll be careful.”

When she had finished, she turned to Keaton. “She needs a hospital.”

“I can’t take her to a hospital.”

“Then understand that you’re taking a serious risk by keeping her here.”

Keaton said nothing.

She wrote down what to watch for and left. Keaton stood in the hallway with the paper in his hand. He had spent years studying what people did when they thought nobody was watching.

✦ ✦ ✦

The lab called on Thursday morning while he was filling a water glass in the kitchen.

“We’ve completed the preliminary analysis.”

“Tell me.”

“There’s an active pharmaceutical compound in both samples, and it isn’t what the label says.”

“What is it?”

The analyst named it, and Keaton didn’t know the name. “Is it a nerve medication?”

“Not in the way the label suggests. We need the quantitative work before we give you a full report. There are signs of a sedative effect, but I don’t want to overstate it.”

Keaton closed his eyes.

“We’ve also found an additional substance in one sample. We’re working on it now. Another twenty-four to forty-eight hours.”

He thanked the analyst and stood a long time with the phone in his hand.

Then he looked the compound up and read the clinical information, the warnings, the effects of long-term use. He didn’t understand all of it, but he understood enough.

Sedation, poor coordination, physical dependence, and severe symptoms if it was stopped. The prescription had been renewed regularly. The dose had gone up. The label had never changed.

The doctor had known. He had known what she was taking and that she couldn’t just be cut off, and he had tried to tell Keaton.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ryla was awake when he went back, propped a little higher on the pillows, her hair damp and her face pale. She drank a little water and watched him put the glass down.

“I found something.” He held up one of the vials.

This is what you were taking? Every night. Sometimes twice.

His hand went still. “Twice?”

When it was bad.

“What was bad?”

She seemed puzzled by the question. My nerves. My legs. Sleep. They said it helped.

“Who did?”

Dr. Albright. He said it was for the pain.

“Did you ever miss a dose?”

She thought about it, and nodded. Sometimes. I couldn’t sleep. I shook. Everything hurt.

His throat tightened. “When?”

Years ago.

He sat down in the chair by the bed. “Did you tell anyone?”

She gave him a look that was almost disbelief, and he understood. Of course she had. She had told the people who were meant to care for her, the doctor and the family, and they had kept giving it to her. Maybe more of it.

“Ryla, I need you to know something. I didn’t know. I thought it was ordinary medicine. I thought stopping it would do no harm.” He signed it too.

I was wrong. She looked away, and her fingers moved on the blanket. I know. It hurt more than anger would have.

He set the vial on the bedside table. “I’m going to get you help.”

I won’t stop your medication again without a doctor. She studied him. You should have asked.

“Yes.”

You should have listened.

“Yes.”

She closed her eyes, and he sat beside her, unable to find any sentence that would make it better.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, while she slept, he laid everything out on the kitchen table: both vials, the lab receipt, Dr. Sethi’s notes, the transcript from Albright’s clinic.

He thought of the neat bedroom at the estate and the measured tonic, Victoria at the bedside with the bottle, Albright saying it would help her sleep, Mrs. Pell bringing it when Victoria was busy.

Laboratory: Final report pending. Additional compound detected. Further identification underway.

He went to the bedroom door. She was asleep with one hand outside the blanket, the fingers still a little curled. He had spent over a year learning how the Whitmores lied and moved money and made a murder look like an accident.

He signed into the dark room, though she couldn’t see it. I’m here.

It didn’t feel like a promise. It felt like a debt.

chapters.title: Two Steps
chapters.desc: At dawn, Ryla puts her feet on the floor.
chapters.content:
At dawn Ryla woke to the sound of her own breathing, small and ordinary. The curtains were drawn against a pale November morning.

The heating had gone off in the night, the air had the cold, dry smell of an old house, and somewhere a pipe clicked in the wall.

For the first time in days the pain had pulled back far enough that she could tell one part of her body from another.

Her head still ached, her muscles felt bruised from the inside, her hands were weak and her legs had a strange, faraway heaviness. But the fever had broken, and the sheets weren’t soaked any more. She could think. Even that felt unfamiliar.

The water glass on the bedside table was empty, a folded cloth beside it, and the two brown vials were gone. Keaton had taken them after the laboratory called. He hadn’t given her anything from them.

He had stayed, though. She remembered waking in the night and finding him in the chair by the bed, head tipped back, one hand on the edge of the mattress, as if he had let himself fall asleep by accident.

When she moved, he woke at once and asked whether she needed anything, and when she shook her head, he watched her a moment and sat back. He hadn’t touched her again. It wasn’t forgiveness or trust, but it was something.

She moved her fingers under the blanket and watched them tremble.

For five years she had measured the world by what she could still do: how far she could reach, how long she could hold a cup, how much strength her fingers had left after a sentence, whether her shoulders would let her sit up.

Her legs had become a fact she didn’t question. They were there, they hurt, they didn’t obey. She had stopped asking them to.

Light gathered behind the curtains. She rolled onto her side, which took effort; her stomach tightened and an ache ran down her back, and she waited for it to pass. Then she pushed herself up.

It took several tries, one hand braced on the mattress and the other on the frame, her arms shaking, and when she was finally upright, she stayed there breathing through her nose. The floor was right there. It had never seemed far away.

Her feet were bare under the blanket, and something old stirred. Not a thought, not a decision: a feeling.

A studio, one foot turned out and the other placed behind it, the floor under the ball of her foot, the tiny adjustments of the ankle, and the knowledge that balance wasn’t something you held still but something you kept negotiating. A teacher’s voice.

Don’t look at your feet. Feel the floor.

She swallowed and pushed the blanket aside. The first attempt was ugly. She swung her legs over the edge, and they went clumsily; her right foot caught on the frame, and she had to lift it into place with both hands. The left followed. Her feet touched the floor. Cold. Solid. She stared at them.

The feeling came up slowly, a report sent from a long way off: the boards against her soles, the uneven weight of her legs.

She curled her toes, and there was a faint movement. She did it again, and her right foot answered. Her breath caught.

Her knees were trembling, but they weren’t dead. She put both hands on the mattress and leaned forward, and her body protested at once: a sharp pull through her thighs, her arms shaking, her vision narrowing. She stopped, waited, and tried again.

For five years she had expected nothing from her legs. The doctors had given her explanations, measurements and careful predictions, and her family had given her a wheelchair, a nurse and a vocabulary of pity.

She had made peace with the chair because the alternative was waiting every day for something that might never come. But the floor was under her, and her feet were on it.

She leaned forward again, and her hips lifted a little. The effort shook her arms and nearly sent her back, and then, without thinking, she shifted her weight. Her right foot pressed down, her knee straightened, her left foot followed, and she stood.

It wasn’t graceful, and it wasn’t straight. Her knees were bent, her shoulders hunched, and both hands gripped the mattress so hard her fingers hurt. But she was standing. The room seemed to step back from her. Her legs were shaking, and they were holding her.

A thin, disbelieving breath came out of her. She let go with one hand, and for half a second she balanced on her own before she grabbed the mattress again. The dancer in her remembered the floor before the rest of her understood what was happening.

She shifted her weight, and one foot moved forward. A small step, heel, then sole, then toes. She caught the bed frame. Her mouth opened, and no sound came. She moved the other foot. A second step.

The room tilted. Her knees gave, she reached for the mattress and missed, and she went down, hip first and then shoulder, pain flashing through her side. She lay there without breath, unable to move. For several seconds, she couldn’t move.

Then she looked down. Her legs were stretched out in front of her, the right foot turned out a little, the left knee bent. They looked like her legs, not a memory of them or something from an old video. Hers.

She touched her thigh. It trembled under her fingers, and when she pressed harder there was resistance. Muscle.

Her eyes filled. She tried to move her foot, and it shifted, a small, uncertain movement. She stared at it, and then she began to cry. Not because it hurt. Because it had moved.

✦ ✦ ✦

Keaton heard the fall from the kitchen: a heavy thud, then something scraping across the floor. He was moving before he had put down his cup.

“Ryla?”

No answer. The bedroom door was open. He saw the empty bed first, blanket thrown back, pillow on the floor, the wheelchair by the window. Then he saw her on the floor several feet from the bed, one hand braced on the boards, legs stretched out, face wet.

For one disorienting second he couldn’t make sense of it. Then the simplest explanation arrived: she had tried to get away and had fallen. His mind ran ahead of his eyes.

The door was open, she was near it, the chair had been left behind, she had been getting stronger, and he had been distracted by the lab report and the doctor and his own mistake. He crossed the room.

She looked up, and he caught her under the arms. “What are you doing?”

Her hands moved at once, frantic, too close to her chest, shaking, and he couldn’t read them. “Stop. Don’t.” She tried again, and he took it for resistance.

He pulled her away from the door. She twisted, and her legs moved, and his grip tightened by instinct. “Ryla, stop fighting me.”

Her eyes went wide. She tried to sign again, and he caught both her wrists. “Enough.” He pressed her arms down against the floor. She struggled under him, not with strength but with panic, hands twisting, her shoulder knocking the boards.

“Stop.”

He wasn’t shouting, which made it worse. He knew that voice, controlled and firm and leaving no room. He had used it on men who lied to him and on people he thought might get away.

Now he was using it on a woman who couldn’t run. Her eyes were locked on his face. She tried to pull one hand free, and he held it down.

“Listen to me.”

She shook her head. Her mouth opened, and at first nothing came. Then something tore its way out of her throat.

“Stop—”

Keaton froze. It was thin and rough at the edges, and unmistakably a human voice.

Ryla stared at him, her lips shaking. “Please—”

He loosened his grip. She tried to pull away, but he still had one wrist.

“I can’t— I can’t—” Her voice broke.

The rest dissolved into a small, frightened gasp. Neither of them moved. The pipe, the clock, the wind at the window all disappeared under the sound of that voice.

For five years she hadn’t said a word or even a whisper, and now, on the floor between the bed and the door, with his hands round her wrists, she had said three. Stop. Please. I can’t.

He let go and moved back so fast his knee hit the bed frame. She pulled her arms to her chest, breathing fast and shallow, her mouth still a little open.

“Ryla,” he said, and she flinched, and he stopped.

He held his hands up, palms open, and knew that didn’t make them harmless. He had pinned her to the floor. He had decided she was escaping before he asked what had happened.

He had treated her panic as defiance, and she had spoken because she was frightened enough to think there was no other way to make him stop.

Red marks were already rising on her wrists where his fingers had been. He moved a hand towards them and stopped.

“I’m sorry.” Her eyes went to his mouth, and he signed it too.

I’m sorry.

He lowered himself to the floor a few feet away. “Can you—”

He didn’t know what he was asking. Whether she could speak again, or move, or forgive him for what he had just done. Every question he could ask would demand something from her. So he stayed where he was.

Ryla looked down at her legs. Her right hand went slowly to her knee, and she tried to straighten it, a small movement, and he saw it.

She moved her foot, and the toes shifted. He looked from her foot to her face, and for the first time he understood.

She hadn’t been trying to escape. She had been trying to stand. He looked at the space between the bed and where she had fallen, then at the wheelchair by the window, then at her legs.

“Ryla...” He could barely hear himself. He lifted his hands.

You stood? She stared at him, then nodded, and her face crumpled. She looked down, and tears dropped onto her nightshirt. Keaton didn’t move. He couldn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was several minutes before she could make herself try again. She was frightened of the pain, and more frightened that she had imagined it.

The two steps were still in her head, but already they felt like someone else’s. Keaton was still on the floor; he had moved further back when she began to shift, giving her room without being asked. He waited. She signed: I stood. He nodded. Two steps.

Something moved round his eyes. “Two?”

She nodded. He looked at her feet and back at her, and neither of them said anything. Neither spoke. May I help you?

She looked at his hands and thought about the way he had grabbed her, his fingers round her wrists, the sound of her own voice. Then she looked at the space between them, and nodded once.

He came slowly and didn’t touch her until she reached towards him, and even then he paused. With one hand behind her back and one under her arm, he helped her sit up, and she winced.

“Stop if it hurts. Yes. I know. Everything hurts.” She gave him a look, and he almost smiled.

He settled her against the bed. “Can you move your foot?”

Her toes shifted. He watched closely. “Again? All right.” She did it again, a faint movement, and he nodded.

Ryla looked at him. Her hands moved. I felt the floor. I remembered how to stand.

There was something terrible in how simple it was. Five years of appointments and explanations and being told what her body could no longer do, and the first sign of change had come when the medicine stopped.

He didn’t want to jump to conclusions or hand her hope that might be taken away again. But he couldn’t look at her legs and pretend he hadn’t seen it.

“Your body may be recovering.” She was watching his face, so he signed it more carefully.

The medicine may have been doing this to you.

Her hands went still. She looked at her knees.

You mean I wasn’t— Her fingers curled. She tried again. I wasn’t supposed to be like this?

Something cold settled under his ribs. He couldn’t answer that yet. “I don’t know.”

“I don’t know how much of it is the medication, or what can recover, or how long it will take. We need a proper assessment. But what you did this morning was real.” She was staring at her legs.

Her eyes filled again. He didn’t reach for her. He let her look.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her voice came back only once more that morning.

Keaton had put a glass of water within her reach and turned away to find a clean cloth, and she watched him.

Her throat felt dry and tight, with an ache along the inside.

She remembered the sound from the floor, from somewhere deep in her chest. Not the voice she had heard in her head for five years. A real one, that other people could hear. He was folding the cloth.

She opened her mouth. “Keaton.”

It was barely audible. His hands stopped, and slowly he turned round. She hadn’t planned to say his name, or anything. It had been there, waiting behind her teeth.

His face was completely unguarded. It wasn’t the careful attention he gave her signing, or the restraint he used when he was trying to understand her. It was shock, and underneath it something painfully close to wonder. He took a step towards her and stopped himself.

“Yes?” His voice had changed.

She swallowed, and it hurt. She tried for something else, and her throat closed, and nothing came. She looked down. He put the cloth aside. He didn’t ask her to say it again or tell her to try. He only nodded.

“I’m here.”

She closed her eyes. She was too tired to answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

By noon she was asleep again, and Keaton sat in the chair by the bed with the lab report open on his laptop.

The final analysis still wasn’t done: questions about the compound, the concentration, the extra substance in one sample. He had asked for a full clinical interpretation and contacted a specialist in medication-induced neurological damage.

He didn’t know what it would show. He did know he couldn’t keep her hidden in a farmhouse and call watching her enough.
