But a hospital meant police questions, the family knowing she was alive, Damien getting the information before Keaton could control it, the FBI agent becoming more than a polite presence. And the twentieth was coming.

She slept with one hand resting on her thigh. He remembered her standing, the first foot and the second, the fall, and then her voice. Stop—please—I can’t— He looked at his own hands.

He had held her down because he thought she was getting away.

She had been on the floor because, for the first time in five years, her body had given her something back, and he had pinned her there and made her use the one thing she hadn’t been able to use in half a decade.

He closed the laptop and went to the window.

The morning had turned into a flat grey afternoon, the fields were wet, and the trees were losing their last leaves.

He thought of Elena and the years she had spent believing that her body, her mind and her work were things she could offer to be loved. He had come to punish the Whitmores for taking her, and he had taken Ryla instead.

A person could be hurt by someone who thought he was protecting her, and made helpless by someone who called it care.

Behind him, Ryla stirred and opened her eyes. Her hand had slipped off her thigh. He didn’t cross the room until she had seen him, and when she had, he waited for her to decide whether she wanted him near.

chapters.title: Speak
chapters.desc: She has a voice again, and he wants to hear it more than he has any right to.
chapters.content:
By evening Ryla had stopped looking at him. He had seen her withdraw before, at the estate, when Victoria talked over her, when Damien touched her shoulder for the cameras, when someone praised her courage as if she had volunteered to be an example. She could make herself smaller without moving.

Her eyes would settle somewhere past whoever was speaking, her hands would lie in her lap, and her face would go so carefully blank that anyone who didn’t know better would call it calm. This was different. This time she had something to hide. Her voice.

She hadn’t tried to speak since the morning, or even to sign. When he asked if she wanted water, she looked at the glass. When he asked if her legs hurt, she looked away.

When he asked if he should call the doctor, she shut her eyes. He gave her room and told himself that was what she needed.

She didn’t touch the dinner he brought at eight. At nine, when he went to check the bruises on her wrists, she pulled her hands under the blanket.

At ten he asked whether she wanted the lamp left on, and got nothing. He stood by the bed watching her breathe.

“Ryla.”

Her eyes stayed on the wall. He signed instead.

Are you frightened of speaking? You don’t have to speak if you don’t want to.

Her fingers didn’t move. He lowered his hands. That should have been enough, and he knew it.

But seeing her silent again brought back something he had spent years refusing to feel. A little girl behind airport glass with her hand up.

A boy who thought leaving was the same as saving someone. A woman who had talked to him through a screen for years until one Sunday she stopped.

He hadn’t been there. He hadn’t heard her last words. He hadn’t known she was dying.

And here was a living person who could speak, who had seen Elena and heard her laugh and remembered the shape of her hands. He wanted to hear her. The want was so huge that it frightened him.

“Look at me.”

She didn’t.

He sat on the edge of the mattress. “Please.”

Her eyes flicked to him. There was no recognition in them now, only wariness. He should have stopped. Instead he reached for her hands, and she pulled them away, and he caught her wrists. “Ryla.”

She struggled, and he pressed her hands down into the mattress. It was quick, instinctive and wrong.

Her eyes widened. He could feel her pulse under his fingers.

“Don’t. Just—” She twisted one wrist, and he held it.

He couldn’t finish. She was looking at him the way she had on the floor that morning. Not angry or defiant. Afraid of what he would do next. He saw it, and still, for one terrible moment, he didn’t let go.

“Say something.”

Her mouth opened, and nothing came.

“Ryla, say something. Anything.”

She shook her head. His grip tightened, and her breathing went ragged.

“Please.”

The word was his, not hers, and he hated the sound of it. “Please. Just—”

He couldn’t bear the silence any more. He wanted to tear through it, through the years taken from her, through the family that had found her silence convenient, through the memory of Elena’s last Sunday call. He wanted something impossible. He wanted to hear what he had missed. And he was making Ryla pay for it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She knew what he wanted, and that was the worst of it. He wanted to hear her voice again and know it had been real, not an accident of fear and a damaged throat. She didn’t understand why.

People had always wanted things from her. Victoria wanted a grateful smile. Damien wanted a sister to sit beside him at dinners and make him look kind.

The doctors wanted cooperation and the physiotherapists wanted effort, and the family wanted her to recover just enough to be presentable and never enough to be inconvenient. Her voice was the one thing nobody had ever asked for.

For five years she had listened to people discuss her body, her future, her money and her care, forgetting she could hear every word. Silence had become somewhere she could go.

Not because she liked it, but because it was the only thing they hadn’t managed to take completely. Now Keaton was trying to take that too.

His hands held her wrists to the mattress, and she could feel her heartbeat in her throat. She tried to sign, and he caught the movement before she finished.

“No.”

That frightened her more than his grip. He looked almost desperate.

“Don’t hide from me.”

She wanted to tell him she wasn’t hiding. That she was terrified, and didn’t know how to use the voice he was demanding. But the words were stuck somewhere under the panic, and her throat closed. She turned her face away.

He let go. The sudden absence of pressure didn’t make her feel safe. She pulled her hands to her chest and curled onto her side, and he moved away from the bed.

He stood with his back to her. Then: “I’m sorry.”

She didn’t answer. When he turned round, the desperation was still in his face, but he seemed to have finally seen what it was doing to him, and to her. He stepped back.

“I won’t touch you.” Slowly, he lifted his hands.

You don’t owe me your voice. Her eyes burned. He lowered his hands.

“I know you can hear me,” he said.

She closed her eyes.

“I know.”

The room went quiet again, and it wasn’t a peaceful quiet.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the kitchen he ran cold water over his hands. The first thing his mind offered him was that he hadn’t hurt her badly: no broken bones, no new injury, nothing lasting.

He stared at his fingers. The sum was obscene. He had spent years building a world where every action had a consequence and every amount could be traced. He knew how to make harm look like an accident, how to make a body vanish from a record, how to turn a woman’s death into a line of expenditure. Now he was measuring his own cruelty by whether it left a mark.

He turned off the tap. In the window he saw his own face, and behind it the boy at thirteen, furious and frightened, standing in an airport with a suitcase and no idea how to keep a promise.

He had told Elena he would come back. He had sent money and called every Sunday and believed it was enough. It hadn’t been.

His phone lay on the counter where he had left it. He picked it up. One new email, from the clinician who had agreed to look at the samples: Preliminary findings expected Sunday morning. Please be available for a call. Do not reintroduce anything until we have spoken. He read it twice. He had no intention of reintroducing anything. He had taken her medicine away, and today he had held her down, and he wasn’t sure which of those the clinician would think worse.

Sunday was the day after tomorrow. He had known it all day without letting himself look at it. For more than a year Sunday had been the hardest day of the week: the hour in the evening when the phone used to ring, and the hour after, when it didn’t. He had filled those hours with work. Files, names, a map of the estate pinned to the wall of a rented flat. Tonight there was nothing to fill them with but a woman down the hall refusing to speak to him, and the knowledge that he had earned it.

He dried his hands and went back.

Ryla was awake, facing the window, her hands folded against her chest. He didn’t go near the bed. He set the chair by the door.

“I won’t ask again tonight.”

She didn’t move. He sat down. The room was dark except for a strip of light under the curtains, and he could see the line of her shoulder under the blanket.

“I was wrong. I thought if you spoke I might understand something. But I was asking you to do it for me. I don’t have the right.” He looked at his hands.

It wasn’t enough, and he knew it. He had taken her out of a house where she was controlled and made himself one more person she had to fear.

He had told himself he was keeping her alive. He hadn’t thought about what it meant to make her feel that her survival depended on pleasing him.

He leaned forward with his elbows on his knees. “I heard you this morning. I heard you say my name. I keep thinking about it.”

She turned her head towards him. He didn’t move.

“I don’t know what I expected, or what I wanted you to say. But I shouldn’t have tried to make you say anything.”

She watched him. Then she slowly brought one hand out from under the blanket. You aren’t them. He waited. But you can hurt me too.

He felt it land. “Yes.”

Her hand dropped. He didn’t defend himself. He didn’t say he had meant well, or that he was grieving, or that he had lost someone. Nothing he could say would stop her wrists aching.

“Yes,” he said again.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had expected him to deny it, to tell her he was different and trying to help and she had misunderstood.

People were good at explaining what they had done to her. Keaton didn’t. He sat by the door.

She had so many questions. Why he had killed the others, why he had chosen her, how he had known Elena, why he looked at her hands.

Whether it was him who had made the sign for breathe. But her throat hurt, and she was tired.

She remembered the first time she had tried to speak after the fall. The rehabilitation wing, a few weeks in, a window full of white sky, Victoria in the chair beside the bed with her coat still on. Ryla had wanted to ask what day it was. What came out wasn’t a word. It was a wet, broken sound, like something being dragged across a floor, and she had watched her stepmother’s face change before it was smoothed back into kindness.

“Don’t strain yourself, darling. There’s no need. We’ll do the talking for now,” Victoria had said.

For now had turned into five years. She had learned that a sound like that made people look away, that a silent girl made them comfortable, and that when they were comfortable they forgot she was in the room. She had hated it, and she had used it. Nobody had ever asked her to give it up. Tonight someone had, with his hands on her wrists, and the old instinct had closed over her like water.

She turned onto her back, and after a while she lifted a hand. He looked up at once. Don’t come closer. Don’t touch me. Stay there.

“All right.”

She lowered her hand. The room stayed dark. A few minutes went by. Then, so she hardly recognised the sound, she spoke.

“Why?”

Keaton went still. Her throat hurt, and she had to swallow before she could go on.

“Why... do you... want... to hear me?” Her voice was weak and hoarse, each syllable scraping the next, and she had to stop. He didn’t prompt her. She tried again.

She couldn’t read his face, and for once that didn’t matter. She had asked, and he answered.

“Because they made sure nobody could.”

She stared at the ceiling. It didn’t quite make sense. It sounded like something he had carried, waiting for somewhere to put it down. She wanted to ask who they were, but she couldn’t.

Not tonight. She closed her eyes. He stayed in the chair, and neither of them slept.

✦ ✦ ✦

Some time after midnight she opened her eyes. He was still by the door, head bowed, hands clasped, his thumbs moving slowly against each other.

He looked exhausted, not in the ordinary way but in a way that had settled into his bones. She wondered whether he had always looked like that. Before the first death. At the gala, watching her hands while everyone else watched her chair.

The mattress creaked when she moved, and he looked up. “Are you in pain?”

She shook her head, and he waited. I don’t know.

“All right.”

She looked at him a moment longer. I’m frightened.

His face changed. “I know.”

Not only of you. Of what happened today. Her throat tightened, and she touched it with two fingers. I don’t know what comes next.

He looked at her. “Neither do I.”

That, at least, felt honest.

He leaned back. “I’ll stay here.”

She nodded once, and he didn’t come any closer. She turned towards the window. Outside there were no cars, no voices, nothing moving in the trees. She didn’t feel safe. But she was no longer alone with the sound of her own voice.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the chair by the door, Keaton listened to her breathing slow without quite settling. He knew the difference now. He had learned it in this house, the way he had once learned the sound of a little girl pretending to be asleep on the other side of a thin wall.

He had wanted her voice tonight because it was the nearest thing left to a voice he would never hear again. That was the truth, and it wasn’t a good one. Ryla hadn’t been put in the world to answer for Elena’s silence, or for his. She had her own, and someone had built it around her on purpose, and he had spent the evening trying to break it open with his hands.

For the first time since he had taken her from the estate, he was afraid of what he might become if he kept confusing the two.

chapters.title: Toxicology
chapters.desc: The laboratory results arrive.
chapters.epigraph: “They let me grieve my own body.”
chapters.content:
The results came on Sunday morning. Keaton had been waiting since the evening before; he checked his phone before sunrise, again while the coffee brewed, and twice during a short call with the clinician who had agreed to review the preliminary findings.

He hadn’t told Ryla. Not to keep anything from her, but because he had learned, late, that information could be one more weapon when it was dropped on someone with no way to prepare.

The email had three attachments, a short covering note and a request that the findings be discussed with a physician in person. He read the report once, then again, and on the third reading he stopped halfway down the second page.

The detected compounds are consistent with prolonged exposure to a compounded preparation capable of producing muscular weakness, altered vocal function and significant central nervous system depression.

He sat still. The report was careful. It didn’t claim to know what had happened to Ryla, or how long, or exactly how much damage, or whether every symptom she had came from the preparation.

But the samples from her bag and the ones from Albright’s contained the same combination. Same preparation, same source. It wasn’t a coincidence or a lab error.

It described three effects. The first was a steady muscular impairment: not destroying the muscle, but stopping it responding normally, so that the body grew heavy and clumsy and ordinary movement took extraordinary effort.

The second was on the voice, leaving it weak and slack and hard to produce, so that speaking felt like forcing sound through a body that had forgotten how.

The third was sedation. Not unconsciousness, but something more useful to anyone who wanted a person awake, compliant and unable to think clearly: a fog, a quiet that could be mistaken for acceptance.

Long exposure could create physical dependence, and stopping could bring on severe withdrawal: tremors, fever, oversensitive nerves and pain.

He closed the report and sat looking at nothing. The second attachment was a short comparison table. Both samples matched. He shut the laptop.

Across the room, Ryla was sitting by the window under a blanket, her hands loose in her lap, watching rain slide down the glass. She had been awake nearly an hour. She hadn’t spoken since the night before, and had barely signed.

He had spent years building a list of the people who took Elena from him, and he had never once asked what had been done to the girl who watched.

He put the printed pages on the table, and she turned her head at the sound of the paper.

“These are the lab results. I want you to read them yourself.”

Her eyes narrowed a little. He waited, and she reached for them. Her hands were steadier than two days ago, though her fingers still shook if she held anything too long.

She squared the paper against the table and began to read, slowly, through a first page that was mostly jargon. At the bottom she paused and looked up.

“They found the same compounds in both samples. The vials from your bag and the ones from Albright’s,” he said.

She went back to the report and turned the page.

There was a diagram of the three effects, with plain words under the lab terms. Muscular impairment. Altered vocal function. Sedation. She read them twice, and her face didn’t change.

He had expected questions, or confusion, or the slow reaction of someone learning that what she believed about her own body might be wrong. Instead she laid the report flat on the table, carefully, and looked at him. How long?

He sat down opposite her. “We can’t tell exactly from these samples. But it fits long exposure. With what you’ve told me about your symptoms and the nightly tonic, it may have been years.”

Her fingers tightened on the edge of the paper. Every night?

“It was made to be taken regularly. Yes.” He understood what she was really asking.

The tonic. The yellow one. The one Victoria gave me.

His jaw tightened. “Yes.”

She seemed not to understand. Not because it was complicated, but because it was so simple.

The woman who stood beside her bed every evening with a glass and a measuring spoon, who called it treatment and told her to be patient, had been giving her something that made her weak.

On the third page there was a paragraph about the voice. Her eyes stopped on it, and she touched her throat.

“Ryla—”

She raised a hand, and he stopped. My voice.

He nodded. “It could have contributed to losing your voice. That doesn’t tell us whether the damage is fully reversible; the specialist will need to see you. But that you’ve started speaking again is a good sign.”

And my legs?

“The same preparation could have caused the weakness, or made it worse. Your body may have been held down for a long time. We need a proper assessment to know what can come back.”

She didn’t answer. Her hands had gone still.

✦ ✦ ✦

Five years. She tried to make the number fit. Five years of waking in a body that felt like someone else’s and being told to accept it.

Of watching other people stand while she waited for someone to move her chair. Of asking for water, for the curtains, for a blanket, for help to the bathroom, and being grateful when anyone remembered to ask if she was comfortable.

She remembered the hospital, the doctors’ careful voices, the physiotherapist telling her to try again, the first time she failed to stand and cried so hard she was sick.

The next appointment, and the next. Victoria beside her bed. You mustn’t give up, darling. The tonic in its small glass, Victoria’s hand holding it, the bitterness, and the heaviness afterwards.

She had thought the heaviness was part of being ill, and the fog was the price of pain relief, and her body was failing her.

And all this time— Her fingers curled, a small, hard movement. There was no sadness in her face now and no tears. Something had gone cold.

She read the words once more. Prolonged exposure. Muscular weakness. Altered vocal function. Sedation. Victoria saying she was doing everything she could. Albright saying recovery needed patience. Waking at night in pain, asking for help, and being told the tonic would settle her.

Being ashamed of her own body, of being lifted, of needing help with the smallest things, of hearing people plan her future in front of her.

And the worst of it: she had believed them. She had believed there was something permanently wrong with her, something that made her hard to love.

She put the report down. They knew.

He nodded. “It looks deliberately compounded. Albright had it in his bag. He was the doctor in charge of your care.”

Victoria knew.

“I believe so.”

She gave it to me. Every night.

“Yes.”

Her lips parted, and he saw her throat move. She looked at the report and then at her hands, and he thought she would cry. Instead she spoke.

“They let me grieve my own body.”

It came slowly, but every word was clear. Her voice was thin and rough from disuse, and there was something in it he had never heard before. Not fear, not pleading. Anger.

“They let me grieve my own body.”

Louder this time. Her throat caught on the last word, and she pressed a hand to it and breathed through it.

He leaned forward without thinking. “Don’t force it.”

She looked at him sharply, and he stopped. She didn’t need him to tell her when to stop. She looked down at the report, and then she laughed, a small, broken sound with no amusement in it.

“Five years. Five years.” Her voice cracked, and she swallowed.

Under the table, his hands were fists.

“They watched me try. They watched me try to stand. They watched me fall. And they knew.” She stopped to breathe.

It was barely audible. “Yes,” he said. He didn’t offer comfort. There was none he could offer without insulting what she had just learned.

✦ ✦ ✦

He had watched people discover the truth about their own lives before. Fraud was rarely one lie. It was a structure of small lies, each built to make the next look reasonable: a missing document, an altered signature, a payment called something else, a number that didn’t belong.

People could live inside it for years, because every new piece of evidence was bent to fit the old ones.

This was worse. Ryla had been made to doubt the evidence of her own body. The tonic hadn’t only weakened her; it had helped convince her the weakness was inevitable, and the people pouring it were the same people telling her they loved her.

It was a system: a body kept weak, a voice kept quiet, a mind kept soft enough to believe what it was told.

He thought of Victoria’s careful hands measuring it, and of her carrying it up to Ryla’s room after Albright died, insisting he had left instructions.

The composed widow, the devoted mother, who looked at Ryla like a tiresome obligation. He had thought the family hated her for the inheritance, or because she reminded them of Edward’s betrayal.

He hadn’t understood they were managing her body, or that the medicine he had dismissed as routine was part of it. And when Albright tried to warn him, he had cut him off for good before he could explain.

He bowed his head. “Ryla. I found the vials in Albright’s bag the night I killed him. I didn’t know what they were. He tried to tell me something about your treatment, and I thought he was bargaining. I should have listened.”

Her face didn’t soften. You didn’t know.

“No.”

But you could have asked. You could have asked me.

It was simple, and it hurt more than he expected. “Yes.”

She looked away, and he let her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Late in the morning the clinician rang. Keaton asked Ryla before he put it on speaker, and she nodded.

The findings were significant, the clinician said, but they didn’t show the full extent of the damage.

The preparation seemed designed to produce several overlapping effects, and after so long, recovery couldn’t be predicted without proper examination. The withdrawal she had been through fitted the report but still needed supervision.

Her voice coming back was encouraging, but her throat needed assessing, and she shouldn’t push through pain or exhaustion. Ryla listened without interrupting. Then she raised a hand, and Keaton said she had a question. She took a breath.

“Can I walk?”

The room went quiet.

“It’s possible some of your weakness was caused by the preparation. I can’t promise how much will return. But standing and taking steps matters. You need a neurological and physical assessment, and it may take time,” the clinician said carefully.

Ryla looked at her legs. “How much?”

“I can’t give you a reliable timeline.”

She nodded. “Will it hurt?”

“Some discomfort, probably, after so long and after withdrawal. But you should never be expected to put up with severe pain without someone looking at it.”

Ryla was quiet. Then: “Was it my fault?”

Keaton’s eyes went to her. The clinician took a moment. “No. Nothing in these findings suggests you caused this. You were given something by the people responsible for your care, and you had every reason to trust them. What happened to you was not your fault.”

Ryla nodded. The call ended a few minutes later, and for a while neither of them spoke.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had thought the truth would feel like freedom. It didn’t. It felt as if someone had opened a door behind her and shown her five years of rooms she never knew existed.

The girl practising standing until her knees shook. The girl apologising to nurses for taking too long.

The girl who stopped asking when she would walk because the answer made her feel stupid.

She wanted to go back into those rooms and find that girl and tell her: You’re not failing. You’re not lazy. You’re not broken. They’re doing this to you. That her legs hadn’t betrayed her, and none of it was her fault. But five years couldn’t be given back.

She looked at the report, then at Keaton. “Did you know?”

“About the tonic? No.”

“Before.”

“About the family? I knew what they did to Elena at the boathouse, and that they lied about her death. I didn’t know this.” She nodded.

She studied him. “Did you know they hated me?”

“I knew they treated you badly.”

A small, humourless smile. “That’s not the same.”

“No.”

“Did you think I was weak?”

He didn’t answer fast enough, and she looked away.

He leaned forward. “I thought you’d been made to bear too much.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

He took the correction. “No. I thought you were fragile. I was wrong.”

She flexed her fingers. The movement still wasn’t right, but it was hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later he helped her from the table to the bed. He asked first, and she agreed, and he took her weight carefully, minding her wrists and the bruises that hadn’t quite faded. When she was settled, he put the report on the bedside table.

“Victoria.” The name sounded strange in her mouth. Not because she had forgotten how to say it. She had never said it meaning this.

“Yes.”

“Albright.”

“Yes.”

“Damien?”

His face went still. “We don’t have evidence yet that he knew about the preparation.”

She thought about it. “He knew I was like this. He knew I couldn’t speak or walk. He never asked why.” Her eyes hardened.

“That doesn’t prove he knew.”

“No. But he didn’t care.” She looked at the window.

There was nothing he could say to that. She shifted her legs under the blanket, small and deliberate, and pressed her heel into the mattress. Her foot moved. A faint crease appeared between her brows, and she tried again. It was still weak, but it happened. Her eyes filled, though nothing spilled over.

“Don’t push yourself,” he said from beside the bed.

“I know.” Two words, quiet and clear.

She watched her foot under the blanket for a while. “I thought I was getting worse.”

He sat down. “I know.”

“I thought... I thought I had to accept it. That I would never... That I would never be myself.” She stopped, frustrated, swallowed and tried again. Her voice gave out, and she shut her eyes. He waited, and she opened them.

“You still are.”

It didn’t look like gratitude. It looked closer to exhaustion. “How do you know?”

He had no answer. After a moment he said, “I don’t.”

She nodded. That was better than pretending.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night he put the lab report in a folder, wrote the date on the cover, and added the names of the compounds exactly as the lab gave them, the comparison and the clinician’s notes. He didn’t write a conclusion. He sat looking at the page.

Six lines on his list, four of them marked. Damien’s still empty, and under it the one with the question mark, which he could no longer read the way he had written it. He had thought the list was an account of Elena’s death.

Now it was also an account of everything the family had been allowed to do afterwards. The preparation hadn’t been a single act. It had taken money, access, medical authority, secrecy and years of patient administration.

Someone had decided Ryla’s body should stay weak, made sure she kept getting it, and watched her fail to recover and called it patience.

He closed the folder. He had thought Victoria’s death would be enough, and Albright’s would settle the medical side. He had been wrong. The report gave him evidence. It had given Ryla something more important: a reason to stop blaming herself.

Down the hall a floorboard creaked, and he went to her door. She was awake against the pillows with her hands on the blanket. He stood and went to the bedroom door. Ryla was awake, sitting against the pillows. Her hands rested on the blanket. She looked at him.

“Keaton.”

He stopped. She glanced at the folder in his hand.

“Don’t let them call it treatment. They’ll say they were helping me. Don’t let them.” Her voice was still weak, and the sentence cost her, but her eyes were steady.

He crossed the room and put the folder on the table. “I won’t.”

She watched him. “I want to know everything.”

“You will.”

“Not what you think I should know.”

“I understand.”

“Everything.”

He met her eyes. “Everything.”

She leaned back against the pillows, exhausted but not beaten. For five years they had made her believe her body was the enemy. Now she knew there had been hands behind the weakness.

Under the anger and the grief and the years she would never get back, something had started to move. Not her legs, not yet.

A decision. She was going to find out what had been done to her, and nobody was going to tell that story in her place again.

chapters.title: The Stage Floor
chapters.desc: A payment in a dead man’s ledger, a stage floor, and the first time Ryla stands with someone holding her up.
chapters.epigraph: “This body is mine now. I’m the one who brought it back.”
chapters.content:
The payment was buried under three layers of ordinary corruption, and Keaton found it on his fourth pass through the scans of Marcus Whitmore’s ledger.

He nearly skipped the entry.

H. Vale — Stage maintenance — $18,000.

It was the date that stopped him: three weeks before Ryla Whitmore’s fall.

The money had gone through a company registered to a dormant Whitmore subsidiary, and the description was carefully dull, a plausible expense for a family that funded arts programmes and sponsored national competitions. But Marcus hadn’t been paying for stage maintenance. He had been paying someone.

Keaton started with the competition. Five years ago Ryla had been one of the youngest finalists in the national contemporary dance championship at the Halden Theatre in New York: a big house with an old stage and a newly renovated backstage.

The public record was easy. The private one wasn’t.

It took him six hours to find the theatre’s former technical director, a retired production manager and the company that had run the security cameras.

A man in black stage trousers came out of the stage-left wing with a cloth and a small maintenance bottle, walked to centre stage, stopped on a particular mark and crouched. The angle hid most of his face.

He wiped the floor once, twice, and a third time with care over a small oval where a dancer would land after a travelling leap. Then he stood, glanced at the wings and left.

Keaton watched it again and saved it, and then he found the name. Harlan Vale: a stagehand at the venue for eleven years, no record, no disciplinary history, married with two children and a small house in Queens. Exactly the sort of man nobody investigates.

He had the name, the payment and the footage. He didn’t have the substance until he found the archived incident report, buried in insurance correspondence. A clear silicone residue had been found on the stage after the accident. Maintenance had first called it contamination from a cleaning product. Two days later, after an “external review”, the report was amended to call it insignificant. The amendment wasn’t signed.

He opened Ryla’s medical folder. There was a photograph of her at the competition under the lights, one arm raised, hair scraped back. She looked young.

✦ ✦ ✦

Keaton had been quiet all morning, and not in his usual way. There was a difference between how he worked when he was concentrating and how he worked when he had found something he didn’t want to say, and this was the second kind.

“There’s something I need to show you.”

Her first thought was Elena. Her second was the family. What?

“Your accident.”

She went still. For five years the accident had been a closed room that other people opened when they wanted to explain her life. The doctors discussed it carefully.

He set the folder on the table. “I found a payment in Marcus’s ledger. To a stagehand, three weeks before your final. I also found security footage from the interval.”

Her fingers curled on the blanket. What did he do?

He sat down opposite her. “I want you to see it. But I won’t play it unless you want me to.”

She stared at him. The question was so simple it almost hurt. She was used to people deciding what she could bear.

“Show me.” Her voice was still quiet; the words came more easily than a week ago, but she couldn’t keep them up for long. He opened the laptop.

The first video was shot from high in the theatre looking down on the stage, the picture washed out, the dancers pale under the lights.

HALDEN NATIONAL CONTEMPORARY DANCE CHAMPIONSHIP — FINAL.

Ryla knew the costume: white, a narrow silver band at the waist, hair pinned back, arms bare. She watched herself walk on and forgot to breathe.

The music started, and her younger self crossed the stage with a certainty that made her fingers tighten. She knew the opening, the turn, the way the light caught her face when she looked up at the balcony.

Her younger self crossed the stage, gathered speed and launched into the travelling leap. Ryla had known for five years what came next. She had never seen it.

The landing foot touched down and shot sideways. Not a stumble or a misjudgement. It slid out from under her as if the stage had turned to ice.

Her body twisted hard, her arms reached for a balance that wasn’t there, and she fell. The side of her head hit the stage. A second later the camera cut to the judges.

Ryla didn’t move. Keaton paused it. On the screen her younger self lay with one arm bent under her and the other stretched out. Ryla’s mouth opened, and nothing came. She looked at Keaton.

“Again.”

He didn’t ask whether she was sure. He played it again.

This time she watched the foot: the instant it touched, the slide, the rest of her following. She leaned in. “Stop. That.”

He scrubbed back. “Here?”

She nodded, and he enlarged it. The picture blurred, but the movement was clear. Her standing foot hadn’t slipped. It had lost its grip the moment it landed and gone somewhere her body hadn’t prepared for.

“I didn’t... I didn’t miss.” Her throat hurt, and she tried again.

“No.”

“I didn’t miss the landing. I knew where I was.”

“Who?”

He closed the video. “Harlan Vale. A stagehand at the theatre.”

“Why?”

“I don’t know yet.”

“Marcus?”

“The payment came from one of his companies.”

She looked down, and said, “He paid someone to make me fall.”

“Yes.”

She turned her face to the window and didn’t speak.

✦ ✦ ✦

He left her with the footage for the afternoon. He didn’t explain the payment again or tell her what to feel.

He followed the money. The company that paid it was registered to an address in Stamford with a nominee director and a closed bank account, and the transfer had run through a consultancy Marcus used for personal expenses. There was a second payment six days after the fall.

H. Vale — Additional services — $7,500.

And a third, four months later.

Confidential settlement — $12,000.

None of it was big enough to stand out in Marcus’s accounts. It was big enough to buy silence.

He sent copies to Detective Calder through the same anonymous courier he had used for the ledger.

The following records relate to the Whitmore family and the injury sustained by Ryla Whitmore five years ago. Please preserve them and investigate the named recipient.

Then he closed the laptop.

There was one more file: the MRI scans. He had asked the rehabilitation centre for the original imaging. The first hospital had passed its records on after a change of ownership, and the second had kept copies for the insurers.

Side by side, the originals and the versions in her rehabilitation file looked the same: same dates, same patient details, matching annotations. But the file data differed. The originals had been made at the hospital.

The ones in her file had been exported and altered later. He didn’t need to understand every medical detail to see it. The originals showed an injury healing. The later ones showed a heavy, lasting abnormality that wasn’t in the original images at all.

The amended rehabilitation report was signed by a specialist who had never examined her.

He printed the original scans, the altered ones and the radiologist’s opinion, put them in a folder and went back to her room. She was awake.

He didn’t hand it over straight away. He put it on the table and sat beside her. “There’s something else.”

He opened it to an MRI report. She read the dates, one after another. The terms were hard, but she could see the pattern: a serious injury with swelling and trauma, then improvement, then resolution.

“These are mine?”

“Yes.”

She turned the page. A second set of images, the same dates, the same patient number, different findings.

“Why are there two?”

“The second set was used in your rehabilitation file.”

She frowned. “Which is real?”

“The first.”

She looked at him.

He pointed to the radiologist’s opinion. “The injury had healed structurally within weeks. The scans don’t show the lasting damage described in the later reports.”

She read it twice, then looked at the dates. “Within weeks? After the fall?”

“Yes.”

The recommendations were familiar. Long-term wheelchair use. No independent weight-bearing. Continued help with daily activities. No unsupervised rehabilitation. She remembered the exercises she had been told not to try, the therapist who stopped her standing, the doctor who said the scans showed no real improvement.

She put the pages down. Her fingers had started to shake.

“How long?”

He understood. “The original scans show it had healed within weeks. I can’t tell you exactly when you should have got your movement back. But the later records were used to justify restrictions the original images don’t support.”

“Five years.” Her voice had nearly gone. She pressed her fingertips to her lips.

“Did they know?”

He took a moment. “The altered reports were used by the people in charge of your care. The originals were available to anyone with access to your records. We still need to find out who changed them and who told them to.”

“Victoria?”

“I can’t prove she altered the scans herself.”

“But she knew.”

He held her gaze. “She knew your condition, what treatment you were getting, and what you were being told.”

Ryla looked down at the altered report. After a while she began to laugh, small and breathless, with no humour in it.

“I asked her. I asked Victoria if I would walk again. She held my hand. She told me to be patient. I believed her.” Her mouth shook. She looked at the page.

Something in Keaton went still. She didn’t cry, and that frightened him more than tears would have.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday evening, when Ryla first asked to stand, he thought he had misheard. She was sitting on the side of the bed with the folder closed on the table and both bare feet on the floor, and she had been looking at them for several minutes.

“I want to stand.”

He put down the glass he was holding. “Not alone. We need a proper assessment. Ryla—”

“I know. I want to try.” It came out sharper than he expected.

He studied her. There was no pleading in her face, no need to prove anything. Only a decision.

He brought the wheelchair closer, changed his mind and pushed it away. “All right. Tell me if you want to stop.”

She nodded. He put his hands at her waist, and she looked down at them before she put both hands on his shoulders. Her grip was so light.

“Ready?”

She breathed in. “No. But do it anyway.” A small, crooked smile.

His mouth moved, not quite a smile, and he took enough of her weight to hold her.

“On three. One. Two. Three.” Her shoulders rose. Her fingers tightened.

He helped her forward. Her legs shook at once; her right knee bent, and she clung to his shoulders while her feet shifted on the floor. He held her. “Easy.”

She tried to straighten. The left leg answered first, then the right, and her hips came up, and for one moment she was halfway upright and her breath caught. Then her knees began to go, and he caught her.

✦ ✦ ✦

They tried again the next afternoon. The clinician had drawn up a cautious plan: until Ryla could be properly assessed, no forcing and no unsupported standing, short attempts, plenty of rest, nothing through severe pain.

Keaton followed it to the letter, and Ryla didn’t always thank him for it.

A faint smile came and went as she started to move. This time she meant to do more of it herself. He stood in front of her with his hands at her waist, steadying rather than lifting.

“Feel your feet. Not your knees. Your feet. Shift forward.” She closed her eyes and breathed in.

Her body moved. Her thighs trembled violently, and she held his shoulders.

“That’s it.”

She pushed. Her hips came up, her knees straightened, and for a second she stood. Not fully, not on her own, but upright. He felt her weight settle into his hands. Her eyes opened, and she looked down. The floor was under her, and she was above it.

“I— I did it.” Her voice failed, and she swallowed.

“Yes.”

“I did it.”

“Yes, you did.”

She stood for three seconds, maybe four. Then her knees gave and he caught her, and her forehead knocked against his shoulder. She stayed there breathing hard while he felt the tremor in her muscles and how much it had cost her.

“That’s enough.”

She nodded against him. He helped her sit, and her fingers stayed curled in his shirt. He didn’t ask her to let go.

By Wednesday, the third day, she had begun to anticipate the pain. Not all of it; some still came without warning, a sting along her calves, a deep ache in her hips, a strange exhaustion after movements that should have been easy.

But she was learning the difference between pain that told her to stop and the ache of muscles waking up after years.

That mattered. So did being able to feel her feet. He had folded a towel under them while she sat down on the bed, practising shifting her weight forward, back, forward again, her hands on his shoulders and his grip firm at her waist.

She breathed out through her nose and shifted forward again. Her weight went over her feet, her legs trembled, and his fingers tightened.

“Don’t let go.”

“I won’t.”

She straightened, and this time she stayed up. One second. Two. Three. Her breath shook. He was close enough that she could see the small lines of tiredness at the corners of his eyes.

“Look at me. You’re standing,” he said.

Her mouth trembled. “Yes.”

He kept his hands where they were, and neither of them moved.

Then he leaned closer, his voice dropping almost to her ear. “This body is mine now. I’m the one who brought it back.”

It was possessive, far too possessive, and she knew it. He had no right to claim what was hers, and it wasn’t an apology for holding her down or a promise never to hurt her again.

But his hands were holding her up, and he was looking at her. She leaned into him.

Not because she believed she belonged to him, but because for five years her body had been treated as something broken to be managed and apologised for, and his grip gave her an edge to push against, somewhere to put what strength she had.

For those few seconds she could feel herself taking up space in the world again. His fingers dug into her waist. She would find bruises there later. Right then she didn’t care, and she leaned harder.

He felt it, and his face changed. He bent his forehead towards her temple. “Stay with me.”

She nodded. Her knees trembled. “Ryla.”

“I’m here,” she said, out of breath.

She was standing, she had spoken, and she was looking straight at him, and for one brief, dangerous moment there was nothing in the room but the two of them and the fact that she was upright.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening he saw the bruises: small dark marks on either side of her waist where his fingers had pressed through her thin shirt. He stared at them, and she noticed.

“What?”

“Your waist.”

She looked down and saw them, and only looked. He came closer but didn’t touch. “I held you too tightly.”

She examined them. “Yes.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Because I don’t want to be one more person who decides what happens to your body.”

She watched him in the quiet. “You already did.”

“Yes.”

She looked at the bruises again. “But today... Today I asked you to hold me. That was different.” She stopped, and he waited.

He understood. It didn’t let him off. It mattered anyway. He moved his hand towards hers and stopped, and she looked at the space between them. After a moment she laid her fingers in his palm, and he closed his hand gently round them.

After she fell asleep, he went back to the table: the original scans beside the altered ones, the footage on an encrypted drive, the payment records in their own folder, copies already with Calder.

He had enough to start building a case against the people who had arranged Ryla’s fall and buried her recovery.

He turned off the lamp. For the first time he caught himself thinking about the day Ryla would be strong enough to stand without his hands at her waist, and whether he would be able to let go. He knew he would have to.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Signed
chapters.desc: Ryla asks why. Keaton shows her a photograph.
chapters.content:
By the fifteenth day, Ryla had learned that recovery didn’t go in a straight line.

Some mornings her legs felt nearly like her own; she could stand with Keaton’s hands at her waist for several seconds and move a little weight from one foot to the other. Other mornings her knees shook before she was out of bed.

Her voice was worse in the evenings, thin and rough with use, as if every word had to squeeze through a narrow passage.

She was starting to recognise when she was pushing too hard, though she hated admitting it. Keaton had become irritatingly good at spotting it first, and at knowing when not to say anything.

That morning she had been watching him work for almost an hour. He sat at the table by the window with documents, the laptop open, two phones beside it and several photographs laid out in a neat row, his breakfast untouched.

She had seen the look on his face several times in the past few days. It came when something confirmed a suspicion he had carried, and it was colder than satisfaction.

The photographs showed the theatre stage, a man coming out of the wings, a close-up of the floor. She knew what they meant, and she knew they weren’t the start of the story. There was something he hadn’t told her.

She had been patient. She had let him give her things in the order he could bear to give them, and collected the pieces he left lying around. But she was tired of being the last person to know what had happened to her.

“Keaton.”

He looked up immediately.

“Yes?”

She shifted in her chair. “Why?”

He waited. She swallowed; her voice was still weak, but she wanted to use it. “Why them? Why did you kill them?”

He didn’t look away.

“Because they killed someone.”

“Who?”

He was quiet a moment, then closed the file. “My sister.”

Ryla’s fingers moved on the blanket. She had known there was someone. She had heard the name Elena, though never enough to understand what tied her to the family. The notebooks, the initials, the old research, the video Preston left.

“Elena,” she said.

His face changed, only slightly, but she saw it. “Yes.”

“Why did they kill her?”

He looked down at the table. “She worked for Damien. She did his research: his dissertation, his papers, the model his fund uses. She thought they were partners. He used her work, and when she became a problem, they decided she was unstable. Preston got her to the boathouse. They drugged her, humiliated her and filmed it. Damien held her under the water.” His voice stayed even.

Ryla stopped breathing. The boathouse. The lights. The window.

“All of them?”

“Not all of them held her under. But they all helped make it possible.”

She looked at her hands. “And you?”

“I found out what happened. I spent a year building the evidence. Then I came here.”

“To kill them.”

“Yes.”

She studied his face. “Why like this?”

“Because they made sure nobody could prove what they’d done. Because they buried her without telling anyone who might come looking. Because they kept using her work after she was dead. And because I wanted them to know.” His jaw moved once.

She understood the last part. She didn’t agree with all of it, and she didn’t think the reasons made the deaths clean. But she understood wanting the people who hurt you to look straight at what they had done.

She looked at the window. “Why the boathouse?”

“Because that’s where she died.”

“Why did you take me?”

His face closed. “At first I thought you were one of them. You lived in that house. You were part of that family.”

“I wasn’t.”

“I know that now. I didn’t know what you’d seen or what you remembered. I thought you might be useful to me.”

A faint, bitter smile. “Useful.”

He didn’t defend it. “Yes.”

She looked at him. “Did you know she spoke to me?”

He went still. “What?”

“Elena. I didn’t know her name. I remember her face. Show me.” She looked at the table.

He understood. He picked up the small folder beside the laptop and held it for several seconds before he took out a photograph.

✦ ✦ ✦

It wasn’t a portrait. A woman stood outdoors with the sun across one side of her face, in a dark sweater with her hair loosely tied back, smiling.

Ryla knew that face. Not at once and not as a name, but as a feeling: someone kneeling beside her chair, someone who hadn’t looked at her legs, someone who waited. Her fingers shook a little as she took the photograph.

“Her.”

“You remember?”

She nodded. “She was at a dinner. At the estate, in the spring before she—” She stopped.

Keaton’s eyes stayed on her face, and Ryla could almost feel the memory coming back in pieces.

A crowded dining room, the clink of silver, Victoria’s voice moving from guest to guest, Damien laughing at something Preston said. Her own hands too tired to type, lying in her lap.

And then the woman, who had been sitting near Damien but not really part of the conversation.

She had seen Ryla struggling with the tablet, and instead of leaning over her shoulder or talking slowly and loudly, she had crouched beside the chair. Long fingers, a small silver ring. She had signed. Your hands are beautiful. Take your time.

Ryla’s breath caught. “She said that.”

His face had lost some of its colour. “What else?”

She looked at the photograph. She remembered being embarrassed, not because the woman had spoken to her but because she had been close to tears. The dinner had been unbearable.

Victoria had spent all evening presenting her as an example of courage, someone had raised a toast to the family’s devotion, and every face had turned to her.

She had wanted to vanish, and her hands were shaking too much to type. The woman had noticed. She hadn’t tried to make her smile. She had tapped two fingers against her own chest. Breathe.

“She did this.” Ryla showed him, two fingers to her chest.

He seemed to forget where he was. She did it again. “Like that.”

“She taught you that?”

“She didn’t teach me. She just did it. She waited until I could breathe.” Ryla touched her chest again.

He bowed his head. His hand on the table had gone completely still.

“Was that something she always did?”

A long pause. “Yes.”

Ryla had never heard him say that. He talked about Elena’s work, her research, what had been stolen and what had been done to her. This was the brother remembering the person behind the evidence.

Ryla ran her thumb along the edge of the picture. “Why didn’t you tell me she was your sister?”

He glanced at the window. “Because I wasn’t ready.”

She thought about that. “She didn’t tell me her name. She was just someone who was kind to me.”

He looked at her. “That was Elena.”

She had known somewhere inside before he said it, but hearing the name made the memory settle. Elena, who told her that her hands were beautiful, who waited, who reminded her to breathe.

“She was your sister.”

“Yes.”

She held the photograph carefully. “I’m sorry,” she said, and he looked away.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was another memory behind the first one, and Ryla hadn’t wanted to look at it. For more than a year she had kept it somewhere she didn’t have to go.

She had told herself it was a dream, or part of one, something her drugged mind had made out of noises and shadows. She had never told Mrs. Pell, or Walter, or anyone. But she was holding Elena’s photograph, and the memory had found its way back.

“Keaton. There was something else.”

He sat up. She put the photograph in her lap and looked at her hands. “That night. At the boathouse.” He didn’t ask which night.

His face went still.

“I saw the lights. From my room.”

The room seemed to pull away from her, and she was back in the house on that August night.

Warm, heavy air, the curtains stirring at the open window, the garden dark except for the lights at the boathouse. She had been awake because she couldn’t sleep, and she had seen movement outside.

People, a group of them, and then the way they were standing, one of them struggling and the others not moving to help. The light from a phone. The water. And a hand coming up out of it with three fingers raised.

She had known the shape before she knew what it meant, and it had felt terribly familiar. Then she had remembered the woman from dinner, her beautiful hands, her patient smile, the two fingers against her chest.

Her eyes filled. “I saw her. I saw someone in the water. I didn’t know it was her. I couldn’t see her face. There were people around her.” Her voice roughened.

Under the table, his hands had become fists.

“I wanted to call for help. I couldn’t. I couldn’t shout. I couldn’t reach my tablet. My fingers wouldn’t work. I tried to reach the table and knocked something over. I tried again. I couldn’t.” Her throat tightened. Her voice broke.

Keaton stood up so fast the chair scraped back. She thought he would leave. Instead he turned away and put one hand flat on the wall, his shoulders rigid.

Instead, he turned away from her and put one hand against the wall. His shoulders were rigid. Ryla watched him.

“I saw the hand. I knew it meant something. I knew it was a person. I couldn’t help her. I was right there. I was so angry with myself. I thought if I’d been faster, if I could have reached—” she said to his back. She made the sign, weakly. She was crying now, looking at a window that wasn’t the estate’s.

“Stop.”

He turned round, and the careful control she knew was gone. His eyes were bright and his mouth tight, and the disbelief in his face made him look younger.

“Ryla.”

She shook her head. “I should have—”

“You couldn’t.”

“I saw her.”

“You couldn’t.”

“I was there.”

“You couldn’t.” His voice broke on it. For the first time since she had met him, he didn’t seem to know what to do with his hands. He wanted to reach for her, she could see, and didn’t know whether he had the right.

“She was my sister,” he said, almost without sound.

“I know.”

“She was... She was the only person I had. I left when she was eight. I told her I would come back. I called every Sunday for nineteen years. I sent money. I paid for her education. I thought she was safe.” His jaw worked. He looked at the photograph in her lap. He pressed his thumb to the bridge of his nose. A laugh with nothing in it.

Ryla couldn’t speak.

“She told me about you.”

She went still. “What?”

“Not your name. She told me about a girl in a wheelchair at a dinner who had beautiful hands. She was so pleased with herself. She said she’d found someone in that house who was still allowed to be a person. She said you were patient with her signing, and you tried even though your hands hurt. She never said your name or which dinner. I didn’t put it together until today. She remembered you.” His face crumpled.

Ryla’s fingers curled round the photograph, and neither of them spoke. Then he lowered himself into the chair, not so much sitting as folding into it, one hand over his mouth, the other arm braced on the table.

The first sound was almost nothing, a breath that didn’t become a breath. Then his shoulders moved.

He bowed his head with his hand over his eyes, trying to keep it in, and it didn’t work.

A quiet, broken sob got out, then another. She had thought of him as a man made of locked doors.

Now she could see what was behind them: a boy at an airport, a little sister behind glass, a promise to come back, nineteen years of Sundays and the one Sunday the call didn’t come.

She put the photograph aside and reached for him.

He didn’t notice her hand until it touched his hair. It was weak and slow and a little unsteady; it brushed the side of his head, missed, and found him again. He looked up.

She had moved to the edge of her chair and couldn’t reach him comfortably, but she tried. She rested one hand on the back of his head and the other against his temple. She looked frightened by what she had just seen, but she didn’t pull away.

He closed his eyes. He had imagined many times what it would be like to learn what happened in the last minutes of Elena’s life. He had imagined finding the person who watched, or helped, or looked away.

He hadn’t imagined a young woman at a bedroom window who could hear everything and couldn’t call out, whose hands had been weakened and voice taken and body trapped in a chair by the same family that killed Elena.

For over a year he had believed Elena died alone. She hadn’t. Someone had seen her, recognised the sign, tried, and been unable to help.

His breath shook. “She was asking for me. That sign. She was asking for me.” Ryla’s fingers moved in his hair.

“I know.”

He shook his head. “No. You don’t understand. She knew I would recognise it. She knew.” He looked down at his hands.

His voice gave out. He bent forward until his forehead rested on her shoulder, careful not to lean too hard; she was still weak, and her arms trembled.

But she held him. For several seconds he couldn’t breathe properly. Then she took one hand from his hair and tapped two fingers lightly against his chest. Breathe.

He went still. She did it again: two fingers, a small tap. The same private sign.

He lifted his head. His eyes were wet.

“She did that to me. At the dinner, when I couldn’t breathe,” Ryla said.

His mouth trembled. Their mother had made that sign for them. It wasn’t in any dictionary. It belonged to a small house in Bridgeport, and after Ruth was gone it belonged to the two of them: when one was frightened, the other tapped two fingers against their chest.

Breathe. I’m here. Elena had carried it into the Whitmore house and into the last year of her life, and used it to comfort a girl she barely knew. And the girl had remembered.

“She gave you that.”

“Yes.”

He looked down, and a tear fell on his hand. “She was still herself. Even there,” he said, almost too low to hear.

“Yes.”

He closed his eyes. For years he had remembered Elena as the girl behind the glass, then the woman in photographs, then a name on a report, then a body cremated without anyone asking about family. He had built his whole life around what was taken from her.

Ryla had given him something else: Elena being kind. Not useful, not brilliant, not dead. Kind. A woman who noticed someone’s hands and waited for her to finish a sentence, and remembered to help her breathe.

His face crumpled again. Ryla leaned forward and rested her cheek on his hair, and he let himself stay there.

He didn’t ask her to forgive him, or tell her she had saved him, or make her responsible for what came next. For once he let himself be held without trying to control it.

✦ ✦ ✦

When he finally lifted his head, his face was wet and he looked embarrassed, which was a new expression on him. Ryla nearly smiled.

“You can cry.”

He let out an unsteady breath. “I know.”

“Do you?” She raised one eyebrow, a small gesture, but hers. He looked down, and something like a smile showed on his face for the first time in days, and didn’t last.

She picked up the photograph again. “She was kind to me.”

“She was kind to everyone.”

“She didn’t know what they were going to do. She didn’t know they would kill her. She still helped me.”

He nodded. She put the picture carefully on the table and touched two fingers to her chest. Breathe.

He looked down and said nothing. Then he turned the photograph towards himself, his thumb at the edge, never over her face.

Ryla’s eyes softened. “She was the first person in that house who didn’t make me feel I was taking too long.”

He closed his eyes. “That sounds like her.”

“Did she know you were coming back?”

It was gentle, and impossible. “I told her I would.”

“Then she believed you. She believed you.” She reached across the small gap between them and touched his hand.

He turned his palm up, and their fingers met. Neither of them spoke for a while.

Outside, the afternoon light faded across the fields, and the heating ticked under the windowsill. For more than a year Ryla had remembered the boathouse as the place where she failed to save someone.

Now the woman had a name and a brother. She had loved someone and been loved, and in the last year of her life she had found time to be kind to a girl nobody else in that house thought worth talking to.

Ryla lifted the photograph once more. “Elena. Elena,” she said, and again.

He bowed his head, and this time when the tears came he didn’t turn away.

chapters.title: The Pact
chapters.desc: Keaton offers her the door. She asks for something else.
chapters.content:
Keaton had prepared three ways to let her go.

The first was practical. A car would take her to a private clinic outside Wrenhaven, and from there she could call a lawyer, Detective Calder or anyone she liked.

He had gathered the medical records, the original scans, the toxicology report and the Harlan Vale payments, and put copies somewhere the Whitmores couldn’t reach.

The second was a list of names: a physician who would examine her without asking about the farmhouse, a lawyer with no ties to the Whitmores, a victims’ advocate who answered to nobody in Wrenhaven. The third was a sentence.

You can leave. He had rehearsed it several times.

He hadn’t rehearsed what he would do if she chose to stay, and that was the problem. He was starting to understand that he wanted her to stay for reasons that had little to do with her safety. He wanted to hear her voice when she woke, to know whether she had slept and whether her legs hurt and whether she had managed to stand.

He wanted to be the person she looked for when she came into a room. He had no right to any of it, and he had already taken enough from her. He found her in the sitting room, standing by the window.

Not for long and not on her own: one hand on the back of a chair, the other hovering near the wall, her knees a little bent. She had been practising without him. He stopped in the doorway.

He crossed the room but didn’t touch her. “Do you want help?”

She thought about it and nodded. He put one hand at her waist and the other round her forearm, and she leaned into it, shifted her weight and took a small step towards the chair.

Her foot dragged a little, and she corrected it and took another. When she reached the chair, she sat with a long, controlled breath.

He almost smiled. Then he pulled the other chair round to face hers.

“Ryla, I need you to understand something. You can leave. I can arrange transport and get you to a hospital, and give you every document I have. You can go to Calder and tell her what happened here, including what I did. All of it. I won’t stop you.”

She looked out of the window. The afternoon was grey and still, the fields had lost most of their colour, and winter was settling in.

“Would you help me get there?”

“Yes.”

“Would you give me my phone?”

“Yes.”

“Would you let me call Walter?”

“Yes.”

“Would you let me tell him where I am?”

Keaton hesitated. Then he answered honestly.

“Yes.”

She looked back at him. “Even if I tell him what you did?”

“Yes, then too.”

She was quiet. He could hear the heating running under the floor.

He said, “I don’t want you to think you owe me anything. Not for the scans, not for helping you stand, not for taking you away from them. I don’t want you to mistake being safe here for having to stay here.”

She looked at her hands, and he thought she might ask why he was saying this now. Instead she asked, “Do you want me to leave?”

It was so direct that he couldn’t hide behind the sentence he had rehearsed. “Yes. I want you somewhere no one can reach you, where you can get better without wondering whether the person beside you might hurt you.” Her face changed, and he went on.

Her expression shifted. He continued.

“I want you somewhere no one can reach you. Somewhere you can recover without having to wonder whether the person beside you might hurt you.”

She looked at him. “That’s not what I asked.”

He looked down. “No.”

“Then answer the question.”

He was silent. Finally he said, “I don’t want you to leave.”

She nodded once. She had expected it. “Thank you. For not lying.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She had thought about leaving many times. In the first days it meant getting away from the man who had kidnapped her: a door, a phone, someone who would believe her.

Then she learned what the tonic had done, and saw the original scans, and remembered the boathouse, and each discovery changed the shape of the world she thought she knew. The farmhouse wasn’t home.

Keaton wasn’t safe just because he could be gentle. She hadn’t forgotten the cold room, the dark, the water over her face, the gun at her temple, her wrists pinned while he demanded she speak.

She hadn’t forgotten that he had chosen to hurt her. But she had also seen him break over Elena, and she had seen something in him she recognised and didn’t much like recognising: a person left with nothing but the need to make someone answer.

“What happens if I leave?”

“You get better.”

“And you?”

“I finish what I came to do.”

“Damien.”

“Yes.”

She looked at the window again. For years the Whitmores had decided what happened to her: where she lived, what she could do, what she took, what she could say.

They had decided she was fragile and then made sure she stayed that way. Even now, part of her still waited for someone to tell her what came next. She was tired of it. She wanted something that was hers.

“Keaton.”

He looked up.

“I don’t want to go back.”

His face became still. She drew a breath.

“I want Damien.”

He didn’t answer. Her voice was quiet but steady. “I want to look at him. I want to hear him explain what he did. I want him to know I remember the boathouse. I want to know why he thought he could do that to Elena, and whether he knew about the stage, and the scans, and what they were giving me.” Her fingers tightened on the armrest.

“And if he won’t answer?”

“Then I’ll know he doesn’t intend to.”

“That may not be enough.”

“It’ll be my decision. Don’t make me one more thing you protect by deciding what I’m allowed to know.” He looked down, and she leaned forward.

His eyes lifted.

“I won’t.”

“Promise me.”

“I promise.”

She studied him. “I don’t want to be sent away because you feel guilty.”

His face tightened. “I’m not sending you away.”

“Good. I want to stay.” She looked at her hands.

Keaton didn’t move.

“Here?”

“For now.”

“With me?”

She nodded.

“With you.”

He searched her face, and she understood why. He needed to know whether she was choosing him or only the one person who had told her the truth. The answer wasn’t clean.

She couldn’t separate gratitude from attachment, fear from wanting, the comfort of him from the relief of finally having someone who spoke the language she had spent years speaking alone. She wasn’t going to pretend she could.

“I don’t know what this is. I don’t know if I trust you. I don’t know if I should,” she said.

“You shouldn’t have to.”

“But I want to stay. And I want Damien.”

Something moved behind his eyes. Not surprise. Recognition. He nodded. “Then we plan for Damien.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, Keaton went to the kitchen to make a call, and she heard him talking about the medical arrangements and the clinician and the evidence he would release if anything happened to him.

When he came back, she was sitting on the bed trying to get the blanket off her legs without twisting too far, and he helped her.

“Thank you.”

He came closer. He looked tired, with shadows under his eyes and his hair a mess from running his hands through it, and the old pale line across one knuckle. His hands.

She had seen them hold a gun, close round her wrists, steady her waist while she stood, and tremble round Elena’s photograph. She didn’t know how to feel about them. Maybe she wasn’t supposed to know yet.

“Keaton.”

“Yes?”

“Sit with me.”

He stopped beside the bed, and she reached for his hand. He let her take it, but his fingers stayed loose.

“What do you think?”

“I think you would have remained in that house. I think the family would have continued giving you the tonic. I think Damien would have found a way to get control of the trust.”

“And Elena?”

He looked at her.

“I think she would still be dead.”

Her fingers tightened round his. She looked at their hands. “Do you think about me?”

He didn’t answer fast enough, and she looked up. “That’s an answer.”

“Yes.”

His jaw shifted.

“Things I shouldn’t.”

“Such as?”

He looked at her. “Wanting to touch you.”

Her breath caught.

“Wanting you to come to me when you’re frightened. Wanting to be the person you trust. Wanting to forget that I’m the one who made you afraid.”

“Can you forget?”

“No.”

“Neither can I.”

He nodded, and she looked at his hand. “Do you want to kiss me?”

His face changed. “Ryla.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“No, it isn’t,” he said.

She slid her hand up his wrist. “Then answer.”

His eyes went to her mouth and back. “Yes.”

“Why haven’t you?”

“Because I don’t know whether you want me or you want not to be alone.”

“Maybe I don’t know either.”

He started to take his hand back, and she held on. “But I know what I’m asking for now. Ask me tomorrow and I might say something different. I don’t know. But right now I want you to kiss me.” He stopped. She lifted her chin.

He didn’t move. “Say it clearly.”

She frowned. “I want you to kiss me.”

“Are you sure? And you want me to stop if you change your mind, at any point?”

“Yes. At any point.”

He leaned in slowly enough that she could have turned away. She didn’t. The first touch of his mouth was almost cautious and lasted barely a second.

Then she caught the front of his shirt and pulled him back, and the second kiss was hungry in a way neither of them was ready for.

She kissed him like someone who had spent years being denied the right to ask for anything, and his restraint began to crack under her hands. His palm came up to her cheek, and she turned into it.

He broke away first, his forehead against hers. “Ryla.” She could hear the warning in it.

She touched his face. “Don’t make me regret asking.”

He closed his eyes. “I’m trying not to.”

“Then stop thinking for a minute.”

When he opened his eyes, she kissed him again, and this time he let himself answer.

There was no innocence in it. They both knew too much about what had brought them into that room. His hands had hurt her. Her body still carried what had been done to it. He had killed four people.

She had spent sixteen days as his captive, and choosing to stay didn’t erase how she had got there. Wanting something now couldn’t make the beginning beautiful. But the wanting was real, and so was her choice.

When he touched her again, he did so slowly, watching her face.

He undid her buttons one at a time and waited after each, and when she pulled his shirt over his head herself, her hands still clumsy, he laughed for the first time in weeks, low against her throat.

She told him what she wanted. When she needed him to wait, he waited. When she drew him closer, he followed.

Neither of them mistook it for a cure. Nobody promised that love would make the past harmless, or that tenderness had turned them into good people.

There was only the hard, deliberate decision to stay present, to talk and ask, and to stop when either of them needed to.

Afterwards, in the quiet, Ryla lay with her head on his shoulder. His hand rested near hers, not holding it, waiting. She found his fingers under the blanket and laced hers through them, and he turned his head.

She thought about it. “Yes.”

“Are you sure?”

“I’m tired.”

“Then sleep.”

She closed her eyes. After a while she said, “Keaton? Don’t disappear before I wake up.”

His fingers tightened. “I won’t.”

She believed he meant it. She didn’t know yet whether that was wise.

They talked about Damien the next morning. Keaton brought coffee for himself and tea for her, and she sat at the table with a blanket round her shoulders, going through the evidence he had laid out the night before.

He had expected her to be quiet. Instead she was focused, with small notes marking several pages.

“This payment.”

“Marcus’s company.”

“Why was it paid twice?”

“The first payment was made before the competition. The second was after the accident.”

“Then the third?”

“A settlement.”

She looked at the date.

“Four months later.”

“Yes.”

“Was that when the original scans were changed?”

“We haven’t established the exact date.”

She nodded. “Then we need to.”

He watched her turn the page. She was learning to use the evidence, not only to read it but to question it.

Ryla looked at him.

“And the stagehand?”

“Harlan Vale. I have his address.”

“Are you going to him?”

Keaton paused.

“I haven’t decided.”

She studied his face. “Don’t kill him.”

His eyes came up. “Why?”

“Because I want to hear him speak.”

He looked at her a moment, then nodded. “All right.”

She went back to the documents. “And Damien?”

He leaned back. “Damien is different.”

“Because he held Elena under.”

“Because he’s the last name on my list.”

“Your list.” He didn’t deny it. She put the paper down.

“Then we need to talk about what happens when you reach him.”

He looked at her.

“What do you want?”

“I want him alive long enough to answer.”

“And after?”

“I don’t know. I want to see his face when he realises I know. I want him to understand I remember the lights, and what was done to my body. I want him to know Elena had someone. Someone who loved her and knew what she was worth.” Her voice weakened, and she stopped to swallow.

Keaton looked down, and she reached across the table and touched the back of his hand. “I want him to know she wasn’t alone in the world.”

He turned his hand under hers. “All right.”

“And I want to be there.”

“Then you’ll be there.”

“Then we plan it properly.”

For the next hour, they did. They split the evidence into three packages: one for Calder, one for the financial regulators, and one for a journalist who had once exposed irregularities at the Whitmore Group. If anything happened to Keaton, the files would go out automatically.

Ryla insisted on her medical records going in, not just the original scans but everything: the altered reports, the prescriptions, how long she had been given the tonic, the names of everyone who approved her treatment.

She wanted the truth written down where nobody could revise it. He agreed.

They talked about how Damien would respond. He would deny the stolen research and the boathouse, call the videos fakes and the financial records misunderstood, and throw the family name, the lawyers, the foundation and everyone who had ever benefited from the Whitmore money at it.

Ryla listened. Then she said, “He’ll talk about me. He’ll say I’m confused, that I’m not well, that you’ve manipulated me. That I can’t make my own decisions.”

“Yes.”

She nodded. “Then I want to speak first.”

He thought about it. “All right.”

“And I want to be awake at midnight on the twenty-first.”

“Your birthday.”

She would turn twenty-five, the trust would be hers, and for the first time the family would have no say over the money, or over her. She looked at the calendar. “At midnight I want to know I’m still here. I want to be awake and see the time change. I want to know they didn’t manage to take that too.”

He nodded. “Then you’ll be awake.”

She stared at him, and then slowly she smiled.

“Good.”

He reached across the table, and she took his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday night, Ryla stood without his help. It wasn’t graceful. Her left hand held the edge of the table and her right hovered beside her, her knees shook at once, and she had to think about every part of it.

But she stood. Keaton watched from a few steps away and didn’t rush to catch her. She had asked him not to.

She shifted her weight. One foot moved, then the other: a small step, and a second. She stopped, breathing hard. His hands stayed close, ready, not touching. “That’s enough.”

“One more.”

“Ryla—”

“One.”

He held her eyes, and then nodded. She took another step. Her knee trembled and her fingers tightened on the table, but she stayed up. When she finally sat down, her face was flushed and her breathing uneven.

She reached for his hand, and he gave it to her.

They sat together in the quiet. Elena’s photograph lay on the table beside the evidence folders, her face turned to the light. Ryla looked at it, then at him.

“We’re going to make them answer.”

“Yes.”

“Together?”

“Together,” he said at last.

“Then that’s the pact.”

He lifted her hand and pressed his mouth to her knuckles. Not a claim. An answer. Outside, winter had settled over the fields. Sixteen days until her birthday, and for the first time he was making a plan with her instead of for her.

chapters.title: Proof of Death
chapters.desc: Damien receives a video. Arabella finds it.
chapters.content:
The first thing Damien noticed was the timestamp.

17 DECEMBER — 21:43:08

He watched the video once without moving, then again.

The camera hung a few feet above dark water, angled down past a wooden post. It was dark, but there was enough light to make out a woman lying face down near the edge, her hair spread round her head and one arm drifting just under the surface.
