Her clothes were pale, and she didn’t move. The picture didn’t shake; whoever filmed it had held the phone steady, as if it needed to be seen clearly.

A dark cardigan over a light shirt. He knew the clothes. He knew the hair, and the small silver bracelet on her wrist. Ryla.

He watched a third time. The body didn’t move. A faint ripple crossed the water, and the video ended. Underneath it, a message.

Unknown number: She’s in the water. Sunday, eleven at night. Come to the boathouse alone, or your police find her first and ask why you were stalling.

For several seconds he didn’t understand it. Then he understood too much. Thursday the seventeenth, a quarter to ten at night. Four days until Ryla’s birthday.

He stood up so fast his chair hit the wall. “No. No,” he said aloud, and again.

He called the number. It rang three times and went to voicemail. He called again and got nothing.

Damien: Who is this?

Damien: Is she alive?

The messages were delivered. Nothing came back. His palms were sweating. He played the video again and watched the body this time, the shoulders, the fingers, the hair, looking for breath. There was none.

He couldn’t tell whether the water covered her face, how long she had been there, or whether it had been filmed minutes ago or hours.

The timestamp might be real. It might be part of the threat. And whoever had sent it knew about the police, and knew he had been stalling.

His stomach clenched. The Scotch, the conversation with Hargreaves. He looked at the study door. Had someone been listening?

He had assumed the room was safe, that the police were chasing the wrong things, and that whoever had Ryla would get impatient and the ransom would turn into a negotiation. It had never occurred to him that the man holding her might have been listening to him.

He called Hargreaves, who answered on the second ring.

“Have you spoken to anyone?”

A pause. “Good evening to you too.”

“Have you spoken to the police? Has anyone asked you about our conversation?”

“What conversation?”

Damien shut his eyes. “Don’t be clever.”

Hargreaves’s voice changed. “What’s happened?”

“She’s dead.”

Silence. “Are you certain?”

“No.”

“Then don’t say that.”

“There’s a video. Her body.”

Hargreaves let out a breath.

“Where?”

“At the boathouse.”

“How do you know it’s recent?”

“There’s a timestamp.”

“Damien, listen to me. Don’t go anywhere. Don’t touch anything. Send me the video.”

“No.”

“Send it to me.”

“No.”

“Then send it to the police.”

Damien turned away from the screen. “You don’t understand. They’ll ask questions.”

“Of course they will. A missing woman has been found dead.”

“Not those questions.”

Hargreaves stopped. When he spoke again, it was carefully. “What have you done?”

Damien’s mouth went dry. “Nothing. I haven’t done anything.”

“Then why are you frightened of the police?”

He could still see Ryla in the frozen last frame. “Because they won’t understand.”

Hargreaves gave a short, humourless breath. “That isn’t an answer.”

Damien hung up. Downstairs the house was silent, the way it had been since his mother died: staff moving carefully, guards in the doorways and corridors, doors locked early, curtains drawn before sunset, everyone living.

He had got used to it, had even started to find the routine comforting. Tonight it felt like a trap. In the drawing room he poured a Scotch with a shaking hand and set the bottle down too hard. No new messages.

Back in the study, the video was still open. He enlarged the last frame. Ryla’s face was turned away, hair across her cheek, and at her wrist the bracelet.

Edward had given it to her when she was eighteen, a thin silver chain with a small engraved charm, and she had worn it every day since, even after the accident.

He had once complained that she never took it off, and she had smiled at him. He remembered the smile now, and it annoyed him. He didn’t want to remember her smiling. He wanted to know whether she was dead.

He wanted a body, one that could be identified and dated so the whole thing could end, and he needed it found before the twenty-first. Not because he cared what day she died.

Because of the trust. If Ryla died before her birthday, the money came back. If she lived to midnight on the twenty-first, it was hers, and the family lost the last thing that kept her quiet.

For a month he had told himself he was trying to rescue her. He had said sister in every conversation with the police, cried on the phone, begged for extensions, called himself desperate.

But when the video arrived, his first thought hadn’t been that Ryla was dead. It had been that the body needed finding before her birthday. His phone buzzed.

Unknown number: Sunday. Eleven o’clock. Alone.

Damien: How do I know she’s dead?

Unknown number: You saw her.

He had seen a body in water and recognised the clothes. He hadn’t seen her face, or her eyes, or a doctor pronounce her dead.

Damien: I need proof.

This answer took longer.

Unknown number: You always did.

He read it twice. There was something familiar in the contempt, and it made his skin prickle.

Damien: Who are you?

No answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

Arabella found the video because Damien had left the laptop open. She hadn’t been looking for it. She had come for the latest financial statements, which Damien had promised to send her father before the morning meeting and hadn’t, and she was tired of reminding him.

She was tired of the house, the police calls, the guards, the whispering, the funerals and the explanations that never explained anything.

Most of all she was tired of Damien. Everyone said he had changed, that he was under enormous pressure, grieving, holding the family together. She had said some of it herself.

But she had started noticing things: the way he watched the gates, checked his phone every few minutes, snapped whenever anyone mentioned Ryla’s birthday, and seemed more frightened of the trust than of the chance that his sister was dead.

The video was paused on the screen. She nearly looked away, and then she saw the pale clothes, the hair, the bracelet. She came closer. “Damien?” Nobody answered. She read the timestamp, and the message underneath.

Unknown number: She’s in the water. Sunday, eleven at night. Come to the boathouse alone, or your police find her first and ask why you were stalling.

She read it twice and pressed play. The woman lay in the water. Her stomach turned. She shut the laptop, and opened it again to be sure she had seen it, and the body was still there. She put her hand over her mouth. “Oh, God.”

Footsteps behind her. Damien stopped in the doorway when he saw her, and neither of them spoke. Then he crossed the room. “What are you doing?”

“What is this?”

He glanced at the screen. “Nothing. Someone trying to provoke me.”

She looked at the laptop.

“Is that Ryla?”

He didn’t answer.

“Damien.”

“I don’t know.”

“You don’t know?”

“I said I don’t know.”

Arabella took a step back.

“She’s lying in the water.”

“It’s a video.”

“Of your sister.”

“We don’t know that.”

It came too fast and too smoothly. His eyes were on the message, not the woman on the screen, and Arabella saw it.

“What does it mean, ‘why you were stalling’?”

His face changed. “Nothing. They’re trying to frighten me.”

“About what?”

He went to the desk. “Arabella, I don’t have time for this.”

She didn’t move. “Have you been stalling?”

He looked up. “Don’t.”

“Have you?”

His expression hardened.

“Do you have any idea what I’ve been dealing with?”

“Apparently not.”

“Ryla has been missing for weeks. The police are useless. Someone has taken her, and now they’re sending me videos of a body.”

“Then call the police.”

He stared at her. “Not yet. I need to know what this is.”

“Call them.”

“Arabella.”

“Call them.”

He reached for the laptop, and she stepped back with it. “Don’t delete anything.”

His eyes narrowed, and for the first time she saw something in his face she couldn’t square with the man she had agreed to marry. Not grief and not fear for his sister. Calculation. She looked at the message again, and back at him.

“Why do you keep talking about the twenty-first?”

He said nothing, and the room seemed to tilt. She remembered him asking about the trust, whether Ryla could legally make decisions while she was in rehabilitation, whether the trustees could step in if she was found incapable.

Victoria calling the birthday a problem. And Elena Ward, a name that had come up in Preston’s video and then sunk under the family’s explanations. She remembered conversations.

Damien asking about the trust. Damien asking whether Ryla could legally make decisions if she remained in rehabilitation.

Damien asking whether the trustees could intervene if she were considered incapable.

She remembered Victoria saying the birthday was a problem. She remembered Marcus’s funeral. The old papers burning. The way Damien had looked at the flames. She remembered Elena Ward.

A name that had surfaced in the video Preston posted, then disappeared beneath the family’s explanations.

“Who was Elena?”

He went still, a pause too long to be an accident. “Why are you asking?”

“Because I heard you say her name. That night, after Preston’s video.”

He looked away. “Someone who worked with me. At Hollis.”

“What happened to her?”

“She died.”

“How?”

His face hardened. “This isn’t the time.”

She looked at the laptop and back at him. “Did you kill her?”

He stared at her, and the silence made her step back. Then he laughed, short and disbelieving. “Don’t be ridiculous.”

She didn’t answer. He came towards her. “You’re letting this get to you. You’ve been listening to people who want to destroy us.”

“Who?”

“Whoever sent this.”

“Then why won’t you call the police?”

“Because I need to handle it first.”

“Handle what?”

He said nothing. She looked at him, and then she understood something that made her cold all the way through. Damien was waiting for someone to make the problem go away.

✦ ✦ ✦

Arabella packed that night, without drama. She didn’t fling things into suitcases or shout down the corridors. She took out what she needed and folded it into two cases. Her engagement ring lay on the dressing table, and she looked at it.

It was beautiful. She had loved it when he gave it to her, and pictured the wedding, the flowers and the speeches, a life where Damien’s charm was just charm. She had never pictured having to ask whether he had killed someone.

The bedroom door opened, and Damien stood there. “What are you doing?”

She closed the suitcase. “Leaving.”

He looked at the cases, then at the ring. “Arabella.”

“Don’t.”

“You’re upset.”

“I’m frightened.”

“Of me?” He seemed genuinely offended, which almost made her laugh.

“Should I be?”

He stared. “After everything we’ve been through?”

“That’s exactly the problem.”

He stepped into the room.

“You’re making a decision based on a video sent by a stranger.”

“No. I’m making a decision based on what you did when you saw it.”

“You don’t know what I did.”

“I know you didn’t call the police.”

“I was trying to establish whether it was real.”

“You were trying to establish whether she was dead.”

His face tightened. “What’s the difference?”

She stared at him. That was it. Not a confession. Something worse: a question he honestly believed had a reasonable answer. She felt she had never seen him before.

“She may be dead.”

“And if she is, what do you expect me to do?”

“Grieve.”

He looked away. Her voice shook. “You haven’t even asked whether she might be alive.”

“I saw the video.”

“Then why are you still thinking about the trust?”

His eyes came back to hers, and she knew she had hit something. He didn’t deny it. He only said, “You don’t understand the situation.”

“Explain why her body needs to be found before the twenty-first.”

Damien’s jaw shifted.

“Because that’s when she turns twenty-five.”

“And?”

He looked at her.

“And the trust becomes hers.”

She stared at him. “So that’s why. That’s why you need her dead before then.”

His face changed. “Lower your voice.”

“Don’t tell me what to do.”

“Arabella, listen to me.”

“No.”

“You are making this worse.”

“I think you already did that.”

He reached for her arm. She moved away.

“Don’t touch me.”

He stopped.

They stood on opposite sides of the room. Then Arabella picked up the ring and laid it on the suitcase. “I don’t know whether Ryla is dead. I don’t know what happened to Elena, or what you’ve done. But I can’t marry a man who watches a video of his sister in the water and thinks about the date on a trust deed.” She looked at him.

Damien went pale. “You’re leaving me over a misunderstanding.”

“No. I’m leaving because I finally understand you.” She lifted the case.

He followed her into the corridor. “Arabella. Don’t do this. Think about what it will look like.”

She stopped at the top of the stairs and turned round slowly. “What it will look like? You still think this is about appearances,” He said nothing, and she looked at him.

She walked downstairs, and nobody stopped her. At the front door she put on her coat while a guard looked away, and she stepped out into the cold without looking back.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday night, a little after half past ten, Damien got another message.

Unknown number: Twenty-nine minutes.

Arabella had been gone three days. Her ring was still on the suitcase upstairs. He hadn’t gone after her. He told himself there was no point; she would calm down, see she had overreacted, come back once she understood the consequences. He knew she wouldn’t.

He opened the laptop and watched the video again, and checked the clock against the timestamp, and picked up his coat. Then he stopped. Alone. The message had said to come alone.

On the security monitor: two guards at the front door, one by the garage, one at the back gate. The two who usually watched the boathouse were in the kitchen, where he had sent them an hour ago without telling them why.

If he left without a word, they would notice. If he told them, whoever had sent the video might see. A new message came.

Unknown number: Bring no one.

Damien: I want to see her face.

Unknown number: You had years to look at it.

He stopped breathing. Years. Not months, not weeks. Years.

He thought of Elena, the university, the papers, the boathouse, the old research, and his stomach knotted. He looked at the frozen image of Ryla and closed the laptop. He couldn’t go to the police.

Not before he knew who had the body and what they knew, and whether the video was real. And certainly not before the twenty-first.

He picked up his keys out of habit, then put them down again; the boathouse was a walk across his own lawn. At the study door he looked back.

His mother’s portrait over the fireplace, his father’s desk under the window, everything where it belonged. He had spent his whole life believing that if he kept the right people close and the right things hidden, he could control what happened next.

Outside, the cold hit him. The boathouse was a dark shape at the bottom of the lawn, and he couldn’t see the water. His phone buzzed once more.

Unknown number: Alone, Damien.

He put the phone in his pocket and started down the lawn.

chapters.title: The Last Night at the Farmhouse
chapters.desc: Keaton is losing time. Ryla dances for him. Across the water, police cars stop outside an empty house.
chapters.content:
Keaton had started forgetting things. Not the important things that could be written down, but small ones. He left the kettle on until it had nearly boiled dry. He walked into the kitchen and stood there with no idea why.

Once Ryla found him at the back door in his coat, staring into the dark garden as if he were expecting someone, and when she asked what he was doing, he said he had heard a car. There hadn’t been a car.

He hadn’t slept properly in three nights. She could hear him moving round the house long after she had gone to bed: working, or sitting in the dark sitting room, or walking the corridor and stopping outside her door. He never came in, and she didn’t ask why.

Sometimes he seemed to lose the present. She would say his name, and he would look at her.

Once, reading a document, his free hand began moving in small private signs she didn’t know, and then he looked up and apologised.

Another time she heard him say Elena’s name, not the way he said it when he told Ryla about her, but like an answer to someone standing just outside the room. There was nobody there.

She said nothing. She had learned that grief could make a person hear what they weren’t ready to stop hearing, and that Keaton didn’t like being watched while he fell apart.

So she watched: the meals he didn’t eat, the coffee going cold by the laptop, the locks checked twice and then a third time as if the second check had never happened, the bruised shadows under his eyes, and the way he had begun looking at her.

On Saturday morning his phone rang while he was rinsing a cup at the sink. He stared at the screen, and Ryla, in the doorway, saw his face. “Calder?”

He nodded and answered. “Vance.”

She couldn’t hear the detective, but she saw the change in him. He put the cup down.

“When?”

A pause.

“No. I haven’t been there.”

Another pause. His eyes moved towards the window.

“Who told you that?”

He listened. “That isn’t enough to establish anything.”

He ended the call and didn’t turn round.

“She’s getting close,” Ryla said.

“Yes.”

“How close?”

“Close enough. She traced the courier who delivered Marcus’s ledger. He remembered the car used for the drop, and she followed it on a road camera to the house by the lake.” He picked up the cup, realised he had already rinsed it, and put it down.

“Your rented house?”

“The lease is in a name that isn’t mine. She knows someone connected to the deaths used it. She rang the bank’s auditor to ask if he’d ever heard of the place.”

“Does she know you’re here?”

“Not yet.”

“How long?”

“I don’t know.” He went back to the table and started gathering papers.

“Keaton. Look at me. You haven’t slept.”

“I’m fine.”

“No.”

His face hardened slightly. “Ryla—”

“Don’t. You keep saying you’re fine when you can’t remember where you put your own coffee. You don’t have to pretend with me.” She came closer one careful step at a time, and he watched her feet until she reached the table and rested a hand on its edge.

He looked away, and she thought he would argue. Instead he said, “I heard her last night.”

Her hand tightened on the table. “Elena?”

He nodded.

“What did she say?”

A small, humourless smile. “Nothing useful. I knew she wasn’t there. I knew it was a memory. I heard her anyway. I heard her laughing.” He looked down at the papers.

“Do you remember what she sounded like?”

“Every day. That’s the problem.”

She didn’t answer. He went back to sorting documents, and she watched his hands, steady now, though she had seen them shake.

“Come with me,” she said.

“Where?”

“Somewhere warmer.”

“It’s warm here.”

“Not where you’re standing.”

He glanced at the window, then at her. She held out her hand, and after a moment he took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

By late afternoon he had packed the evidence into three envelopes, one for Detective Calder, one for the financial regulators, one with the medical records and original scans, and arranged for them to go out if he didn’t call a particular number by midnight. Ryla watched him seal the last one.

“You’re planning to leave tonight.”

“Yes.”

“Without me?”

“I haven’t decided.”

She frowned. “You said we were doing this together.”

“We are.”

“Then don’t make plans that leave me behind.”

He put the envelope down. “Calder is closing in. If she finds this place, I want you not to be here.”

“Why?”

“Because I don’t know what she’ll do when she finds me.”

“She’ll arrest you. And she’ll find me. So why would I be safer somewhere else?”

He didn’t answer.

“You want to disappear before she gets here.”

“I want to keep you out of the middle.”

“I’m already in the middle.”

“That doesn’t mean you have to stay there.”

She shook her head. “You don’t get to decide that.”

The old instinct came back into his face, the urge to arrange and control and move the pieces before anyone else could touch them. Then he looked at the envelopes and seemed to remember. “You’re right.”

“I know.”

He almost smiled. She pulled out a chair and sat. “How much time do we have?”

“Until midnight. Perhaps less.”

“Then stop wasting it. Tell me what goes where.”

He did. They went through every envelope, file and name. Ryla checked dates, Keaton explained the chain of custody, and they worked out what Calder would ask and what they could prove.

By the time they finished, the light was going. Her legs hurt and her voice was tired, but the work had steadied her.

“You should rest,” he said.

“So should you.”

He didn’t argue. She stood, and this time she didn’t reach for the table.

✦ ✦ ✦

The floor was cold under her bare feet. She had taken off her socks and tied her hair back, and she stood in the middle of the sitting room with her arms loose and her sleeves falling over her wrists.

Keaton was in the doorway. He hadn’t asked what she was doing; he had only watched her push the chair aside.

“Ryla.”

“Stay there.”

He stopped. She took a breath and began. There was no music. She didn’t want any. She wanted to hear her own feet on the boards and the small sounds her body made as it shifted, and her breathing.

The first movement was barely there: a slow turn of the wrist, a shift through the shoulders. Then she lifted one foot and set it down a few inches away.

Her knee trembled, and she held her balance. The movement travelled up through her spine and into her arms, and she reached out with one hand, then the other, towards something she couldn’t quite touch. Her body remembered more than it could do.

It remembered the shape of a turn, the line of an arm, the way a dancer moves through space without asking the floor’s permission.

But memory wasn’t strength. Her left leg shook, and she stopped. Keaton took a step forward.

“Don’t.”

He stopped. She closed her eyes, breathed and began again. This time she let her arms move more freely, shifting her weight from one foot to the other, slow and uneven, and turned, not all the way, but enough to feel the old direction of movement inside her.

For one moment she looked like the dancer she had been.

Then her knee went, and she landed hard on one hand and hip. Keaton was moving before she hit the floor, but she pushed herself up before he got there.

“I’m all right.”

“Don’t move. Let me see.”

“I said I’m all right.”

He stopped. She breathed through it. Her palm stung, her hip throbbed, and her leg shook with the effort of holding her up.

He waited. Then: “May I help you?”

She nodded, and he helped her sit. For a while neither of them spoke. Then she looked at the floor.

“I used to do that.”

“I know.”

“No. You don’t. I used to do it without thinking. I used to know exactly where my body was, how much space I needed, where my weight was going before I moved.”

“Now I have to think about everything.”

Keaton lowered his eyes. Ryla rubbed her palm.

“I hate it.”

“I know.”

She looked at him.

“I don’t want you to tell me I’m doing well.”

He nodded.

“All right.”

“I don’t want you to tell me I’m brave.”

“I won’t.”

“I want you to watch.”

He looked at her. She held his gaze.

“That’s all.”

He nodded.

“Then I’ll watch.”

She rested for several minutes and stood again. This time he stayed close enough to catch her without touching her.

Her arms rose, smaller now, and her body shook. She turned halfway, stepped forward and shifted back. One step, another. Her foot slipped, and she caught herself, and then her knees went.

He caught her before she hit the floor, and she hung against him, breathless and trembling. Then she let herself lean into his chest.

“I can’t.”

He held her carefully. “You can stop.”

She shook her head. “Not because you want me to.”

“Then stop because you want to.”

She was quiet, and after a moment she nodded.

He helped her to the sofa, where she leaned back, exhausted, and he knelt to look at her palm. A small graze, nothing serious. He brought a clean cloth and wiped the dust away.

“You looked at me like I was doing something important,” she said.

“You were.”

“It was only a few steps.”

“It wasn’t. I’ve seen people stand up in front of a thousand witnesses and mean nothing. I’ve watched people sign their names to things that ruined lives. You stood up when nobody was asking you to.” He went back to her hand. He folded the cloth.

She looked away. He held her hand in his palm. “I watched.”

“Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner the farmhouse was quiet. Ryla had showered and changed into soft clothes; her legs ached and her palm was bandaged, and the walking stick the clinician had sent on Thursday leaned by the bed. Keaton had checked the locks, then checked them again. She found him standing at the bedroom window.

“You’re doing it again.”

He turned.

“What?”

“Looking outside.”

He glanced at the dark garden.

“Calder could be here by morning.”

“Then let her come.”

He looked at her.

“She’ll arrest me.”

“Yes.”

“She’ll ask you questions.”

“Yes.”

“She’ll want to know what happened here.”

Ryla nodded.

“Then I’ll tell her.”

He looked at her.

“You don’t have to protect me.”

“I know.”

“Ryla.”

“I know.”

She came closer, slowly, without the chair. When she reached him, she put her hands on his face.

“You look exhausted.”

“I am.”

“Come to bed. Keaton. Come with me.” He glanced at the window, and she touched his cheek.

He let her lead him away. He was careful with her.

Not because he thought she would break, but because he had finally begun to understand that care wasn’t the same as control.

He asked before he touched the places that still hurt. He slowed when she told him to, followed when she moved his hand, answered when she whispered his name.

Hearing her voice in the dark was different from anything before. He hadn’t demanded it or frightened it out of her. She had chosen to give it to him, a few soft words at a time against his ear, and he listened.

They didn’t talk about the people who had died.

They didn’t talk about the police or the evidence or the birthday.

For a little while, there was only the warmth of the room, the quiet between their breaths, and the fragile intimacy of two people who knew they couldn’t make the past disappear.

Afterwards she lay with her cheek on his shoulder and his hand on her back, and she could feel how much tension he was still holding.

“You’re thinking.”

“Yes.”

“About Elena?”

He nodded. She lifted her head.

“Tell me something about her.”

He looked at her.

“Now?”

“Yes.”

He considered. Then he said, “She used to steal the sugar packets from cafés.”

Ryla blinked.

“Why?”

“She liked collecting them. She said every café had a different design.”

“Did she use them?”

“No. She kept them in a tin.”

Ryla smiled.

“That’s ridiculous.”

“She was very serious about it.”

“Did you steal them too?”

“Only when she wasn’t looking.”

Ryla laughed. It was small and tired, but real, and he looked at her, surprised.

“What?” she asked.

“Nothing.”

She settled against him again.

“Tell me another.”

He did. He told her about Elena’s habit of reading the last page of a book first, about the way she used to argue with him over mathematics, about how she would sign I told you so with an expression so smug that he sometimes wanted to throw a pillow at her.

Ryla listened, and at some point he stopped talking, and his breathing changed. She lifted her head. He was asleep. Not dozing, not listening for a car, but properly asleep, the strain gone from his face and his hand loose on her back.

She thought about the man who had brought her here: the man who hurt her, who held her while she cried, who had just told her about his sister stealing sugar packets. She didn’t know what to call what was between them.

She knew it was dangerous, that tenderness didn’t cancel violence, that a person could be loved and still be accountable. She also knew that, for the first time in a long while, Keaton was asleep. She didn’t move.

✦ ✦ ✦

Some time after two, Ryla woke. The room was dark, and Keaton was sitting at the foot of the bed, fully dressed, looking at his phone.

“What happened?”

He turned at once. “Nothing.”

The screen showed a camera feed: a driveway, a dark house by a lake, three cars with their lights turning.

“The rented house,” she said.

He nodded.

“Calder?”

“With a warrant, by the look of it.”

The last of her sleep vanished. “Will she find this place?”

“There’s a fuel receipt in a kitchen drawer over there. I never thought anyone would look. By morning.” He stood.

He looked at her.

“Ryla—”

“We go together.”

He hesitated. She stood. Her legs shook, but she stayed up.

“Can you walk?”

“Not far.”

“Then we’ll take the chair.”

She looked at it. “No. Leave it. Bring the stick. Lend me your arm. Leave the chair.”

He went to the wardrobe. Ryla looked round the room: the bed, the small table, Elena’s photograph, the clothes folded over the chair.

The place where she had learned her body hadn’t betrayed her, where she had stood for the first time, where Keaton had slept beside her. It wasn’t home. But it had held the last few weeks of her life. She reached for the photograph. Keaton watched her.

“Bring it,” he said.

She looked at him. He picked up the bag.

“She should come with us.”

Ryla placed the photograph carefully inside. Then she sat at the table by the window and wrote, slowly, on a sheet of his paper.

When she had finished, she folded the wheelchair herself, footrests tucked in, cushion on the seat, handles turned towards the door, and stood it against the wall. She left the note beside it. Then she looked at him.

“Are you ready?”

He looked at the window, and she thought he might be hearing Elena again. Then he turned back. “No.”

She nodded. “Me neither.”

He reached for her hand, and she took it, and they left the room together. Behind them the farmhouse was quiet. Somewhere on the road, Calder was getting closer.

chapters.title: Resurrection
chapters.desc: Sunday, eleven o’clock, the Whitmore boathouse.
chapters.content:
At half past ten, Ryla was standing in the dark.

Not well. Keaton had found her a place at the far end of the boathouse, beside the last post, where the boards were dry and she could rest one hand on the wood. In the farmhouse kitchen she had tried three times to stand for ten minutes, and managed it twice. Tonight she needed less than that. She needed to be on her feet when the lights came up, and to stay there long enough for Damien to see.

“You can sit until you hear him,” Keaton said, low. He had set a folding stool behind her. She hadn’t used it.

“If I sit, I’ll think about getting up.”

“Then think about something else.”

“Such as?”

He considered. He was crouched by the junction box on the wall, where he had spent twenty minutes with a torch in his teeth, and the switches he had rewired were taped together under his hand so that one movement would throw them all. “The water’s lower than it was in the summer. About a foot,” he said.

She looked at it. Black, flat, the slip running down into it like a tongue. Somewhere under there was the place where Preston had been found, and before him Elena. She had watched this building from her window for five years and never wanted to set foot in it.

“That’s not something else,” she said.

“No,” he admitted.

Her left leg had begun its small, familiar tremor. She shifted her weight to the right and held the post, and the tremor eased. Through a gap in the boards she could see the lawn and, far up it, the house, with three windows lit upstairs. One of them was hers. Someone had left the lamp on.

“He might not come alone.”

“He will. He wants to see the body before anyone else does. He’ll want to know it’s finished.” Keaton’s voice didn’t change.

“And if he brings the gun?”

“He’ll bring the gun.”

She should have been more frightened by that. Instead she felt very clear, the way she had at the farmhouse table with the evidence spread out in front of her and every line of it true.

Keaton straightened and came to stand beside her, not touching her. “You don’t have to do this part. I can do it alone.”

She looked at the water. “I know. That’s why I’m doing it.”

He looked at her for a long moment. Then he touched two fingers to his chest. Breathe. She made the sign back. He went to the switches and then into the dark by the door, and she was alone with the water.

At five to eleven she heard the gravel.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven that Sunday night, the slip was empty.

Damien stood at the edge of the water with a torch in one hand and a gun in the other, trying to understand it. There was no body.

No pale sleeve under the surface, no hair drifting against the posts, no silver bracelet caught on the edge of the jetty. Only black water, a strip of wet timber and the reflection of the boathouse roof. He swept the torch left, right, towards the reeds, and back.

“Hello?”

It came out embarrassingly small. His phone said one minute past eleven. The last message was still on the screen. Come alone. He had. He had walked across the grounds with the torch off until he reached the water, and brought the gun because he had no intention of being caught helpless.

Getting out of the house had been easier than it should have been. Since his mother died, the security men had stopped watching the family and started watching the gates, as if whatever had come for the Whitmores would have the manners to use the drive. He had told the man on the terrace that he couldn’t sleep and wanted air. The man had looked at his face and believed him. Damien hadn’t slept properly in a week. It was the first true thing he had said to anyone in days.

He hadn’t told security, or Hargreaves, or the police. He had done exactly what he was told, and the slip was empty. He turned slowly. The boathouse stood behind him with dark windows, and the lawn ran back towards the house, where a few security lights marked the edge of the grounds. He had been coming here for years.

He knew where the boards creaked, where the water was shallow, where the old ropes hung, which side of the slip got slippery in winter. He knew where Elena had gone into the water, and where he had held her. His fingers tightened on the gun.

Something moved behind the boathouse, and he spun round. “Who’s there?”

Nothing. He went towards the sound with the torch cutting through the dark. “Show yourself.”

A faint rustle, then silence. He looked back at the water. Maybe the body had been moved. Maybe the video was older than it said. Maybe this was a trick to get him out here, away from the house and the guards.

He lifted the gun a little. “Do you think this is funny?”

His voice cracked, and he hated that. He hated the cold and the dark, and standing in a place he had once controlled, unable to see past the end of his own torch. His phone buzzed, and he flinched.

Unknown number: Look at the water.

He turned the torch on the slip. Nothing.

Unknown number: You should know what you’re looking for.

His mouth went dry. He knew exactly what he was looking for. A dead girl. Proof that the problem was finished.

He stepped closer. The water slapped against the timber, and for one terrible second he saw a pale shape under the surface and jerked back. Then it was gone. Only a reflection, his own face broken up by the ripples.

“Enough! Come out!” It burst out of him, and he raised the gun.

The lights came on all at once: the boathouse lamps, the lights along the slip, the floodlights under the roof. White light poured over the water and turned the dark lawn into a stage. Damien blinked, his torch useless, and turned sharply.

And saw her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was standing at the far end of the boathouse. Not in the wheelchair, not leaning on the wall, not being pushed into the light by someone else’s hands.

Standing, in flat shoes on the cold boards, a dark coat over a plain dress, her hair tied back, one hand resting lightly on a post and the other at her side.

She was pale and thinner than he remembered. Her left leg trembled, and she held her weight carefully, every movement still taking thought. But she was on her own feet.

Damien stared. The torch slid out of his hand, hit the boards and rolled, throwing a frantic circle of light across the floor.

“No.”

Ryla didn’t smile. “Hello, Damien.”

Her voice carried across the water, clear and quiet and entirely hers.

He stopped breathing. He knew that voice. He had heard it in the three years before the accident, before the hospital rooms and the tablets and watching her talk through a screen.

He remembered her laughing when she was younger, complaining about the music at one of his parties, asking him to bring her a glass of water. He had spent five years telling himself he would never hear it again. Now it was standing in front of him.

“Ryla?”

She tilted her head. “Yes.”

He stared at her legs, then her face, then her mouth, looking for the trick. “You’re—”

“Alive.”

He shook his head. “No.”

She took a step towards him, slow and careful and unmistakable, and he recoiled. “No.”

She stopped and looked at the gun in his hand. “Were you expecting someone else?”

The video, the water, the body, the timestamp. His eyes went to the slip, looking for the place where he had seen her lying. “How—”

“Did you think I was dead?”

He swallowed. “I saw you.”

“You saw a video.”

“I saw your body.”

“You saw what someone wanted you to see.”

He looked at her again. Her face was real, and her voice. Her hands were moving slightly at her sides; they were still weak, but they weren’t trapped in her lap any more. He backed away another step.

“This isn’t possible.”

“You’ve said that about me before.”

His face changed. He remembered telling visitors her recovery was unlikely, and brushing off the doctors who wanted to investigate further, and sighing while she typed.

He remembered standing at the foot of her bed telling her she had to accept her limitations. Looking at her now, he knew she remembered all of it.

He raised the gun. “Stay there.”

She didn’t move. “Damien.”

“Stay where you are.”

She looked at the weapon. Then back at him.

“You’re frightened.”

“Shut up.”

“You came here expecting a body.”

“Shut up.”

“And now you don’t know what to do with me.”

His face twisted.

“You’re not real.”

She gave a small, tired smile.

“That’s what they told me about my recovery.”

He raised the gun higher.

“Don’t come closer.”

“I haven’t.”

“Don’t move.”

She stood still. For the first time in five years he was looking at her with no wheelchair between them. He couldn’t hide behind the old arrangement, talk over her, turn to Mrs. Pell to interpret or tell her to type. She was standing in front of him, speaking in a voice he had believed was gone for good, and looking at him.

“How long?” he asked.

Ryla frowned.

“What?”

“How long have you been able to—”

“Speak?”

He nodded.

“Not long.”

“Your legs?”

“Not long.”

He stared.

“Who did this?”

She looked at him.

“You did.”

He flinched. “No.”

“You and the others.”

“I didn’t know—”

“You didn’t know what?”

He had no answer. She took another step, and this time her foot came down more firmly. Damien raised the gun.

“Stop!”

She stopped. The barrel pointed at her chest.

She looked at the barrel without expression. Then she looked at him. “Are you going to shoot me? You’d need my body before midnight.”

His face went white.

✦ ✦ ✦

He fired. The sound tore through the boathouse, and the bullet hit the post behind her. She flinched; her shoulder came up and one foot slid back, nearly taking her balance with it. But she didn’t fall.

Damien stared at the hole in the wood, then at her. He had missed because his hand was shaking. He raised the gun again.

“Don’t.”

The voice came from behind him, and Damien froze. He knew it. Not from the video or the police.

From the study, from the bank review, from the quiet man who had sat across the desk asking about missing documents and irregular payments, a voice he had heard so often in the house that he had stopped noticing it.

“Put the gun down.”

Keaton Vance stood a few feet behind him in a dark coat. His face was calm, but there was something in his eyes Damien had never seen across the desk. Not professional curiosity or polite disapproval. Recognition.

Damien looked from Keaton to Ryla and back, and understood. The auditor. The killings, the video, the messages, the boathouse. All of it had been him.

“You.”

Keaton didn’t move.

“Put the gun down.”

Damien’s breathing became shallow.

“You did this.”

“Yes.”

“You killed them.”

“Yes.”

“Preston. Marcus. Albright. My mother.”

Keaton’s face didn’t change.

“Yes.”

Damien looked towards Ryla.

“And you brought her here?”

“She came here.”

“She’s supposed to be dead.”

Keaton glanced at Ryla.

“She isn’t.”

Damien laughed, thin and disbelieving. “You think this is clever?”

“No.”

“You think you can walk into my house, kill my family, take my sister and—”

“Your sister is standing right in front of you.”

Damien turned on her. “You don’t understand what he is.”

Ryla held his eyes. “I understand more than you think.”

“You were never supposed to be involved.”

She looked at him.

“I was in the house.”

“You didn’t see anything.”

“I saw her.”

Damien’s face tightened. Ryla took a breath.

“I saw her in the water.”

There was no sound but the water against the slip. Then he said, “You were at the window.”

She nodded.

“You saw?”

“Yes.”

Something in his face began to come apart.

“You couldn’t see who it was.”

“I knew it was a person.”

“You didn’t do anything.”

It was out before he could stop it. Ryla went still, and Keaton’s eyes sharpened, but she answered first, without raising her voice.

“I tried. I tried to reach my tablet. I couldn’t move my hands. I couldn’t shout. I tried.” She looked at him.

Damien stared, and then looked away.

Keaton stepped closer. “Put the gun down, Damien.”

Damien turned. “Or what?”

“You know what.”

Damien seemed to think about firing again, and his finger tightened. Ryla watched his hand, then glanced at Keaton, a small movement, a warning.

Keaton saw it and didn’t move. He waited. Damien’s breathing grew louder, the gun stayed up, and the water moved under the boards.

“You’re not going to kill me,” Damien said.

“Why?”

“Because you want me to confess. You need me to say it. You need me to tell her.” Keaton didn’t answer, and Damien gave a thin smile.

Ryla was pale, but she didn’t look away. Damien lowered the gun a fraction. “Fine. Let’s talk.”

Keaton’s eyes stayed on the gun. “Put it down first.”

Damien looked at him, then at Ryla, and for the first time he seemed to understand that the night wasn’t going to end the way he had planned.

chapters.title: Across an Ocean
chapters.desc: A dissertation, a photograph and a hand raised above the water.
chapters.content:
The gun hit the floor before Damien understood what was happening.

One moment he was holding it, the next his wrist was caught and his arm wrenched behind him, and something cracked, a short, sickening sound. The pain came a fraction later, and he screamed. The gun skidded across the boards and fetched up against a post.

“Don’t move,” Keaton said.

Damien tried to tear himself free, and Keaton tightened his grip, and fresh pain shot through his hand. His knees went, and he lurched forward and caught himself on the rail with his good arm. “Let go!”

Keaton let go. Damien staggered away clutching his right hand to his chest. The fingers were already swelling, and blood ran from a split across the knuckles onto his white shirt. He turned with his face twisted. “You bastard!”

Keaton stood a few feet away. At the far end of the boathouse Ryla hadn’t moved. She was pale and her shoulders were tight, but she was still on her feet.

“Who the hell are you?”

Damien’s voice broke. He gave a sharp, disbelieving laugh, and when he asked again it was almost pleading. He searched Keaton’s face for the man from the study, the auditor who asked about missing accounts and sat across from him while he talked about Elena. The man who had listened.

“Why are you doing this? Is it the money? The fund? Whatever you think I owe you, I can—” said Damien’s.

“Stop.”

It was the first word Keaton had said since he broke his hand. Damien stopped.

Keaton reached inside his coat, and Damien flinched and shielded his hand, but what came out was a thick bundle of papers held with an old elastic band, the edges worn soft, some pages marked in pencil, and a photograph with its corners curled from years of handling.

Keaton walked up to him and dropped them. The papers scattered across the boards, and the photograph landed face up. Damien looked down, and the world narrowed.

✦ ✦ ✦

A young woman sat at a desk with her hair tied back carelessly and a pencil between her fingers, smiling at whoever held the camera.

Not the polished smile of her university photographs or the careful one she wore beside important people. A private smile, the kind you give someone you trust.

Damien had seen that face across library tables, in cafés, in the passenger seat of his car. He had watched it change when she was tired, when she was pleased with an idea, when she was trying not to laugh at him. Elena.

The top page of the papers was covered in equations and handwritten corrections, with her name in neat black ink in the corner.

ELENA WARD

Dissertation Draft — Risk Propagation in Interdependent Financial Systems.

He crouched awkwardly, guarding his hand, and picked it up with his left. There were notes in the margins, and some of them were his: a question about a variable, a correction to the model, a suggestion for calculating exposure across linked portfolios. His handwriting. His ideas, or what he had later presented as his own. He dropped the page. “No.”

He looked at the photograph again. “Where did you get this?” No answer. He picked up another sheet: a draft of the paper that became the basis of the fund’s risk model, the paper his dissertation cited, the paper that made his name. Her equations, her notes, her corrections to his corrections. And in the bottom margin, a small handwritten line.

Tell D. the third assumption doesn’t hold if the exposure is correlated.

His throat tightened. He remembered her saying it across a table, pushing her glasses up with the back of her wrist.

He remembered laughing and telling her she was being too cautious, and her explaining it again, and him using the revised model in a presentation the next week.

He hadn’t thought about that conversation in years. He hadn’t needed to. The work had become his, and the girl had disappeared.

“Where did you get these?” he whispered.

“They were hers,” Keaton said.

“Who are you?”

Keaton didn’t answer. He looked at the photograph, and something passed over his face, not softness but something more painful, a man looking at a place he couldn’t go back to. Then he looked at Damien. “Do you remember her?”

“Of course I remember her.”

“Do you?”

“Yes!”

“Then say her name.”

Damien’s lips parted.

“Elena.”

“Her full name.”

“Elena Ward.”

Keaton nodded once.

“Good.”

The word was quiet.

Damien looked from him to the papers. “She had no one.”

It came out too fast. He seemed to hear himself, and his eyes flicked to Keaton’s face, and then he said it again, louder. “She had no one! She was nobody!”

Ryla’s face changed. Keaton didn’t move. Damien’s breathing went ragged. “She was nobody. A scholarship student. No family here, no connections. Nobody knew who she was,” he said, as if saying it could put the world back where it belonged.

Keaton looked at him.

“You knew.”

“I—”

“You knew her.”

Damien shook his head.

“She was nobody.”

“She told you about her brother.”

Damien went still. The boathouse seemed to lose the last of its sound, and even the water under the slip went quiet. Keaton took one step closer. “Didn’t she?”

Damien stared. His hand throbbed, and he could feel blood running between his fingers.

Keaton’s face didn’t look the way it had in the study any more. There was something else under it that Damien had missed, something Elena had once tried to describe.

“She told you,” Keaton said again.

Damien’s eyes went to the photograph, to the name on the dissertation, back to Keaton, and something stirred. Not the boathouse, not yet. Something much smaller.

A quiet evening, a glass of wine, a woman beside him with bare feet and her hair over one shoulder, speaking low because the rest of the house was asleep. He remembered her saying she had a brother. He remembered laughing.

Keaton had imagined this moment many times. In some versions Damien begged; in others he denied everything until the evidence was laid in front of him.

He remembered the little pause before she answered when she was thinking, the tilt of her head when he made a joke, the way she sometimes signed and spoke at once though she knew he could read every movement of her hands.

He remembered her saying she was happy, and believing her.

And now the man who had taken her stood with her work at his feet, insisting she had been nobody. Keaton looked at Damien’s broken hand, the hand that had held Elena under. He felt no triumph, only an old, familiar emptiness.

Keaton raised his right hand. Thumb out, index finger up, little finger up, the middle two folded into his palm. A small shape held above the dark water.

Damien stared. Keaton held it, then lowered his hand and spoke.

“From across an ocean.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The memory came back whole, all at once, with the terrible clarity of something that had been waiting for years.

His apartment, rain on the windows, Elena on the floor beside the sofa sorting papers she had brought home, in one of his old shirts with the sleeves rolled to her elbows. He had been reading something on his phone.

“Damien?”

He had looked up. She was smiling, not the bright public smile she used around people who mattered to him, but a smaller, almost shy one.

“There’s something I should tell you.”

She hesitated. “I have a brother. An older brother.”

“A brother?”

She had looked at the window. “He lives abroad. Edinburgh first, then London.”

She had gone back to sorting the papers, but he could see that she was waiting for him to ask more. So he had.

A faint smile. “I know how it sounds. He left when I was little. He was adopted. He changed his name.” She spoke carefully then.

“Adopted?”

“Yes.”

“So you’re not even Ward anymore?”

“I am.”

She had looked at him.

“He isn’t.”

“He had to leave. It was his chance. He was very young.”

“How old?”

“Thirteen.”

It had seemed a strange story to Damien: a poor family, a brilliant boy, a Scottish professor, an adoption. He hadn’t understood why it mattered. She went on. “He gave up his name so I could keep mine.”

He looked at her, and she smiled again. “He was the only person who ever loved me from across an ocean.”

Those were the words, exactly. Now they seemed to rise out of the water itself.

He had asked whether she still talked to him.

“Every Sunday, if we can.”

“Every Sunday? That’s sweet.” He had meant it as a joke, or maybe kindly. He couldn’t remember.

Then she had lifted her hand: thumb, index finger, little finger, the same shape Keaton had just made. “I love you,” she had said.

He had laughed, a short, amused sound. “What’s that?”

“Sign language.”

“I know what sign language is.”

She had rolled her eyes. “Then why ask?”

“What does that one mean?”

She looked at her hand. “It’s something my brother taught me. It means I love you.”

He had reached for her hand. “I wasn’t.”

She had let him take it, and they had sat in the quiet for a while.

“Please don’t tell anyone about him yet.”

“Why?”

“Because I want to keep him separate from all this. From the Whitmores, the university, everything.”

“Does he know about me?”

She nodded. “He wants me to be careful.”

Damien had laughed. “Smart man.”

She had squeezed his fingers. “He loves me.” And Damien, who had never thought that sentence mattered, kissed her forehead and changed the subject.

The memory let him go. He was in the boathouse, the photograph was on the floor, and the distant brother he had laughed at had come across an ocean.

His mouth opened, and nothing came. Then: “Ward. You’re a Ward. You were a Ward.”

“Yes.”

Damien’s eyes widened. “She said— You’re her brother.” He stopped and looked at the papers, the photograph, the hand, and at last at Keaton.

Keaton didn’t need to answer. Damien backed away. “No. No, no—” he said, barely audible. He searched Keaton’s face for anything that might contradict it, and it was all there: Elena’s eyes, her stillness when she listened, her hands. He had invited this man into his study and poured him whisky. He had talked about the murders with him, complained about Elena’s work in front of him, called her nobody.

He had laughed at the only person who was ever going to come for her.

“And you— She said you were abroad.” He looked at the water, the slip, the place where he had held Elena under, and his face crumpled.

“She said you had changed your name.”

“Yes.”

“She said you were a good man.”

Keaton’s jaw tightened, and for the first time that night his composure slipped. Damien saw it. He had always known how to find the soft place in a person, and he reached for it.

“She thought you were coming back. She waited for you. Every Sunday, she told me. She waited for your calls. She didn’t know you were going to—”

“Stop.”

“She didn’t know—”

“Stop.” Keaton’s voice was quiet, but something under it had finally broken through.

Damien stared at him, then at his own hand, blood gathering in the creases of the palm. He remembered another hand rising out of the water with three fingers lifted, Elena struggling, trying to breathe, her fingers breaking the surface.

He had thought it meant nothing, that she was reaching for help from someone who didn’t exist. Now he understood. It had been for the brother she loved, somewhere beyond the water, who never knew she was dying.

“You saw the sign,” Damien said.

“On Preston’s video. The one he told you he’d deleted.”

“And you knew.”

“I knew what it meant.”

Damien’s breath caught. The hand above the water, the photograph, the dissertation, the man in front of him. It all fitted. She had been calling to someone who wasn’t there, and now he was.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ryla had been watching Damien’s face, and she saw the moment he understood. He looked like a man finding out that the past had been standing behind him the whole time.

She had seen grief like that in Keaton when she told him about the dinner and the window. Now it had something else beside it: a quiet, terrible finality.

Damien looked at her. “Ryla. I didn’t know.”

He seemed to expect her to say something, to comfort him or help him find a version where he hadn’t understood what he was doing. She gave him nothing.

“You knew she was a person. You knew she was alive. You knew she had a family, and someone waiting for her,” she said.

His mouth trembled. “Ryla—”

“You knew.”

She didn’t shout. She didn’t need to.

Damien turned to Keaton. “I didn’t know he would come.”

“That was the point. You never thought anyone would come. You thought she had no one. You thought nobody would ask questions, or remember her well enough to notice what you’d taken. You were wrong.” Keaton glanced at the photograph.

Damien shook his head. “You don’t understand what she was like.”

Keaton’s eyes sharpened. “Tell me. Tell me what she was like.”

Damien faltered and looked at the photograph, searching for a version of Elena that belonged to him. “She was brilliant. She was good at what she did.”

“Her work.”

“Yes. Her work.”

Damien’s face tightened. “She helped me.”

“She did more than help you.”

“She wanted to.”

“She wanted to be credited.”

Damien looked away. “She knew I would—”

“She asked you to keep her brother a secret.”

Damien stopped, and Keaton took a slow breath. “She trusted you with the one person she had spent her whole life trying not to lose. And you laughed when she told you how much he loved her. You didn’t just take her work. You took the part of her life she trusted you with,” he said, still low. He looked at the papers between them.

The silence was unbearable. Damien sat down heavily on a wooden bench with his broken hand against his chest, and he looked older and smaller. Not because he had grasped what he had done, but because he finally knew who had come to collect.

✦ ✦ ✦

Keaton had thought that if Damien remembered and understood, something in him might settle at last. It didn’t.

The boathouse was still the boathouse, the water was still dark, and Elena was still gone. He was standing where she had died, still trying to understand how a person could vanish so completely.

“Do you know what she called me?” he said.

Damien lifted his eyes. “What?”

Keaton’s mouth tightened. “Not Elias. Not Keaton. She called me Eli when she wanted something. Nobody else ever has. When she wanted me to carry her. When she wanted the last piece of bread. When she was frightened.” The name sounded strange in the cold air, small and private, and Damien didn’t understand it.

He looked at the water. He had spent more than a year trying to make the world understand that Elena had existed: that she had worked and loved and been loved, that she wasn’t an unstable girl who wandered into a lake, that she hadn’t been unclaimed, that someone had been waiting for her call.

He had made a list because the world gave him nobody to hold responsible, and crossed the names off one by one, and none of them had brought her back.

Not the first, and not the man sitting in front of him. On the last call he had told her to ring him if anything felt wrong. She said she would. He had believed her, and he had been too far away.

When he opened his eyes, Damien was watching him. “Why didn’t you come sooner?”

The question was so absurd that for a second Keaton couldn’t answer. Then he said, “I did. I came as soon as I knew. You made sure there was nothing left to come back for.” His eyes went to the slip.

The phone in Damien’s coat began to ring. Neither man moved. Ryla looked towards the sound, and Damien slowly reached for it with his left hand. SIMON HARGREAVES. He let it ring out. Then a message came.

Simon Hargreaves: I’ve given the police everything. Don’t call me again.

He read it, and his face changed.

“What?” Ryla said.

He looked up at her, then at Keaton. “You’re not the only one who’s been keeping records.”

“Do you think you can just kill me and walk away?”

Keaton’s gaze moved to the phone.

“Who is that?”

Damien looked at the screen again.

“Hargreaves. My lawyer. He knows about the trust and the money. He knows what happened.”

Ryla’s face sharpened. “Then he’ll tell the police.”

Damien looked at her, and his smile went. “He’ll tell them whatever keeps him out of prison. And it sounds as if he’s started.”

Keaton watched him carefully. “Then perhaps you should start telling the truth.”

Damien looked at him, and for the first time he seemed to understand the night wasn’t finished. He looked at Elena’s photograph and the papers, at the brother who had crossed an ocean, and at Ryla, standing where the dead girl should have been.

Somewhere beyond the boathouse, a siren started up, faint and far off, and getting closer. Keaton turned his head towards the road. Ryla looked at him, and neither of them spoke.

chapters.title: Held Under
chapters.desc: The same slip, the same water.
chapters.content:
The siren was getting closer, and Damien heard it too. His eyes went to the road and back to Keaton, his broken hand pressed to his chest with blood slipping between the fingers, the phone in his other hand gone dark.

For a few seconds nobody spoke. Then Damien laughed, an ugly, breathless, half-hysterical sound.

“Well. I suppose this is where you decide what kind of man you are.”

Keaton looked at him.

He glanced at the water. “You’re going to do it, aren’t you? After all the trouble you’ve gone to.”

Keaton said nothing. Ryla stood a few feet away with one hand on the post, watching Keaton, not Damien. He could feel her attention, but he couldn’t look at her. He was looking at Damien’s right hand, the one that had held Elena under.

He had pictured that hand for more than a year: round a glass, signing a document, reaching for a door handle, lifting a phone to call someone who would tell him the girl was dead. In his dreams it was always wet.

“Do you remember?” Keaton asked.

Damien frowned. “What?”

“The water.”

Damien’s face changed, and he glanced at the slip. “Keaton—”

“Do you remember her?”

His mouth tightened. “Yes.”

“Then say it.”

“I remember.”

“Say her name.”

Damien looked at him.

“Elena.”

Keaton took a step towards him. “Again.”

“Elena.”

“Again.”

“Stop.”

“Say her name.”

“Elena Ward!”

It hit the rafters. Keaton stared at him. For months he had imagined hearing Damien say it, the name coming back into the world out of the mouth that had tried to erase it.

He had expected some release, the pressure in his chest finally letting go. There was nothing. Only the name, and Damien, and the water.

“She was alive,” Keaton said.

Damien shook his head. “I know.”

“She was breathing. She was trying to get out.”

“Keaton—”

“She was trying to get out.”

Damien backed away, and his heel hit the edge of the slip. “Don’t.”

Maybe he had said the same word to Elena. Maybe something else. Keaton would never know. He hadn’t been there. He had been asleep in another country with his phone beside him, waiting for Sunday.

Damien lifted his good hand. “Whatever you think you’re going to get out of this—”

Keaton seized his coat and dragged him towards the water. Damien fought, but the broken hand made him clumsy; his shoes scraped over the boards, and he hit Keaton’s shoulder with his left fist and tried to twist away. Keaton drove him down, and his knees cracked on the timber, and he cried out. “Get off me!”

Keaton caught the back of his neck. For one suspended second he saw two scenes in the same place: a woman at the edge of the water with her hand rising above the surface, and the man under his palm, under the same lamps, at the same slip.

“Please,” Damien said.

The arrogance had gone out of his face, and the certainty, and the easy confidence that other people would always arrange themselves around him.

There was only fear, real fear. Keaton had wanted to see it. He had thought it would be enough. He tightened his grip and pushed him into the water.

The cold swallowed Damien’s voice. He came up once, coughing and flailing, and his good hand caught the edge of the boards, and Keaton took him by the coat and hauled him back.

“Keaton!” The name came out broken by water and panic, and Keaton heard the plea under it. He heard something else too: a voice from more than a year ago, muffled and fading, a body fighting something it couldn’t beat. He pushed Damien under again. The water broke round them. Damien thrashed, his good hand clawing at Keaton’s sleeve, the broken one jerking uselessly at his chest, his shoes kicking against the submerged edge of the slip. Keaton held on.

He had rehearsed this until it felt familiar: the walk across the lawn, the boards, the water waiting underneath. He had imagined counting, making Damien live through every second he had taken from Elena.

But time didn’t behave the way it had in his head. It stretched and broke apart. There was no clean measure of suffering, no exact number to hand back. Only a man fighting to live, and Keaton holding him down, and the water.

Damien came up again, no longer shouting words, only gasping, and his eyes found Keaton’s. For an instant there was recognition in them. Not of the auditor or the brother, but of one person understanding that the other had decided he wasn’t going to be allowed to leave.

He tried to speak, and water filled his mouth. Keaton heard himself say something, maybe Elena’s name, maybe nothing, and pushed him under once more.

He counted, not because it made anything fair but because his mind needed something to hold. One, two, three. The last call. Four, five. Elena laughing at something stupid. Six, seven.

The airport glass. Eight, nine. Her small hand raised on the other side. Ten, eleven. His promise to come back. Then the numbers lost their order and became noise in his head.

Damien’s movements changed. Keaton didn’t look away. He had imagined turning his head at the end and refusing to watch, but he couldn’t.

He hadn’t seen Elena’s face when she died, or held her hand, or heard her last breath. So he watched this one, until the water stopped fighting, and then he kept his hand where it was longer, and another.

The water settled. He let go. Damien drifted against the edge of the slip with his face turned half towards the lights and his broken hand floating near the surface, the hand that had once held someone else under.

Keaton stood up, his knees soaked and his coat clinging to his legs, breathing in short, ragged pulls. There was no satisfaction, no sudden peace, no sense of justice finally arriving. He had killed the man who killed his sister, and Elena was still dead.

✦ ✦ ✦

The boathouse had gone quiet. The siren was louder, but he couldn’t tell any more where it was. His fingers were trembling. He opened them, closed them, opened them again.

There was water on his palms, and he rubbed them together, and it didn’t help, so he rubbed harder until the skin went red.

There was a small cut on one knuckle he didn’t remember getting. A drop of water slid off his wrist, then another. His mind was going somewhere else.

The lamps were too bright, the boards felt wrong under his feet, the air smelled of wet wood and something metallic. He could hear someone breathing.

He looked up. A girl stood by the post, small, with dark hair tied back, looking at him.

“Lena?”

She didn’t answer. He took a step towards her. “You’re here.”

Ryla’s face changed. “Keaton?”

The name didn’t reach him. He was somewhere else, years ago: a kitchen with a cracked window, a small girl at the table swinging legs that didn’t reach the floor, a tin of sugar packets, a schoolbag too big for her shoulders, a hand raised behind airport glass. He had promised. He had promised. Somewhere years ago.

A kitchen with a cracked window. A small girl sitting at a table, swinging her legs because they didn’t reach the floor. A tin full of sugar packets. A schoolbag too large for her shoulders. A hand raised behind airport glass. He had promised. He had promised.

“Lena,” he said again.

Ryla took a careful step closer, and he looked down at his hands. “Where is she? Where did she go?”

His voice had gone small. He turned to the water.

“She was here,” said Ryla.

Ryla looked at Damien’s body, and then at Keaton.

His hands hung at his sides, opening and closing on nothing. Ryla took another step. “Keaton, look at me.”

He didn’t. “She was right here. I saw her.”

Her throat tightened. “You’re at the boathouse.”

He looked at her.

“Where?”

“At the Whitmore boathouse.”

He stared at her. The words meant nothing to him; she could see it. His eyes went back to the water. “I was supposed to come back.”

She couldn’t move. Then she understood. His eyes were on the place where his sister had died, and he no longer saw Damien at all.

The road was right there. Past the lawn and the trees, the gravel drive led to the main gate, and the sirens were close enough that she could hear the pitch change as the cars turned in.

She could leave the boathouse, walk to the first officer she saw and tell them everything.

Keaton had made that possible. He had laid out the evidence and prepared the documents and given her the means to leave him behind. He had told her she could tell Calder everything he had done. She could do it now and leave him standing by the water.

Instead she looked at his hands, and then his face. “Keaton.”

He didn’t respond. She came closer slowly. His eyes were following something she couldn’t see, his breath came too fast, his shoulders were hunched up, and his fingers had curled so tight that the tendons stood out.

“Keaton, I’m coming closer.” He didn’t seem to hear. She reached him and slid her palm under his wrist.

She put her palm beneath his wrist.

His arm jerked. “Don’t,” he said, barely audible.

She stopped. “It’s me.”

He stared at her, trying to recognise her, his eyes moving over her face for something familiar. “Lena?”

Her chest hurt. “No. Ryla. I’m Ryla. Ryla.” He didn’t answer. His eyes went to her mouth, and she said it slowly.

She thought it had reached him. Then his gaze dropped to the water again.

“She’s gone.”

Ryla’s fingers closed gently around his wrist.

“I know.”

He shook his head.

“I couldn’t—”

His voice broke.

“I couldn’t get there.”

Ryla looked at him.

“I know.”

He looked at her again, and this time there was something like fear in his face. “I was too late.”

She didn’t tell him he wasn’t, or that he had done everything he could. She wouldn’t make a lie out of the thing that had destroyed him. “You’re here now,” she said.

His hand trembled. She wrapped both of hers round it and held it until the fingers uncurled, and he stared down at them.

There was a streak of blood on his cheek where Damien’s fist had caught him. She lifted her coat sleeve and wiped it away gently, and he flinched. She stopped.

“Don’t.”

She lowered her hand. “All right.”

“I killed him.”

“Yes.”

His breathing quickened.

“I killed him.”

“I know.”

“I—”

He couldn’t finish. Ryla glanced at the water. Damien was still there, and the sirens were closer. She knew what came next: officers on the grounds, the body, Keaton, the evidence waiting at the farmhouse, questions, handcuffs, consequences. She wouldn’t pretend otherwise. But Keaton was looking at his hands again.

“There’s water,” he whispered.

Ryla took his hand.

“Yes.”

“It’s still there.”

She turned his palm upwards.

“Look at me.”

He didn’t.

She moved closer until he couldn’t avoid her face. “Keaton. You’re not in the water. You’re standing beside me. Feel my hand.” His eyes finally met hers.

He didn’t move.

“Keaton. Feel it.”

Slowly his fingers closed round hers, barely at all, but enough. She held on.

“Can you walk?”

He didn’t seem to understand the question.

“Can you walk with me?”

A small nod. She turned towards the steps up from the slip. Her legs were tired, the boards were wet, and her left knee was already trembling, but she took one step, and then another.

Keaton didn’t move. He was still staring at the water.

“Come on.”

“Where?”

“Out.”

He looked at his shoes, then his hands. “I can’t.”

She went back to him. “You can. Not alone.”

Something shifted in his face. He looked at her hand and then at her, and when she started walking, he followed.

One step, then another. He was unsteady; he stumbled once, and she nearly lost her own balance holding on to him, and he grabbed the rail. She stopped.

“Take your time.”

He stared at her, and the words seemed to reach him. A long time ago a woman had crouched beside Ryla’s wheelchair and told her the same thing, and the memory went through her as she tightened her grip on his hand.

They walked to the end of the slip. At the top of the steps he stopped and looked back.

The water was dark again, the lamps reflected on it, the body half hidden by the edge of the boards, and the boathouse stood exactly as it had on the night Elena died.

“She was here.”

“Yes.”

He swallowed.

“I thought if I—”

He stopped. She waited.

“I thought if I did it the same way...”

His voice disappeared. Ryla looked at the water and understood what he couldn’t say. He had wanted to give something back. Not only death: the helplessness, the terror, the knowledge that a person could struggle and struggle while someone else decided whether they could breathe.

He had wanted Damien to feel it. But the water hadn’t given Elena back. It had only taken another person.

She turned to him. “You can’t bring her back.”

“I know.”

“And you can’t make what happened to her unhappen.”

“I know.”

She held his hand. “But you can come out of here.”

He looked at her, and nodded, and she led him up the steps.

The first police car came through the main gate with its lights turning.

From the top of the steps, Ryla could see the whole lawn: blue light washing over the front of the house, officers getting out of cars, a torch beam already swinging towards the gardens. In a minute, perhaps two, someone would think of the boathouse. The road was right there. So were they.

She could raise her hand. She could call out in the voice she had only just got back, and they would come running, and they would take him, and she would be the poor Whitmore girl who had survived. She looked at Keaton.

He was watching the lights without recognising them. Water was still running out of his sleeves.

Below them, tied to the slip where Damien turned slowly against the posts, was the old rowing boat her father had taught her to row the summer she was sixteen. The oars were still in it. Nobody in that house had touched it since.

Across the lake, there were no lights at all.

“Keaton.”

He turned.

“Look at me.”

He did.

“The police are here. If you stay, they’ll take you, and they’ll be right to,” she said.

He nodded.

“I’m not going to let them.”

He only looked at her. Then something came back into his face, enough to understand what she meant.

“Ryla. You don’t have to—”

“I know I don’t. I’m choosing.” She took his hand.

She led him back down the steps, past the place where Damien lay in the black water, and into the boat.

It rocked under them. She nearly fell, caught the side, and didn’t let go of him. She untied the rope with fingers that had spent five years unable to hold a glass.

“Row. That way. Where it’s dark,” she said.

He only looked at the oars. Then his hands remembered, the way her feet had remembered the floor, and he pulled.

Behind them, a torch found the boathouse. Someone shouted. Someone else called for a medic. The boat slid out of the light.

Ryla sat facing the estate and watched it grow smaller: the house where she had been kept, the window she had watched from, the slip where two people had drowned. Nobody on the lawn looked at the water. Nobody ever had.

Keaton rowed in silence. Once he stopped and stared at his hands on the oars, and she leaned forward and covered them with hers until he began again.

The water closed behind them, black and flat and still.

chapters.title: Midnight
chapters.desc: Ryla turns twenty-five.
chapters.content:
The coat was too big for her. Keaton’s coat hung from her shoulders almost to her knees, the sleeves over half her hands, still damp and smelling of rain and cold air and him.

Ryla sat on the edge of the public landing on the far side of the lake with her feet against the lower boards.

Across the water, the estate was wide awake. Police lights moved through the grounds and torches crossed the lawn, and somewhere inside the boathouse, small and far off, people were working round a body that had once been her brother.

On this side there was nothing: the landing, an empty car park, the car Keaton had left there two days ago, and the two of them. Her phone said one minute to midnight. The date hadn’t changed yet.

She had spent five years being told to wait. For the pain to ease, her legs to strengthen, her voice to come back, her body to cooperate. For the next appointment, the next assessment, the next dose.

For her family to stop looking at her like a burden they had inherited. She had waited so long that she had nearly forgotten what it was to arrive anywhere.

Now she was on a dock in a man’s coat, with a dead man across the water and police searching the house she grew up in, and her birthday was a few seconds away. The seconds changed. 49. 50. 51.

She heard footsteps. Keaton was standing a little way behind her. There was a blanket in the car that he hadn’t touched.

He had changed into the dry shirt from the bag on the back seat, and his hands had shaken so badly that she had done the buttons. His hair was still wet, and there was a faint red mark on his cheek where she had wiped the blood.

He looked at her phone. “Almost.”

She nodded. He didn’t come closer. After tonight, she didn’t know whether she wanted him beside her or needed him to stay where he was. Perhaps both.

The seconds ran out, and the minute turned over. 00:00. The twenty-first of December. Ryla Whitmore was twenty-five.

For a few seconds nothing happened. No music, no applause, no cake, no family gathered round with borrowed affection, nobody asking her to make a wish.

Somewhere inside a legal system that didn’t care whether she was on a dock or in a hospital bed, the trust became hers: seventy per cent of the Whitmore fortune, the voting rights, the controlling interest, everything her father had left her. She looked out over the water.

“Happy birthday,” Keaton said, roughly.

She smiled. “Thank you.”

He looked at her a long moment. “You made it.”

She turned to him. “I did.”

For the first time in five years there was nobody standing between her and the future with a prescription bottle. Nobody had the authority to decide what she did with her body, her money or her name.

She was still weak. Her legs still shook and her voice still tired easily, and the date changing hadn’t healed anything. But she was twenty-five, and the money was hers.

“Do you think he knew? My father, when he wrote the trust,” she asked.

Keaton thought about it. “I think he knew what they were capable of.”

She nodded slowly. “He wanted me to have something they couldn’t take. Then I suppose he did one thing right.” She pulled the coat tighter.

Keaton didn’t answer. He stood beside her in the cold, looking at the same water. Neither of them mentioned Elena or Damien. For once Ryla didn’t need the night to mean anything. It was enough that she had reached midnight.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little after two, the three packages went out, minutes apart. Keaton had never trusted a single point of failure.

Each held a different part of the structure, each backed by records that could be checked independently, the originals preserved and the copies encrypted, and the recipients chosen so that no one person could make it disappear.

Detective Nora Calder received the original post-mortem report, the cremation authorisation, Marcus’s payment ledger and the correspondence connecting the Whitmore estate to the suppression of Elena Ward’s death.

Walter Greaves received the documents concerning the trust, the medical records, the laboratory findings and the original rehabilitation scans. He also received instructions from Ryla concerning the legal control of her assets.

Three national newspapers and several investigative journalists received separate evidence packages, including the original video Preston had filmed, the financial records, the wiretap transcript and the payment made to Harlan Vale.

The lab results showed the tonic contained compounds that had nothing to do with its label, consistent with long exposure to substances that weakened the muscles, damaged the voice and created dependence.

The competition footage showed a stagehand wiping something clear onto the landing mark during the interval. The original scans contradicted the ones used to keep Ryla in her chair. And the wiretap held Damien’s voice.

A missing girl is worth nothing for seven years. A dead one is worth everything by Christmas.

It was in the transcript and the audio, and it could no longer be waved away as a claim made by a man who had killed four people. It existed in too many places.
